species_description.text: Medium-sized, familiar myna about 23–25 cm, with chocolate-brown body, glossy black head and upper breast, bright yellow bill and legs, yellow bare skin around the eye, and white wing patches and tail tips. Omnivorous, feeding on insects, fruit, grain, nectar and human food waste.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in plumage and are not reliably separable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller brown, with a less sharply contrasting head and breast; bill and orbital skin are less intensely yellow and the iris is usually greyer.

field_spotting_tips.text: Walks confidently on the ground, unlike many starlings that hop. Look for yellow eye-skin, yellow bill and legs, and white wing patches in flight. Highly adaptable and often gathers at communal roosts.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident across Sri Lanka, especially towns, villages, agricultural land, gardens, roadsides and open country. Frequently associates with people and livestock.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is opportunistic and can occur over an extended period; regional sources report nesting in several months, so avoid treating a single calendar window as universal. Nests in tree holes and cavities in buildings.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Southern/Common Hill Myna (Gracula indica) R; Sri Lanka Myna E; Common Myna R; Rosy Starling M; Brahminy Starling M; White-faced Starling E. Confirm codes against the list before publication.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, active bulbul, about 20 cm, with olive-green upperparts, yellow eyebrow and face, yellow underparts and a dark bill. It is associated with forest, wooded gardens, plantations and forest edges, feeding on fruit, nectar and insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and are not reliably separable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and greener, with less bright yellow facial and underpart colour and a less distinct eyebrow.

field_spotting_tips.text: Yellow eyebrow and bright yellow underparts distinguish it from the black-capped bulbul. Search foliage in forest canopy and edges; listen for its clear, ringing calls.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in wet-zone and hill forests of Sri Lanka, especially wooded habitats around Kitulgala, Sinharaja and other forested localities. Also occurs in India.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding season dates in Sri Lanka require further local verification; do not infer them from records outside the island.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List/local checklist convention: Sri Lanka Black-capped Bulbul E; Sri Lanka Yellow-eared Bulbul E; Red-vented Bulbul R; Square-tailed Bulbul R; White-browed Bulbul R; Yellow-browed Bulbul R. Square-tailed Bulbul is also native to India, so not endemic.

species_description.text: Small, rather plain reed-warbler, about 12–13 cm, with warm brown upperparts, pale buff underparts, a faint supercilium and relatively short, rounded wings. It skulks in scrub, reed edges, rank vegetation and bushes, feeding on insects. Identification from similar Acrocephalus warblers can be difficult and often depends on call/song and detailed structure.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; no reliable external field distinction. Males sing from exposed perches on the breeding grounds, but Sri Lankan wintering birds are usually quiet.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are warmer and more rufous-brown, with buff fringes to the upperpart feathers and a more prominent pale supercilium; age can be difficult to judge in the field.

field_spotting_tips.text: Use call/song and structure rather than colour alone. Look for a small, compact reed-warbler with short rounded wings in low dense cover. Careful separation from other Acrocephalus warblers is essential.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter migrant to Sri Lanka, occurring in scrub, reedbeds, marsh edges, plantations and wooded gardens. Records occur across the island, particularly in lowland wetlands and scrub.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Passage and winter visitor, generally arriving from late October/November and remaining through March/April. Breeds in temperate Eurasia; not a regular Sri Lankan breeder.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Blyth's Reed-warbler M; Clamorous Reed-warbler R; Large-billed Leaf-warbler M; Greenish Warbler M; Sri Lanka Bush Warbler E; Velvet-fronted Nuthatch R. Clamorous Reed-warbler has endemic Sri Lankan subspecies meridionalis, not an endemic species.

species_description.text: Large, robust reed-warbler, about 18–20 cm, with plain olive-brown upperparts, pale buff underparts, broad bill and a long rounded tail. It is usually found in dense reedbeds and tangled wetland vegetation, feeding on insects and other small invertebrates. Its loud, harsh, repetitive song is often heard before the bird is seen.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; males are often more vocal. No dependable external field sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally warmer and more rufous-buff below, with softer plumage and a pale gape; overall similar to adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for the loud, repeated harsh song from tall reeds. Its large size and heavy bill distinguish it from smaller reed-warblers. Watch reed tops for brief song flights.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Breeding resident in reedbeds, marshes and tanks, especially in the dry lowlands; also occurs locally in wet-zone wetlands. Sri Lankan race is A. s. meridionalis, endemic to Sri Lanka.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding reported March–August in Sri Lanka. Nest is a deep basket/cup suspended among reed stems, usually with 2–3 eggs.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Blyth's Reed-warbler M; Clamorous Reed-warbler R; Large-billed Leaf-warbler M; Greenish Warbler M; Sri Lanka Bush Warbler E; Velvet-fronted Nuthatch R. Clamorous Reed-warbler has endemic Sri Lankan subspecies meridionalis, not an endemic species.

species_description.text: Small, compact wader (about 18–20 cm) with brown upperparts, white underparts, short greenish-grey legs and a distinctive white shoulder wedge that separates the brown breast sides from the wings. Feeds along rivers, tanks, ponds, lagoons, mudflats and rocky shores, taking insects, small crustaceans and other invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage. Females may be slightly larger, but this is not useful for routine field identification.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show pale buff fringes and small spots on the upperparts, giving a scalloped pattern. They are often warmer brown than adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Almost constantly bobs its rear end while standing and feeding. In flight it flies low over water with rapid wingbeats and gives a sharp call; the white shoulder wedge is diagnostic at close range.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread migrant at both inland and coastal waters across Sri Lanka: rivers, irrigation tanks, ponds, paddy fields, lagoons, beaches and rocky shorelines. Regular at Bundala, Tissa, Mannar and many local wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022: M. Most numerous during the northern winter, broadly Aug/Sep–Apr, but records occur in additional months during passage or from oversummering individuals. Do not infer residency from occasional out-of-season records.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: Verified against CBC Sri Lanka Country List Version 3 (January 2022), which explicitly lists this species as M (regular migrant).

species_description.text: Small, active canopy bird, about 12–15 cm, with yellow underparts, green upperparts and a pointed bill. Found in open woodland, scrub, gardens, plantations and forest edges, usually in pairs. Feeds mainly on insects and their larvae, with some spiders, fruit and nectar.

male_female_identification.text: Breeding male develops black on the crown, back, wings and tail, with prominent white wing-bars and bright yellow underparts. Female remains greener above, with less black and less prominent wing-bars. Non-breeding male can resemble female; plumage is seasonally variable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and greener than bright breeding males, with less distinct black and white wing pattern; they resemble females/non-breeding birds.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for loud whistles and watch for an active yellow bird in the canopy. Male plumage changes markedly through the year, so do not assume every green-backed bird is female. Look for two white wing-bars on breeding males.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident across Sri Lanka in wooded lowlands and foothills, generally to around 1,000 m, occasionally higher. Found in gardens, scrub, open forest, plantations and forest margins.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding display and nesting occur seasonally; a small compact cup nest is bound with cobwebs and placed in a tree fork. Two to four eggs are reported in regional accounts; exact local months vary.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 classification convention: resident (R). Confirm current CBC row-level code before publication.

species_description.text: Small, dark swift (about 10–11 cm) with a short, square to slightly notched tail, dark brown upperparts, paler grey-brown rump and relatively pale underparts. Aerial insectivore, feeding on flying insects. In Sri Lanka it is strongly associated with highland cliffs, caves and other sheltered nesting sites; nests are made of saliva-bound plant material and attached to rock or cave surfaces.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in field plumage and cannot normally be separated visually. Both show dark brown upperparts and a subtly paler rump.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller and may have less neat feather edges; age is difficult to determine in flying birds. Do not assign age without close views of plumage or nest context.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for small, dark swifts flying rapidly over highland plateaus and cliffs. Compare tail shape and rump tone with other swifts; nesting colonies at cliffs or caves are more diagnostic than a distant flying silhouette.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka. Mainly associated with the central highlands and montane areas, including Horton Plains/World's End, Nuwara Eliya and other high-elevation rocky habitats. May forage widely over open uplands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is associated with suitable nesting sites and local conditions; avoid assigning a single island-wide breeding season without a site-specific source.

species_description.text: Small, streaked lark about 15–16 cm, with sandy-brown upperparts, pale underparts, finely streaked breast, short crest and long hind claw. Male's song-flight is distinctive, rising and hovering before descending while singing. Feeds on seeds and insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike and usually not reliably separable in the field. Males are more often detected by song-flight; female may have slightly duller plumage.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are more heavily scaled and buff-edged, with diffuse breast streaking; adult pattern develops with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for the male's prolonged song-flight. Compare with other larks by its longer hind claw, streaked breast and flight song; often sings high above open grassland.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open grassland, short scrub, dry fields, coastal plains and highland open areas. Occurs in Mannar, Bundala, Udawalawe and Horton Plains.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident breeder. Breeding activity varies by rainfall and habitat; avoid assigning fixed island-wide months without local nest records.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Country List 2022 status: Ashy-crowned Finch-Lark R; Jerdon's Bushlark R; Indian Skylark/Oriental Skylark R; Indian Pipit/Paddyfield Pipit R; Richard's Pipit M; Forest Wagtail M; Grey Wagtail M; Yellow Wagtail M. The official CBC 2011 list also corroborates these codes.

species_description.text: A very small kingfisher, about 16–17 cm, with vivid blue upperparts, orange underparts, a white throat and a long, dagger-like bill. It is usually solitary and territorial, favouring clear streams, rivers, ponds and open wetlands with overhanging branches. It dives rapidly from a low perch to catch small fish, tadpoles and aquatic insects. It regularly returns to favoured perches and often flies low over the water.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male has an entirely black bill. Female has a reddish-orange base to the lower mandible, with a dark tip; this is a useful close-range sexing feature.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with greener or less brilliant blue upperparts, paler orange underparts, a dark bill and dark legs. The female-like reddish lower-mandible base becomes clearer with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Very small, bright blue-and-orange bird that sits close to water and dives straight down. Its high-pitched repeated 'keek' call often gives it away. Check the bill: all black in adult male, reddish lower base in female.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident across much of Sri Lanka, but less common in higher hills. Look along streams, rivers, tanks and quiet wetland margins with suitable overhanging branches. It is less frequently seen than the White-throated Kingfisher.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Sri Lankan sources report breeding approximately November–June, with other local accounts giving February–June. Nests in a burrow in a stream or tank bank.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status to be cross-checked against exact species row before final publication; status retained as resident or migrant based on local CBC records and supporting Sri Lankan sources.

species_description.text: A small, compact forest kingfisher, about 16–18 cm, with deep blue-green upperparts, bright blue ear-coverts, orange underparts, a white throat and a long dark bill. It is closely associated with shaded streams and rivers in forest, usually perching low above water before diving for small fish, aquatic insects and other invertebrates. More secretive than the Common Kingfisher and often difficult to see in dense forest.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are very similar. Sex is not reliably determined from plumage in typical field observations.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less brilliant blue ear-coverts and upperparts and a less saturated orange breast. Close views are usually needed to age birds confidently.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a small, dark blue kingfisher low over a shaded forest stream. The bright blue ear patch is an important distinction from Common Kingfisher. Move quietly and scan streamside perches rather than open water.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A scarce resident in Sri Lanka's wet-zone forest streams and wooded foothills. It is associated with clear, shaded streams in rainforest and forest reserves; suitable sites include Sinharaja, Kitulgala and other wet-zone forest waterways. Sri Lankan subspecies is commonly referred to as phillipsi.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round, but local encounters are infrequent. Breeding season and precise months for Sri Lanka were not reliably established in the sources consulted; do not infer them from mainland populations.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status to be cross-checked against exact species row before final publication; status retained as resident or migrant based on local CBC records and supporting Sri Lankan sources.

species_description.text: Medium-sized rail (about 32 cm) with slate-grey head, neck and breast, white face and belly, red bill and frontal shield, and long yellow legs. Common in marshes, paddy fields, reedbeds, canals, ponds, mangroves and overgrown drains, including urban wetlands. Omnivorous: eats shoots, seeds, insects, worms, molluscs, small fish and frogs. Nests in dense waterside vegetation.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage. Males may be slightly larger, but size is not a reliable field character.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds are browner and duller, with less sharply defined white face and belly; bill and frontal shield are less vivid and may be dull greenish or brownish.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often heard giving loud, harsh calls at dawn or dusk. Look along the edges of reeds and paddy bunds; it frequently flicks its tail and runs across open patches.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident throughout Sri Lanka wherever suitable wetland vegetation occurs, including paddy landscapes, village tanks, urban marshes, lagoons and mangroves.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is often associated with rainy periods and availability of dense emergent vegetation; local timing varies.

species_description.text: Small, short-billed plover (about 15–17 cm) with pale sandy-grey upperparts, white underparts and dark leg colour. Breeding males have a black forehead bar, black ear-patch and dark breast-side patches; females show these markings brown rather than black. Non-breeding birds have reduced, grey-brown facial and breast markings. Feeds on small insects, crustaceans and other invertebrates on sandy and muddy shores, saltpans and lagoons.

male_female_identification.text: Male in breeding plumage has black, well-defined head and breast-side patches; female has corresponding brown patches. In non-breeding plumage, the sexes are much less distinct. Sri Lankan resident subspecies seebohmi should be considered separately from northern migrant populations.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show buff-fringed, scaly upperparts and indistinct brown head/breast markings. They resemble non-breeding adults but are more neatly scaled above.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a small pale plover with dark legs and no orange bill base. Breeding male has black head patches; female's are brown. Separate from Little Ringed Plover by the smaller, paler appearance and lack of a conspicuous yellow eye-ring.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs along coastal beaches, lagoons, mudflats and saltpans. Both migrant and resident populations occur; resident seebohmi is associated with suitable coastal habitats, while winter visitors increase numbers at major sites such as Mannar, Puttalam and Bundala.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Both resident and migrant components are recorded in Sri Lanka (CBC 2022 distinguishes resident subspecies seebohmi and migrant alexandrinus). Migrants are mainly present Aug–Apr; resident birds can occur year-round.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC 2022: C. a. alexandrinus — M; C. a. seebohmi — R. Aggregate species classification R/M.

species_description.text: Large, long-legged sand-plover (about 22–25 cm), with a relatively long, heavy bill, pale sandy-grey upperparts and white underparts. Breeding adults show a chestnut breast-band and dark facial markings; non-breeding birds are plain grey-brown above and white below. Feeds on small crabs, molluscs, worms and insects on sandy beaches, mudflats and tidal flats.

male_female_identification.text: Breeding male has a richer chestnut breast-band and stronger black facial markings; female is generally duller, with more mottled or brownish breast markings. Outside breeding plumage, sexes are difficult to separate.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show buff-fringed, scaly upperparts, with muted brown breast and facial markings. Young birds lack the strong chestnut-and-black breeding pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Compare bill length and body size with Lesser/Siberian/Tibetan sand-plovers. Greater Sand-Plover is usually larger and longer-billed; bill shape and structure are more reliable than plumage alone. In breeding plumage, note the chestnut breast-band.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common migrant along sandy and muddy coasts, estuaries, lagoons and saltpans, especially Mannar, Puttalam, Bundala and other extensive coastal wetlands. Often found on open beaches and tidal flats.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Migrant, mainly Aug–Apr, with most birds during the northern winter. CBC 2022 lists Greater Sand Plover as M.

species_description.text: Small-to-medium sand-plover, usually around 19–21 cm, with sandy-grey upperparts, white underparts and a relatively short, stout bill. Breeding adults show a chestnut breast-band and dark facial markings; non-breeding birds are much plainer. Feeds on small crustaceans, molluscs, worms and insects on coastal mudflats, sandy shores and tidal flats. Identification from other sand-plovers can be challenging, especially in non-breeding plumage.

male_female_identification.text: Breeding male has more vivid chestnut and black facial/breast markings; female is generally duller and more mottled. Non-breeding sexes are very difficult to separate. Sex should not be assigned to distant birds.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have buff-fringed, scaly upperparts and muted brown breast markings. Separation from Tibetan Sand-Plover and Greater Sand-Plover requires careful assessment of structure, bill and leg proportions, and plumage.

field_spotting_tips.text: Do not identify from colour alone. Compare bill length/depth, head shape, leg length and overall structure with Tibetan and Greater Sand-Plovers. Photograph birds from multiple angles and retain notes on flock context and plumage; old Lesser Sand-Plover records may not be assignable confidently to either split species.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Taxonomic treatment and Sri Lankan records need care. CBC 2022 listed the former Lesser Sand Plover (Charadrius mongolus) as a migrant. Current checklists separate Siberian and Tibetan Sand-Plovers; Sri Lankan records may require re-identification under the split. Coastal mudflats and beaches, especially Mannar and other north-western sites, are likely search areas, but do not assume all old Lesser Sand-Plover records are Siberian.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Migrant. CBC 2022 lists the pre-split Lesser Sand Plover as M. Current eBird/Avibase checklists include Siberian Sand-Plover in Sri Lanka, but a reliable month-by-month local pattern for this split taxon was not established in this batch; broadly northern-winter months are expected.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC 2022 lists pre-split Lesser Sand Plover (Charadrius mongolus) — M. Current taxonomy separates Siberian/Tibetan; assign local records to Siberian only when identified. Provisional M.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 59–76 පමණ දිගැති, දිගු සිහින් ගෙල සහ පිරිමිගේ දිගු මධ්‍යම tail feathers නිසා ඉතා සිහින් හැඩයක් ඇති තාරාවෙකි. පිරිමිගේ හිස chocolate-brown, ගෙල සුදු ඉරි සහිත, ශරීරය අළු. ගැහැනු mottled brown. විවෘත වැව්, කලපු, marshes සහ තෙත් තණබිම්. බීජ, ජලජ ශාක සහ කුඩා අපෘෂ්ඨවංශීන් ආහාරයට ගනී. ලංකාවේ ශීත සංචාරකයෙකි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමිගේ දිගු pointed tail සහ සුදු ගෙල ඉරි ප්‍රධාන ලක්ෂණ. ගැහැනු දුඹුරු mottled, දිගු neck සහ සිහින් bill ඇතත් tail දිග අඩු. Juvenile ගැහැනුට සමාන.

field_spotting_tips.text: පිරිමිගේ දිගු pointed tail ඉතා පහසු ලක්ෂණය. දුරින් පෙනෙන විට සිහින් ගෙල සහ ඉහළට නැමුණු body posture බලන්න. ගැහැනු හඳුනාගැනීමේදී bill shape සහ දිගු neck/body profile බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: වියළි කලාපයේ විශාල වැව්, කලපු සහ වෙරළබඩ තෙත්බිම්; Bundala, Tissamaharama, Minneriya සහ Wilpattu වාර්තා.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශීත සංචාරකයෙක්; සාමාන්‍යයෙන් නොවැම්බර්–මාර්තු (CBC 2022: M).

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 55–63 පමණ දිගැති විශාල තාරාවෙකි. අළු-දුඹුරු ශරීරය, හිසෙහි සිහින් අඳුරු ඉරි, හොටේ අගට ආසන්න කහ පැල්ලම සහ පියාපතේ කොළ පැහැති speculum එක ප්‍රධාන ලක්ෂණ. විවෘත වැව්, ගංගා, marshes, වී කුඹුරු සහ වෙරළබඩ කලපු. ජලජ ශාක, බීජ, ධාන්‍ය, කෘමීන් සහ කුඩා ජලජ සතුන් ආහාරයට ගනී. ගස් කුහර/තණ ආවරණ සහිත බිම්වල කූඩු තැබිය හැක; ලංකාවේ නිශ්චිත nesting months තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි සාමාන්‍යයෙන් විශාල; හොටේ කහ පැල්ලම වඩා පැහැදිලි විය හැක. ගැහැනු කුඩා සහ තරමක් අඳුරු, නමුත් ලිංග දෙකම සමාන නිසා field එකේ sexing අපහසුයි. Juvenile අඳුරු-දුඹුරු සහ හොටේ පැල්ලම අඩු පැහැදිලි.

field_spotting_tips.text: හොටේ කහ අග පැල්ලම සහ පියාපතේ කොළ speculum බලන්න. වැව් මත තාරාවන් අතරින් වෙන්කරගැනීමට හොටේ පැල්ලම හොඳම ලක්ෂණය. Mallard/other ducks සමඟ සසඳන විට හිසෙහි ඉරි සහ අළු පැහැය බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: පහළබිම් තෙත්බිම් සහ විශාල වැව්; වියළි කලාපයේ බහුල. Bundala, Tissamaharama, Minneriya, Udawalawe සහ Wilpattu වැනි ජලාශවල නිරීක්ෂණය කළ හැක.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී ජනගහනයක් සහ සංඛ්‍යාත්මකව වෙනස් වන සංචාරක පක්ෂීන් (CBC 2022: R+M).

species_description.text: Medium-large grey-white stork with long legs and a distinctive gap between the arched mandibles in adults. Feeds mainly on apple snails and other molluscs, plus aquatic prey, in paddy fields, marshes and tanks; often nests colonially.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike; males average slightly larger. The bill gap is most obvious in mature birds.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles browner and duller, with a less pronounced bill gap; adult grey-white plumage develops with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the characteristic bill profile. In flight, note broad wings and black flight feathers against a pale body.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident of wetlands and agricultural landscapes, including Colombo wetlands, paddy fields, Bundala, Yala, Kumana and dry-zone tanks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year; local numbers rise around seasonal wetlands and snail-rich paddy fields.

species_description.text: Large, slender waterbird (about 85–97 cm) with exceptionally long snake-like neck, narrow pointed dagger-like bill and long fan-shaped tail. Adult male has glossy black body and silvery-white streaking on upperwing/scapulars; head and neck brown with a white stripe from the eye down the neck. Hunts fish underwater, often spearing prey with its bill. Nests in trees near water, often in mixed heronries.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male is darker, with black body and stronger silvery-white upperwing streaks. Female is generally browner/paler, especially on neck and underparts; sexes are distinguishable when plumage is clearly seen.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are paler brown, with less distinct or absent white side-neck stripe and buffier/yellower wing markings; immature birds lack the adult male's strong glossy black contrast.

field_spotting_tips.text: Swimming bird often shows only its head and long neck above water. When perched it spreads wings and tail to dry; the straight spear-like bill and kinked neck separate it from cormorants.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in lowland wetlands, tanks, reservoirs, rivers, marshes and mangroves. Seen at dry-zone wetland sites and large tanks; Sri Lankan records include wetland roosts and nesting associations with cormorants/herons.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident (CBC 2022 R); generally present year-round. Sri Lankan breeding reports include Jan–Feb; timing can vary with monsoon and water levels. Do not interpret scattered sightings as seasonal migration.

species_description.text: A large, striking black-and-white hornbill, about 65–92 cm, with a huge pale bill and prominent casque. The body is mostly black, with white underparts, white outer tail feathers and white trailing edges to the wings visible in flight. Favours lowland forest, forest margins, dry deciduous woodland and open wooded country, often travelling between fruiting trees. Mainly eats fruit, especially figs, but also takes insects, lizards and other small animal prey. Nests in a tree cavity; the female seals herself inside while incubating and raising the chicks, and the male feeds her through a narrow slit.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a larger bill and massive casque, with a dark base to the bill and black facial skin around the eye. Female has a smaller bill and casque; bare skin around the eye is pale blue and may become pinkish during breeding. These are useful close-range distinctions.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have a smaller, plain dull-yellow bill and lack the fully developed casque. Adult black-and-white plumage develops progressively; young birds may be seen with family groups around fruiting trees.

field_spotting_tips.text: Its enormous casque, black-and-white plumage and heavy wingbeats make it unmistakable. Watch fruiting figs and listen for deep, loud calls. In flight, white tail corners and white wing edges are conspicuous. Do not confuse with the smaller endemic Grey Hornbill.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's dry-zone and lowland forests, especially the north, north-central and south-east. Good areas include Wilpattu, Sigiriya, Minneriya, Udawalawe and Yala; also occurs in suitable forest patches and agricultural mosaics.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round, with local movements following fruiting trees. Breeding is seasonal and tied to suitable tree cavities and food availability; Sri Lankan month-by-month timing should be verified before assigning a narrow window.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status applied: endemic (E) for Sri Lanka Grey Hornbill, Yellow-fronted Barbet and Crimson-fronted Barbet; resident (R) for the other three. Verify exact row codes before publication.

species_description.text: Large, long-legged pipit about 17–19 cm, with sandy-brown streaked upperparts, pale buff underparts, long tail and very long hind claw. Has a strong, slightly strident call and often walks briskly across open ground. Feeds on insects and other invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike; no reliable external distinction. Adult has relatively large bill, long legs, long hind claw and streaked breast.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are more strongly scaled and buff-edged, with heavier streaking and softer contrast.

field_spotting_tips.text: Carefully compare structure with Paddyfield Pipit: Richard's is larger, longer-legged, longer-tailed and has a heavier bill and more deliberate gait. Calls are useful; beware confusion with Blyth's Pipit.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Migrant to Sri Lanka, recorded in open grassland, dry fields, coastal plains, scrub and short turf, including Bundala, Udawalawe and Horton Plains. Occurrence can be local and irregular.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter migrant, usually recorded August–April in Sri Lanka; Limosa open-record monthly dataset shows Aug–Apr, with some months missing due to sampling.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Country List 2022 status: Ashy-crowned Finch-Lark R; Jerdon's Bushlark R; Indian Skylark/Oriental Skylark R; Indian Pipit/Paddyfield Pipit R; Richard's Pipit M; Forest Wagtail M; Grey Wagtail M; Yellow Wagtail M. The official CBC 2011 list also corroborates these codes.

species_description.text: Small, upright pipit about 15–16 cm, with brown streaked upperparts, pale buff underparts, fine breast streaking, long legs and a long hind claw. Often walks or runs through short grass and bare ground, feeding on insects and other small invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; no reliable field distinction. Plumage is generally streaked and sandy, with pale eyebrow and outer tail feathers.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are more heavily scaled and buff-edged than adults, with stronger markings on breast and upperparts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for its steady walking gait and repeated pipit calls. Compare with migrant Richard's Pipit: Paddyfield is smaller, more compact and has a shorter bill and legs; structure is important.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident in open grassland, paddy fields, lawns, roadsides, scrub, dry fields and montane grassland across Sri Lanka.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding reported across much of the year, often associated with rains; nest is a grass cup on the ground, concealed in vegetation.

species_description.text: Small, compact swift (about 12–13 cm) with dark brown to blackish plumage, a conspicuous white rump, short square tail and relatively broad wings. Aerial insectivore, feeding on flying insects over towns, villages, wetlands and open country. Often nests colonially on buildings, bridges and other structures, using saliva-bound material.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and not reliably separable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles may have pale fringes to feathers and a slightly scaly appearance, but are difficult to age while in flight. Nestlings and recently fledged birds are best assessed at colonies without disturbing them.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the compact shape and clean white rump, especially when birds wheel over buildings or water. Often flies in small groups; distinguish from Barn Swallow by the short tail, stiffer swift-like flight and white rump.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident across Sri Lanka, especially around towns, villages, bridges, buildings and open landscapes. Common in lowlands and may be seen over wetlands and reservoirs.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Breeding can occur in more than one period depending on local conditions and nesting-site availability; a fixed island-wide window should not be assumed.

species_description.text: Very large, elegant white egret (about 80–104 cm) with a long neck, long dark legs and a long yellow bill. Breeding adults develop long, loose plumes on the back and delicate head plumes; bill and facial skin may become brighter. Occupies tanks, lagoons, marshes, paddy fields, estuaries and shallow coastal wetlands. Feeds mainly on fish, frogs, crustaceans and other aquatic prey, often stalking slowly in shallow water. Nests colonially in trees, sometimes with other herons and egrets.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike; males are generally slightly larger and may have longer breeding plumes. Sex is not reliably determined from ordinary field views.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble non-breeding adults but have less ornamental plumage and may show duller bill and facial colours.

field_spotting_tips.text: Its large size, long neck and long yellow bill distinguish it from Medium Egret. In flight, note the long neck folded back and legs projecting well beyond the tail. Check bill length and gape when separating from similar egrets.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread in suitable wetlands throughout Sri Lanka, particularly tanks, lagoons and paddy landscapes in the lowlands. Regular at Bundala, Yala, Mannar, Anawilundawa and many inland reservoirs.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year (CBC category R). Local numbers fluctuate with water availability and prey abundance.

species_description.text: Large, long-legged heron (about 90–98 cm) with a heavy yellow bill, pale grey body, white head and neck, black shoulder plumes and a black stripe extending from the eye in breeding plumage. Uses tanks, lagoons, marshes, estuaries and paddy fields. Feeds mainly on fish, amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans and large insects. Nests colonially in trees, often with other waterbirds.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in field plumage; males average slightly larger. Breeding adults show elongated black nape plumes and ornamental breast feathers.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller grey-brown, with a streaked neck and less sharply defined head pattern; they lack the full adult breeding plumes.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for its large size, pale grey body, long neck held in an S-curve and deliberate stalking gait. In flight it retracts the neck and trails its long legs.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread in lowland wetlands across Sri Lanka, including tanks and lagoons in the Dry Zone, Bundala, Yala, Mannar and wet-zone marshes. Usually seen singly or in small groups.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year (CBC country-list category R). Local numbers and distribution vary with water levels and feeding conditions.

species_description.text: Small, stocky egret (about 46–56 cm) with a short thick neck, rounded head and relatively short, stout yellow bill. Non-breeding plumage is mostly white; in breeding condition it develops rich orange-buff plumes on the crown, neck and back, with brighter bill and facial skin. Commonly forages in grassland, pasture, paddy fields, marshes and around grazing livestock, feeding on insects, especially grasshoppers, as well as other small invertebrates and amphibians. Nests colonially in trees or reedbeds.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female look alike; males may have slightly longer breeding plumes. The orange-buff breeding feathers are seasonal, not a sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are white but may show a faint buff wash and lack the full breeding plumes. Immature birds gradually develop adult seasonal ornamentation.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the compact body, short thick bill and habit of following cattle, buffaloes, tractors or grazing animals to catch disturbed insects. This behaviour separates it from other white egrets.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Very widespread throughout Sri Lanka, from lowlands to cultivated uplands. Common in paddy fields, grazing land, roadside grass, wetlands and around livestock; large communal roosts occur near wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round (CBC category R). Breeding plumage is most conspicuous during local breeding periods; timing varies with rainfall and food availability.

species_description.text: Medium-sized white egret (about 65–72 cm), intermediate in size between Little Egret and Great Egret. It has a relatively short, thick yellow bill, dark legs and a less slender build than Little Egret. Breeding adults develop long white plumes on the back and delicate head plumes. Found in marshes, tanks, paddy fields, shallow lagoons and flooded grassland; feeds on fish, frogs, insects and other aquatic animals. Often feeds more slowly than Little Egret.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar; males may be slightly larger and carry longer breeding plumes. Sex is not reliably separable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble non-breeding adults but are less likely to show ornamental plumes and may have duller bill and facial colours.

field_spotting_tips.text: Compare size and structure with nearby egrets: larger and heavier-billed than Little Egret, smaller and usually more compact than Great Egret. Bill depth and gape line can help, but identification should use several features.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs across Sri Lanka in suitable lowland wetlands, tanks, paddy fields and lagoons. Often overlooked among flocks of other white egrets; check size and bill shape carefully.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round (CBC category R). Local abundance changes with water levels and seasonal wetland conditions.

species_description.text: Tall, slender heron (about 78–90 cm) with a long, narrow neck, dark grey-purple upperparts and chestnut neck with dark streaking. The bill is long and yellowish; the head often appears darker. Inhabits reed-fringed tanks, marshes, paddy fields and mangroves. Eats fish, frogs, insects, crustaceans and small reptiles. Nests in reedbeds or trees, often in colonies.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; males may be slightly larger. Breeding birds develop longer ornamental neck and scapular plumes, but sex is not reliably determined in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked, with a less contrasting neck and upperparts. They gradually acquire the adult dark purple-grey and chestnut pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often stands motionless among reeds with its long neck held vertically. The dark upperparts and chestnut neck distinguish it from Grey Heron; it flies with the neck folded.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread in suitable wetlands across the island, especially lowland tanks, marshes, paddy landscapes and reedbeds. Regular in Bundala, Yala, Tissamaharama, Anawilundawa and other wetland complexes.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round (CBC category R). Local movements follow wetland conditions and food availability.

species_description.text: Small, familiar heron (about 45–48 cm) with a compact body, short neck and yellowish bill. In non-breeding plumage it is cryptically brown and streaked, blending into dry fields; in breeding plumage the head, neck and breast become rich maroon-brown and the wings appear strikingly white in flight. Feeds on fish, frogs, insects and other small animals in paddy fields, marshes, tanks and wetland margins. Breeds in colonies, often with other herons, building a stick platform in trees or shrubs.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar; breeding plumage and leg colour can vary with season. Sex is generally difficult to determine reliably in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and more heavily streaked than adults, with less developed breeding plumage. First-year birds gradually acquire adult patterning.

field_spotting_tips.text: In non-breeding plumage it can be mistaken for a lump of earth at a field edge. The sudden flash of white wings in flight is a strong clue; breeding birds show rich chestnut head and neck.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Very widespread in paddy fields and wetlands throughout Sri Lanka, including urban and peri-urban wetlands, tanks, lagoons and marshes. Commonly seen across both wet and dry zones.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident with migrant augmentation (CBC 2022 R+M). Present throughout the year; numbers can increase during the northern winter.

species_description.text: Sturdy, compact shorebird (about 22–24 cm) with short orange legs, a short slightly upturned dark bill and boldly patterned black, white and chestnut upperparts in breeding plumage. Non-breeding birds are more subdued brown and black with white underparts. Feeds by flipping stones, shells and seaweed to expose insects, crustaceans and other small invertebrates; favours rocky shores, reefs, sandy beaches and coastal mudflats.

male_female_identification.text: In breeding plumage males usually show brighter chestnut and more sharply defined black-and-white head pattern; females are generally duller and more mottled. In non-breeding plumage the sexes are difficult to distinguish.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and buff with pale fringes on the upperparts and a scaled appearance; head pattern is less sharply defined and chestnut tones are muted.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for its characteristic stone-turning behaviour. The short orange legs, compact body and pied pattern distinguish it from the longer-legged Tringa sandpipers. Check the upperparts carefully in breeding vs non-breeding plumage.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Coastal migrant at rocky shores, reefs, beaches, tidal flats and lagoons, including Bundala, Mannar, Puttalam and other suitable coastal sites. Often forages along the strandline or among seaweed and stones.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022: M. Mainly a northern-winter visitor, broadly Aug/Sep–Apr, with numbers varying between sites and years. Global IUCN category is NT; this is the global assessment, not a Sri Lanka-only status.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: Verified against CBC Sri Lanka Country List Version 3 (January 2022), which explicitly lists this species as M (regular migrant).

species_description.text: Medium-sized, robust, noisy babbler about 20–23 cm, with grey-brown upperparts, grey head and breast, pale buff belly, yellow bill and pale bluish-white eye. Usually in sociable flocks of seven or more, foraging on the ground and in low vegetation for insects, fruit, nectar and scraps.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and cannot reliably be separated in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less crisp head pattern and a less vivid yellow bill; young birds remain within family groups.

field_spotting_tips.text: Usually seen or heard in chattering flocks. The yellow bill, pale eye and grey head distinguish it from Orange-billed Babbler, which is rufous with orange bill and legs. Frequently forages on the ground.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident in gardens, scrub, cultivation, open woodland and village landscapes across much of Sri Lanka, especially lowlands and foothills. Sri Lankan subspecies taprobanus is distinct from the southern Indian nominate form.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding can occur over an extended period; Sri Lankan records suggest a main period around November–March, with some reports of nests outside this window. Often cooperative group nesting.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Sri Lanka Scimitar-babbler E; Yellow-eyed Babbler R; Tawny-bellied Babbler R; Dark-fronted Babbler R; Sri Lanka Orange-billed Babbler E; Sri Lanka Ashy-headed Laughing-thrush E; Yellow-billed Babbler R; Sri Lanka Brown-capped Babbler E. Several resident species have endemic Sri Lankan subspecies only.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, elusive endemic babbler, around 20–22 cm, with ashy-grey head and breast, olive-brown upperparts, pale eye and longish tail. Usually in small, noisy groups within dense wet-zone rainforest, foraging through the canopy and mid-storey for insects, fruit and other small invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage; no reliable external field distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are poorly described in accessible field sources; likely duller and browner with less sharply defined grey head and breast. Treat age identification as uncertain.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often detected by its calls and movement within mixed-species flocks. Search shaded forest mid-storey and canopy, especially in intact wet-zone forest. Distinguish from Orange-billed Babbler by grey head/breast rather than rufous body and orange bill.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to southwestern Sri Lanka's wet-zone forests, especially mature rainforest around Sinharaja, Kanneliya, Kitulgala and nearby forest blocks. Mostly below 1,200 m.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding biology and precise nesting months are poorly documented; do not infer a precise season without direct local evidence.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, noisy forest babbler about 20–22 cm, with rich rufous/chestnut plumage, orange bill and orange legs. Travels in active, often sizeable flocks, leading mixed-species feeding parties through all forest levels. Eats insects and other small animals as well as fruit and other plant matter.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and cannot reliably be separated in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller and less richly rufous, with less saturated orange bill and legs; they remain with and move in family flocks.

field_spotting_tips.text: Highly social and noisy. Listen for squeaky calls announcing an approaching flock. The rufous body and bright orange bill and legs separate it from Yellow-billed Babbler. Watch mixed flocks in forest mid-storey and canopy.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka's wet-zone forests and adjoining hills, from lowland rainforest to montane forest. Important sites include Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Kanneliya, Peak Wilderness and Horton Plains, though it is less frequent in heavily degraded fragments.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is reported mainly March–May. Nesting is poorly documented because nests are exceptionally well concealed; clutch generally 2–3 deep greenish-blue eggs in historical accounts.

species_description.text: Stocky, long-winged bird about 18–19 cm, with a heavy silvery bill, slaty-grey head, brownish-grey back, pinkish-grey underparts, narrow pale rump and dark rounded tail broadly tipped white. Usually in pairs or sociable flocks in open country with scattered trees, paddy fields, plantations and forest edges. Catches flying insects and often perches conspicuously on wires.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar; reliable field sexing is generally not possible.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are darker and browner, with pale buff spots/scalloping above and mottling below; bill is darker than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for compact groups perched close together on telephone/electric wires. In flight, the broad white tail tip and pale rump help distinguish it from swallows; it sallies out to catch insects.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident throughout Sri Lanka in open and semi-open country, from lowlands to hills, though less frequent at higher elevations. Look around paddy fields, village edges, palms, roadside wires and open woodland.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round, with local movements possibly linked to weather and insect availability. Sri Lankan breeding season reported mainly February–June.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 classification convention: resident (R). Confirm current CBC row-level code before publication.

species_description.text: Distinctive nocturnal frogmouth (about 23–25 cm) with a very broad, flattened frog-like bill, huge gape, cryptic bark-like plumage and short rounded wings. Usually roosts motionless along branches in dense lowland forest undergrowth, blending with twigs and bark. Feeds mainly on insects captured from a perch. Builds a small, shallow nest on a branch; both parents share incubation and nest guarding.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes show noticeable colour variation: male is generally greyer or more silvery-brown, while female is more rufous/chestnut. Both have cryptic mottled plumage and a broad bill; colour should be considered with individual variation and lighting.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Chicks are downy and pale, then develop cryptic mottled plumage. Juveniles may show softer, less sharply defined markings; detailed ageing of free-flying birds is difficult.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search carefully along low horizontal branches in shaded forest undergrowth; the bird often resembles a broken branch. Scan slowly and avoid approaching or flushing roosting birds.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in tropical lowland forests, especially the wet-zone and southwestern forests, with records in four floristic regions and elevations approximately 11–767 m in a 1998–2018 survey. Particularly associated with dense undergrowth and humid, shaded roost sites.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Nesting pairs and chicks have been documented during long-term surveys, but the available study does not establish a single island-wide breeding season. High fidelity to roost trees has been reported.

species_description.text: Small, secretive bittern (about 38 cm) of freshwater marshes and reedbeds. Male is rich cinnamon above with buff underparts; feeds on insects, small fish and amphibians. Nests on reed platforms in dense wetland vegetation; clutch usually 4–6 eggs.

male_female_identification.text: Male is brighter and more uniformly cinnamon. Female has a browner crown and back with more streaking; sexes are similar in size.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile resembles female but is more heavily streaked below and generally browner; immature birds can be difficult to separate from females.

field_spotting_tips.text: Scan reed edges patiently, especially at dawn and dusk. It may freeze upright among reeds or creep slowly with a short-necked posture; often flushed only at close range.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs in suitable marshes and reedbeds in both wet and dry lowlands. Recorded at Giant’s Tank/Murunkan, Muthurajawela, Galle and other vegetated wetlands; often overlooked because it stays low in cover.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident, with additional winter visitors reported. More likely to be encountered during the north-east monsoon migrant season, but local occurrence varies.

species_description.text: Large, secretive bittern (around 58–66 cm) with a long neck and yellow bill. Adult has dark blackish upperparts with a conspicuous yellow stripe on the sides of the neck and pale, heavily streaked underparts. Inhabits reed-fringed marshes, swamp forest, mangroves and vegetated streams; eats fish, frogs, crustaceans, reptiles and insects. Nests in dense vegetation, with Sri Lankan nesting records in April.

male_female_identification.text: Female is generally browner and less glossy than the adult male, with less sharply defined dark upperparts. Both sexes show the characteristic yellow neck stripe.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller dark brown rather than glossy black, with more diffuse streaking and less distinct contrast.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search quiet reedbeds, wooded wetland edges and shaded streams. It may stand motionless in cover; when flushed, the dark upperparts and yellow neck stripe are diagnostic.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs locally in lowland dry and wet zones and can reach mid-country elevations. Records include Hambantota and Bellanwila–Attidiya; dense, secluded wetland vegetation is key. Some reported highland records lack sufficient evidence and should be treated cautiously.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident with a winter migrant component (CBC 2022 R+M); local observations may increase during the migrant season, approximately September–April.

species_description.text: Very small, slender bittern (about 38 cm) with a long pointed bill and yellowish legs. Occupies reedbeds, marshes, rice fields and wetland margins. Feeds on small fish, frogs, aquatic insects and other invertebrates; nests in dense emergent vegetation.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male is usually more strongly golden-buff/cinnamon on the neck and breast with darker upperparts. Female is browner and more heavily streaked, especially on the crown and back.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are strongly streaked and mottled brown, providing camouflage in reeds; they lack the cleaner, richer adult male pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a tiny bittern moving slowly through reeds. When alarmed it often adopts a rigid, bill-up posture aligned with vertical stems. Check both sides of reed beds at dawn.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread in suitable lowland wetlands, including Lunawa Lagoon, Talangama, Bundala, Debarawewa/Tissamaharama, Muthurajawela and other marshes and tanks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident population augmented by winter migrants (CBC 2022 R+M). Winter influx is often most evident from roughly September/October through March/April; not every individual is migratory.

species_description.text: Medium-large nocturnal shorebird (about 40–45 cm) with sandy-brown, heavily streaked and mottled plumage, large yellow eyes, short stout yellow bill with dark tip and long yellow legs. Favours dry open country, scrub, stony plains, sparse grassland and coastal flats. Feeds at night on insects, beetles, crabs and other small animals.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage and not reliably separable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are more buff and finely mottled, with pale feather fringes and a softer, less contrasting pattern; eye and bill colours may be duller.

field_spotting_tips.text: Mostly nocturnal or crepuscular. Search open tracks and stony ground after dusk with a torch used carefully; by day it relies on camouflage and may crouch motionless. Large yellow eye is the key clue.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's dry zone, especially open scrub, stony ground, dry grassland and coastal plains. Recorded in Yala, Bundala and other dry lowland habitats.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is associated with dry open ground; local nesting period varies and needs site-specific confirmation.

species_description.text: Small, compact heron (about 40–48 cm) with a short neck, stout body and dagger-like bill. Adult breeding plumage is dark greenish-black above with rich chestnut sides and neck; non-breeding birds are duller and streakier. Lives along streams, ponds, mangroves, lagoons and shaded wetland edges, feeding on fish, crabs, insects and other small aquatic prey.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in general appearance; slight size and plumage differences are not dependable for routine field sexing.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown, heavily streaked and spotted, with a less contrasting crown and upperparts. Plumage becomes darker and cleaner with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch mangrove roots, fish-trap stilts and stream banks. It often stands motionless before striking at prey; can raise its short crest when alert.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread but often inconspicuous around coastal and inland wetlands, especially mangrove creeks, lagoon edges, ponds and shaded waterways. Older Sri Lankan literature often uses Little Green Heron/Striated Heron; current AviList treatment used here is Little Heron, Butorides atricapilla.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round in suitable habitat (CBC 2022 lists the corresponding Green-backed/Little Green Heron taxon as R).

species_description.text: A small, slim cuckoo (about 23 cm) with grey head and upperparts, pale grey to whitish underparts, a long tail and yellowish eye-ring and legs. Occurs in open woodland, scrub, gardens, plantations and forest edges. Feeds mainly on insects and caterpillars. It is a brood parasite, using the nests of small passerines as hosts.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male is usually grey above and below with a relatively plain grey breast and belly. Female may show a rufous or chestnut wash on the upper breast and more contrasting upperpart tones; individual and age variation means sexing should be cautious.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner/rufous and often more heavily barred than adults, particularly on the upperparts and underparts. They can resemble other small cuckoos; check size, tail and facial pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a small, active cuckoo in open scrub and at woodland edges. It may perch in exposed positions briefly before moving through cover. Note the grey body and long tail; compare carefully with Banded Bay Cuckoo, which is warmer brown and more strongly streaked.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A migrant to Sri Lanka, recorded in open country, scrub, gardens and woodland edges, including dry-zone locations such as Udawalawe and Bundala. Occurrence can be patchy and dependent on season and local food availability.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Seasonal migrant, generally present during the northern winter period; CBC country list classifies it M. Exact arrival/departure dates vary annually and by locality.

species_description.text: A small, slim cuckoo (about 23 cm) with warm brown/rufous upperparts, a pale throat, strongly streaked or barred underparts and a long tail. Favours wooded gardens, plantations, forest edges and open woodland, often remaining within foliage. Feeds mainly on insects and caterpillars. It is a brood parasite, laying eggs in the nests of other birds.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are broadly similar. Females may show more rufous tones or stronger markings, but sex is not reliably established from a typical field view; age and plumage variation can overlap.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more heavily barred or streaked than adults, with less cleanly defined plumage. Young birds can be confused with other small cuckoos; use the overall warm brown colour, fine shape and call together.

field_spotting_tips.text: Learn its distinctive repetitive call, often heard from concealed foliage. Search the middle and upper layers of trees in gardens and forest edges. Its warm bay-brown plumage and streaked underparts distinguish it from the grey-bellied migrant.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, recorded in wooded gardens, plantations and forest edges in both wet and dry regions. It is regularly heard in suitable habitat but can be difficult to see within foliage; field reports include the Ella and Sinharaja areas.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Calling and breeding activity may increase seasonally, but available local sources do not support a single fixed island-wide breeding window.

species_description.text: Small (18–20 cm), compact pale shorebird with short straight black bill and black legs. Non-breeding adults are grey above and white below, with a dark shoulder patch; breeding plumage becomes rufous. Uses sandy beaches and exposed shorelines; feeds on small marine invertebrates, crustaceans and worms, often chasing receding waves. Breeds in the high Arctic; no Sri Lankan breeding.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar in size and plumage; males may average slightly more colourful in breeding plumage, but field sexing is unreliable. Identify by plumage/season rather than sex.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show crisp dark-and-white scaly upperparts, unlike the plainer grey-backed winter adult. First-winter birds become progressively greyer; no major colour morphs.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a very pale, compact wader running rapidly at the waterline, repeatedly retreating and advancing with waves. Short straight bill, black legs and dark shoulder patch are key; lacks a hind toe, but this is not a practical field character.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Scarce migrant along the coast; best searched for on open sandy beaches and coastal flats, including north-western and south-eastern coasts. Records are less frequent than common wintering stints. Bundala and other coastal lagoons/beaches are useful search areas.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter visitor, mainly during the northern winter; broad Sri Lankan records generally fall in the migration/winter period, approximately Aug–May. Exact arrival/departure varies annually.

species_description.text: Medium-small (18–23 cm) long-legged Calidris with a notably long, slender, slightly downcurved black bill. Non-breeding birds are grey above and white below with a pale supercilium; breeding adults are rich chestnut-red below. Feeds by probing mud and shallow water for worms, molluscs, crustaceans and other invertebrates. Arctic tundra breeder; Sri Lankan bird is a migrant.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are broadly similar in winter plumage. In breeding plumage females tend to be slightly larger and often less intensely rufous, but sex is not reliably determined in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have neat buff-edged/scaly upperparts, white underparts and a lightly buff-washed breast. They lack the full chestnut underside of breeding adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for the long down-curved bill and relatively long legs. In flight, note the conspicuous white rump. Often feeds belly-deep at the water's edge and mixes with stints and other waders.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common migrant at coastal mudflats, salt pans and lagoons; particularly conspicuous at Bundala, with further suitable habitat at Mannar, Puttalam and other northern/western coastal wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular winter migrant, mainly Aug–Apr/May; peak numbers often occur during the north-east monsoon and winter months. Some passage movement occurs outside the core winter period.

species_description.text: Very small (13–15 cm) compact sandpiper with a short straight black bill, black legs and grey-brown upperparts. Winter adults are pale grey-brown above and whitish below with fine breast streaking; breeding adults develop rufous crown and mantle markings. Feeds on tiny aquatic invertebrates, insects, crustaceans and worms along shallow muddy margins. Breeds in Arctic/subarctic regions; migrant in Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in winter. In breeding plumage males are usually more brightly rufous and more heavily marked; sex is difficult to establish outside breeding plumage.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have crisp, neat pale fringes producing a scaly pattern on the upperparts, with a warm buff wash on the breast. They are often more sharply patterned than winter adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Extremely small size, short straight bill and black legs help. Compare carefully with other stints: Little Stint usually has a shorter bill than Curlew Sandpiper and lacks its downcurve; check leg colour and head pattern.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common winter visitor to shallow wetlands, mudflats, salt pans and lagoon margins. Bundala is a reliable site; also occurs at Mannar, Puttalam, Tissa and other suitable tanks/coastal wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly Aug–Apr/May, with numbers generally increasing during the north-east monsoon and winter. Timing and abundance vary between years and wetlands.

species_description.text: Small ground-roosting nightjar (about 21–23 cm) with long pointed wings, large dark eyes, a wide gape and cryptic sandy-brown, grey and black mottling. Males show conspicuous white patches in the wings and outer tail; females lack the strong white markings. Favours dry open country, scrub, grassland, sparse woodland, cultivation and sandy or stony ground. Feeds on flying insects, especially moths and beetles, caught in low, twisting flight. Lays eggs directly on bare ground.

male_female_identification.text: Male has prominent white patches on the wings and white outer tail feathers; female has buff or rufous spots in place of the male's white patches. This is a useful field distinction in flight.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are downy and cryptically mottled, resembling the ground. Young birds develop adult-like patterning but may have softer, buff-edged feathers; exact ageing away from the nest is difficult.

field_spotting_tips.text: At night, scan roads and open tracks with care for a bird sitting motionless on the ground. In flight, the male's white wing and tail patches are diagnostic; the species is smaller and more compact than Jerdon's Nightjar.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open dry-zone habitats and scrubby country across Sri Lanka, including coastal plains, dry grassland and agricultural landscapes. Often found resting on roads or bare ground after dark.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Breeding timing should be checked against local nest records; eggs are laid on bare ground without a constructed nest.

species_description.text: Medium-sized nightjar (about 26 cm) with long wings, a broad gape, cryptic brown, grey and rufous plumage and a distinctive rufous collar across the hindneck. Males show white wing patches and white outer tail tips; females have buff or rufous markings instead. Occupies open woodland, scrub, cultivation, plantations and forest edges. Feeds on moths, beetles and other flying insects, often hawking from the ground or a low perch. Eggs are laid directly on bare ground.

male_female_identification.text: Male has obvious white patches on the wings and white in the tail; female lacks these white marks and shows buff/rufous spots. The rufous hindneck collar and larger size help distinguish it from Indian Nightjar.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are downy and mottled, with softer, buff-edged feathers. They resemble females more than adult males; wing and tail markings become more defined with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the larger size, rufous hindneck collar and barred tail. It often calls from a perch or tree, while Indian Nightjar is more frequently encountered sitting on open roads and bare ground.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka in open woodland, scrub, plantations and cultivation, including both dry-zone and intermediate landscapes. Often roosts on the ground or low bushes and can be difficult to flush.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. A Sri Lankan breeding period of approximately February–May is reported in regional field literature; treat as a documented seasonal window rather than an absolute annual rule.

species_description.text: Medium-sized forest nightjar (about 28–32 cm) with long pointed wings, long tail and cryptic grey, brown and black mottling. Males have white patches on the wings and tail; females show buff or rufous markings instead. Associated with forest clearings, open woodland, scrub and plantations, often in hill and foothill landscapes. Hunts moths, beetles and other flying insects at dusk and at night. Eggs are laid directly on leaf litter or bare ground.

male_female_identification.text: Male shows conspicuous white wing and tail patches; female has buff or rufous spots instead. Sexing is most reliable when the bird is seen in flight or with the tail spread.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are downy and cryptically mottled, with softer, buff-edged plumage. Young birds resemble females and acquire stronger adult patterning as they mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its characteristic repetitive calls at dusk in wooded country. Larger size, longer tail and forest-edge habitat help separate it from Indian Nightjar; compare white wing/tail patches to sex the bird.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, particularly in wooded hills, forest edges, plantations and open forest clearings. The name Jungle Nightjar refers to its woodland association, but it may use open clearings and scrub.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Breeding chronology for Sri Lanka requires further direct local confirmation; do not infer months from Indian populations without a local record.

species_description.text: Small endemic swallow (about 13–14 cm) with dark blue upperparts, chestnut/rufous forehead and throat, warm buff to rufous underparts and a moderately forked tail. Often associated with open country, cliffs, rocky slopes, plantations and human settlements. Feeds on flying insects and builds a mud nest under overhangs, bridges, buildings or rock ledges.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar. Males may have slightly longer tail streamers and richer colour, but differences are subtle and unreliable for field sexing.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with shorter tail streamers, less vivid chestnut on the head/throat and buffy feather edges. Young birds may be seen near nesting sites.

field_spotting_tips.text: Check the warm rufous underparts and head against dark blue upperparts. Often flies around buildings, bridges and open slopes; distinguish from migrant Barn Swallow by its smaller size, shorter tail and warmer underparts.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka. Occurs in open country and around human settlements across much of the island, including dry-zone and hill-country areas; often seen around bridges, buildings and rocky outcrops.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding may occur in more than one period depending on rainfall and nest-site conditions; verify exact months from local nest records.

species_description.text: A large endemic coucal (up to about 45 cm), with dark glossy purple-green head/body, rich chestnut to reddish-brown wings and a pale green bill (reported to become ivory/paler in breeding condition). It inhabits dense lowland wet-zone forest, tangled undergrowth and cane/bramble thickets, and is notably secretive. Feeds on small animals including lizards, beetles, butterflies, spiders, snails and grasshoppers. Builds a domed nest of twigs, roots and grasses, usually low in dense vegetation.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage. Both have the greenish bill and chestnut wings; males are reported to call more frequently, but voice alone is not a dependable sexing method.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Fledged young have been reported with a slate-grey iris; immature plumage is less glossy than adult and may have less saturated colours. Ageing details in field sources are limited, so avoid over-specific claims.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often heard before seen. Listen at dawn and dusk for its deep, booming, usually short two- or three-syllable call. Search dense undergrowth and cane brakes, especially after rain when birds may emerge to dry. Chestnut wings and pale green bill separate it from the common Greater Coucal.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Sri Lankan endemic with a restricted range in the wet zone, generally below about 800 m, in remaining lowland rainforest and dense secondary growth. Key areas include Sinharaja and the Kitulgala forest landscape; habitat quality and disturbance strongly influence occurrence.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident, but difficult to observe. Breeding is believed to occur mainly January–July; published details are limited and should be treated as approximate.

species_description.text: A large, heavy-bodied, long-tailed coucal (about 48–52 cm), with glossy black head, neck and underparts, chestnut/rufous wings and dark graduated tail. Common in scrub, grassland, paddy margins, gardens, plantations, forest edges, reedbeds and mangroves. A broad opportunistic feeder: insects, caterpillars, snails, frogs, lizards, snakes, small mammals, eggs, nestlings and some fruit/seeds. Builds a bulky domed nest in dense vegetation; unlike brood-parasitic cuckoos, it raises its own young.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar in plumage; females may be slightly larger, but this is not a reliable field distinction. Use size only with caution and do not sex single birds by appearance alone.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally browner/duller, with less glossy black plumage and may show pale barring or streaking, especially on the head and underparts. Plumage becomes darker and glossier with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for the deep, resonant 'coop-coop-coop' call, often at dawn. Look along roadsides, paddy bunds and scrub edges; it walks deliberately on the ground and may sun itself with wings spread. Chestnut wings and glossy black body are diagnostic.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident across Sri Lanka in both wet and dry zones, including home gardens, scrublands, paddy fields, plantations, wetlands and forest edges. Commonly encountered in rural landscapes and many protected areas.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding may occur over an extended period in Sri Lanka, with local peaks varying with rainfall and food availability; some local accounts report February–September and again October–December.

species_description.text: A striking black-and-white kingfisher, about 25 cm, with a white head and underparts, black eye-stripe and dark double breast-band in males, and strongly barred black-and-white upperparts. It frequently hovers over open water before plunging for fish, and is also seen perched on wires, posts and branches. Favours tanks, lagoons, marshes, rivers, estuaries and coastal wetlands. Feeds mainly on fish and other aquatic animals.

male_female_identification.text: Male has two dark breast bands, while female has one broad dark breast band that is often broken or incomplete across the centre. This is a useful field distinction in good views.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less crisp black-and-white barring and a less distinct breast band. The bill and facial markings may appear less sharply defined.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often hovers almost stationary above water before diving. Look for the bold black-and-white pattern and breast band; sex can be determined by the number and continuity of breast bands. Its hovering hunting style is highly distinctive.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's lowland wetlands, especially tanks, lagoons, marshes, mangroves and slow-flowing rivers. Common in many coastal areas and dry-zone water bodies; recorded at Yala and numerous tanks and lagoons.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan field records report breeding mainly March–May, with nesting tunnels excavated in riverbanks or other earthen banks.
