species_description.text: A tiny, compact forest kingfisher, around 13–14 cm, with a blackish crown and back, bright turquoise-blue markings, orange-rufous underparts and a short red bill. It is usually secretive, keeping low in dense vegetation beside shaded forest streams, pools and creeks. Feeds on small fish, aquatic insects and other small invertebrates, making short sallies from low perches. Nests in a tunnel excavated in an earth bank, often close to a stream.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar and are not reliably separable in ordinary field views. Subtle differences in colour or bill may occur, but should not be used without close examination.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds are generally duller, with less saturated blue and orange, and a shorter-looking bill. Reliable ageing often requires close photographs or direct comparison with adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search slowly along shaded, clean forest streams, watching low branches and streamside roots. Its tiny size, orange underparts and vivid blue-black upperparts are key. Pause frequently and listen for its high-pitched calls; avoid disturbing streamside nest banks.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's wet-zone forest streams and adjoining mature forest. CBC records include Boralugoda, Puwakpitiya/Avissawella and Bodhinagala; also sought in suitable lowland rainforest and foothill stream habitats.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. It is elusive and can be difficult to detect outside breeding or territorial activity. No robust Sri Lanka-wide breeding-month window was confirmed in this research batch.

species_description.text: Compact, ground-feeding forest dove (about 23–28 cm) with brilliant emerald-green wings and back, maroon/purple-brown body, grey crown and distinctive orange-red bill and legs. Male has a white forehead patch; female lacks the white patch and is generally duller with a greyish face. Uses forest, dense woodland, plantations and shaded gardens, feeding on fallen seeds and fruit on the ground.

male_female_identification.text: Male shows a conspicuous white forehead patch and brighter plumage; female lacks the white forehead patch and has a greyer, more subdued face. Both have green wings and red legs.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less brilliant green wing coverts and no clear adult male forehead patch. Adult colours intensify as feathers mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often detected when it walks quietly on the forest floor or flies up with a flash of green and chestnut. Scan shaded tracks and fruiting/seed-rich ground; the male's white forehead patch is useful for sexing.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident across Sri Lanka in wet, intermediate and dry-zone wooded habitats, including forest undergrowth, plantations and shaded gardens. Occurs in many protected areas and forest reserves.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding may occur in more than one period depending on rainfall and local conditions; nesting dates vary regionally.

species_description.text: Small, compact plover (about 17–19 cm) with brown upperparts, white underparts, white collar and a dark breast-band. Non-breeding birds have a duller brown breast-band and facial markings; breeding adults show a black forehead, eye-stripe and breast-band, orange legs and an orange bill base with black tip. Feeds on small insects, worms, crustaceans and other invertebrates on mudflats and sandy shores.

male_female_identification.text: Male in breeding plumage usually has a broader, darker breast-band and more extensive black on the face; female tends to show browner, less extensive black. In non-breeding plumage, sexes are difficult to separate.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have buff-edged, scaly upperparts, a less complete breast-band and duller facial markings. Young birds can be confused with other small ringed plovers.

field_spotting_tips.text: Check the complete dark breast-band, orange bill base and orange legs. Distinguish from Little Ringed Plover by the orange bill base and usually more obvious orange legs; compare leg colour and facial pattern carefully in poor light.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Uncommon migrant on coastal mudflats, beaches, lagoons and saltpans, particularly north-western and southern shorelines including Mannar, Puttalam and Bundala. Occurrence is local and can vary between years.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly a winter visitor, broadly Aug–Mar, with many records during Oct–Feb. CBC 2022 lists it as M.

species_description.text: කුඩා-මධ්‍යම ප්‍රමාණයේ marsh tern එකකි (සෙ.මී. 23–27). අභිජනන සමයේ හිස කළු, යටපස අළු/කළු; ශීත පිහාටුවල හිස සුදු සහ කණ අසල අඳුරු ලපයක් ඇත. කලපු, වැව්, වගුරු හා විවෘත ජල තීරුවල කෘමීන්, කුඩා මසුන්/උභයජීවීන් අල්ලයි. ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ අභ්‍යන්තර තෙත්බිම්වල බහුලව පෙනේ.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි හා ගැහැනු පෙනුමෙන් සමානයි; අභිජනන සමයේ දෙපාර්ශ්වයටම කළු හිස හා අඳුරු යටපස ලක්ෂණ ඇත.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile හි ඉහළපස දුඹුරු පැහැති කොරපොතු රටා සහ හිස/පපුවේ අසම්පූර්ණ අඳුරු ලකුණු ඇත; ශීත adult සමඟ වෙන්කරන විට පිටේ රටාව බලන්න.

field_spotting_tips.text: ජල මතුපිටට පහතින් පියාසර කර කෘමීන් අල්ලන හැසිරීම බලන්න. අභිජනන සමයේ කළු හිස/යටපස, non-breeding හි සුදු හිස සහ කණ ලපය හඳුනාගැනීමට උපකාරී.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: දිවයිනේ පහළබිම් තෙත්බිම්, වැව් හා කලපු පුරා; Tissa, Bundala, Udawalawe, Anuradhapura tanks සහ වෙනත් විශාල ජලාශ. සමහර අවස්ථාවල කඳුකර ජලාශවලද වාර්තා.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022 අනුව M; නමුත් Limosa/eBird වැනි සමුච්චිත වාර්තාවල වසර පුරා දත්ත පෙනිය හැක. අභිජනන/දේශීය ගමන් සහ වාර්තා සලකා නිශ්චිත seasonal classification තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: කුඩා-මධ්‍යම marsh tern එකකි (සෙ.මී. 23–27). අභිජනන පිහාටුවල හිස හා යටපස කළු, ශරීරය අළු සහ පියාපත්වල සුදු පැහැති ඉදිරි/පසු අග පැහැදිලි වේ; ශීත පිහාටුවල හිස සුදු සහ කණ අසල කළු ලපයක් ඇත. වැව්, වගුරු, කලපු හා වෙරළබඩ ජලයේ කෘමීන් සහ කුඩා මසුන් අල්ලයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි හා ගැහැනු බාහිරව සමානයි; ලිංගය ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ වෙන්කිරීම සාමාන්‍යයෙන් නොහැක.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile හි පිට හා පියාපත්වල දුඹුරු/කළු කොරපොතු රටා, හිසෙහි අසම්පූර්ණ අඳුරු ලප සහ අළු යටපස ඇත. Whiskered Tern සමඟ වෙන්කරන විට පියාපත් රටා සහ වලිගය බලන්න.

field_spotting_tips.text: Whiskered Tern සමඟ සසඳන විට පියාපත්වල සුදු පැහැති ඉදිරි/පසු කොටස් සහ වලිග හැඩය බලන්න. breeding plumage හි සුදු පියාපත් අග වඩාත් පැහැදිලිය.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් passage/winter visitor ලෙස wetlands: Bundala saltpans, Tissa, Yala, Anuradhapura වැව් සහ වෙනත් විශාල ජලාශ. දකුණු/වයඹ තෙත්බිම්වල වාර්තා ඇත.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022 අනුව M. ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ වාර්තා බොහෝවිට සංක්‍රමණ සමය හා ශීත කාලය තුළ; Limosa dataset හි ජනවාරි–මැයි සහ අගෝස්තු–දෙසැම්බර් වාර්තා ඇත.

species_description.text: Green leafbird about 17–19 cm, with black face/throat mask, bright yellow-orange forehead and blue moustachial markings. Brush-tipped tongue for nectar; eats fruit, nectar and insects in forest, wooded gardens and plantations.

male_female_identification.text: Male has more extensive black face/throat mask and brighter golden-orange forehead. Female is greener on face/throat with less extensive black; variation among subspecies.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles greener and duller, with reduced black mask and less bright forehead; adult facial pattern develops progressively.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for varied melodious song; scan canopy and flowering trees. Often joins mixed flocks. Compare blue moustachial stripe and face pattern with Jerdon's Leafbird.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's wooded lowlands and foothills, especially dry/intermediate-zone forest, gardens and plantations.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding window not reliably established; do not transfer mainland dates without local evidence.

species_description.text: Green leafbird about 17–18 cm, with black face/throat, blue moustachial stripe and yellow-orange forehead; female greener and less strongly marked. Inhabits woodland, forest edges, plantations and gardens; eats insects, spiders, fruit and nectar, often high in canopy and may imitate other birds.

male_female_identification.text: Male has strong black face/throat mask and blue moustachial stripe; female has greener face/throat, less black and duller facial colours.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles greener and duller, with incomplete/absent black mask and less developed blue moustachial stripe.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for green canopy bird with black face and blue moustache; listen for rich song and mimicry. Compare facial mask with Golden-fronted Leafbird.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's wooded lowlands and foothills, especially dry/intermediate woodland, forest edges and plantations; local rather than abundant.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. No reliable Sri Lankan breeding-month source located in this batch; leave local timing unassigned.

species_description.text: Medium-sized gull (about 42–46 cm), with pale grey mantle, white body, red bill and legs. Breeding adults have a rich chocolate-brown hood; non-breeding adults show a white head with dark ear-spot. Feeds on fish, insects, crustaceans and other small aquatic prey; frequents coastal lagoons, estuaries, mudflats and large inland wetlands. Breeds on inland lakes in central Asia.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in plumage; male is slightly larger on average. Seasonal hood is a breeding-plumage feature, not a sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show brownish mottling on the upperparts and dark markings on the tail/wing; first-winter birds become greyer but retain some brown. Non-breeding adults have a white head and dark ear spot.

field_spotting_tips.text: Medium-sized gull with red bill/legs; in winter identify the dark ear-spot on white head, pale grey mantle and red legs. Breeding hood is chocolate-brown, not black; compare with Black-headed Gull.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter visitor to Sri Lanka, often on coastal lagoons, estuaries, saltpans and mudflats. Bundala and other large southern/eastern coastal wetlands are productive; north-western coast also worth checking.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Limosa records Jan–May, Jul–Aug and Oct–Dec; core Sri Lankan occurrence is during the northern winter, with records varying by year. Monthly database presence should not be read as proof of equal abundance each month.

species_description.text: A large, conspicuous woodpecker, around 29–31 cm, with a black-and-white patterned body, white nape and pale underparts; the wings and back are boldly marked, and the bill is long and strong. It favours dry scrub, open woodland, thorn forest and scattered trees in the dry zone. Feeds on ants, termites and beetle larvae, probing and hammering on trunks and branches. Nests in a cavity excavated in a tree.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a red crown; female has a black-and-white crown without the red. The white nape and bold black-and-white pattern are shared by both sexes.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and less sharply patterned, with a less distinct crown and nape. The red crown develops in young males as they mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the bold black-and-white plumage and white nape in dry scrub and open woodland. It is much less frequently encountered than the common flamebacks. Male's red crown separates it from the female.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident, mainly in the dry zone and arid lowlands, particularly northern and south-eastern Sri Lanka. Records include Anuradhapura, Wilpattu, Yala, Bundala and other dry scrub/woodland sites; uncommon and local.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Specific breeding months in Sri Lanka were not sufficiently verified in this batch; nesting occurs in tree cavities.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): resident (R) for all non-endemic woodpeckers; endemic (E) for Crimson-backed Flameback. Red-backed Flameback Dinopium psarodes is now treated as a separate endemic species; taxonomy differs from older CBC treatment. Confirm latest CBC row mapping before publication.

species_description.text: A large endemic flameback, about 29–32 cm, with a crimson-red back, golden-yellow crown and crest, black-and-white patterned face and underparts, and a long, stiff tail used for support while climbing. The Sri Lankan species is strongly associated with mature forest and wooded landscapes, where it forages on trunks and large branches for ants, termites and beetle larvae. Nests in a cavity excavated in a tree.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a red crown/crest; female has a black crown with white spotting, while both sexes have the crimson back. The colour of the crown is the clearest sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less intense red on the back and less sharply defined head pattern. Young males gradually acquire the red crown; young females retain a dark, spotted crown.

field_spotting_tips.text: Largest of Sri Lanka's woodpeckers. The crimson back and golden crest are striking; listen for loud calls and drumming in mature forest. In flight, look for the large size and contrasting pale underparts. Do not confuse with the smaller Red-backed Flameback.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident in Sri Lanka, widespread but local in forested lowlands and hills. Notable sites include Sinharaja, Horton Plains, Yala, Wilpattu and other mature forest blocks; occurs from lowlands to montane forest.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding and nest records occur in the first half of the year in some local accounts, but a robust national month range was not established in this research batch.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): resident (R) for all non-endemic woodpeckers; endemic (E) for Crimson-backed Flameback. Red-backed Flameback Dinopium psarodes is now treated as a separate endemic species; taxonomy differs from older CBC treatment. Confirm latest CBC row mapping before publication.

species_description.text: Small, long-tailed grassland babbler about 18 cm, with warm rufous-brown upperparts, cinnamon wings, pale underparts, a conspicuous yellow orbital ring and a short pale eyebrow. Feeds on insects, spiders, berries and nectar, clambering through tall grass, reeds and thorny scrub.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; no reliable external field distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less conspicuous yellow eye-ring and less contrasting facial markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the bright yellow eye-ring and long graduated tail. It skulks in tall grass but sometimes climbs to exposed reed tops to call. Do not confuse the yellow eye-ring with the pale eyebrow of other babblers.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in dry and intermediate zone grassland, scrub, reedbeds, paddy margins and open thorny vegetation across Sri Lanka. The Sri Lankan subspecies is Chrysomma sinense nasale, endemic to the island; the species is not endemic.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding has been reported mainly November–July, with a peak around February–May. Often in pairs or small groups outside the breeding season.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Sri Lanka Scimitar-babbler E; Yellow-eyed Babbler R; Tawny-bellied Babbler R; Dark-fronted Babbler R; Sri Lanka Orange-billed Babbler E; Sri Lanka Ashy-headed Laughing-thrush E; Yellow-billed Babbler R; Sri Lanka Brown-capped Babbler E. Several resident species have endemic Sri Lankan subspecies only.

species_description.text: Large dark stork with glossy black body, contrasting white woolly-looking neck and lower belly, long red legs and heavy black bill. Forages in wetlands, flooded fields and forest-edge pools, taking fish, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes very similar; males average larger. White neck and dark body are main field marks.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds browner and less glossy, with less sharply contrasting neck and bill; adult pattern develops progressively.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search quiet wetland edges and flooded fields, especially early morning. Often solitary; distinguish from Black-necked Stork by white neck and lack of extensive white wing panels.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident but generally uncommon and local. Quiet tanks, marshes, paddy fields and forest-edge wetlands in dry/intermediate zones; records include Yala, Kumana and north-central dry zone.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident; encounters sporadic and depend on suitable feeding habitat.

species_description.text: Small sunbird about 10 cm. Breeding male appears glossy metallic purple-blue to blackish depending on light, with dark throat and breast and greyish-brown lower belly; female is olive-brown above with yellowish underparts and a faint pale supercilium. Feeds on nectar and small insects, often perching at flower bases.

male_female_identification.text: Male's metallic purple-blue plumage can look almost black in shade; female is olive above and yellowish below with a faint eyebrow. Male is generally darker below than Purple-rumped Sunbird.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Non-breeding or eclipse males lose much of the iridescent breeding plumage and can resemble females; juveniles are dull olive-brown with yellowish underparts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Use direct sunlight to reveal the male's purple iridescence; in shade it may appear black. Usually perches to feed rather than hovering frequently. Check for the lack of Purple-rumped Sunbird's bright yellow belly and purple rump.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident, mainly in dry-zone Sri Lanka, in open country, scrub, gardens and flowering trees. Occurs in lowlands and around settlements.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Breeding in Sri Lanka mainly January–June, before the monsoon; local nesting may vary with rainfall and food availability.

species_description.text: Medium-sized sunbird about 13 cm, with a relatively long, curved bill. Adult male is glossy purple-blue with a maroon breast band and grey-brown belly; small yellow/crimson pectoral tufts may show in display. Female is grey-olive above and yellowish below, without the male's iridescence.

male_female_identification.text: Male glossy purple with maroon breast band, grey-brown belly and long bill; female plain grey-olive above and yellowish below. Loten's is longer-billed than Purple Sunbird; male has a maroon band.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young males resemble females until iridescent plumage and breast band develop; juveniles are duller olive-brown with pale yellowish underparts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Compare with Purple Sunbird: Loten's has a longer bill, male maroon breast band and brownish wings. It often hovers at flowers more than Purple Sunbird.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, particularly dry and intermediate zone gardens, scrub, open woodland and flowering trees. Species also occurs in peninsular India.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Sri Lankan breeding reported February–May. Nest is a hanging pouch, sometimes built close to or within social spider webs.

species_description.text: Large harrier (about 48–56 cm) with long wings and tail, flying low over marshes and open grassland. Adult male is pale grey with black wing tips; female and juveniles are brown with streaked underparts and a pale head with dark facial markings. Hunts small mammals, birds, frogs and reptiles by quartering low over reedbeds, paddy fields and grasslands. Nests on the ground in dense wetland vegetation in its breeding range outside Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Strong sexual dimorphism: adult male is grey above with pale underparts and black wing tips; adult female is larger and brown with streaked underparts and a pale facial disc. Adult males and females are readily distinguishable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble females but are often richer rufous-brown below with less streaking; first-year plumage can be difficult to distinguish from adult female.

field_spotting_tips.text: Identify by low quartering flight over open ground, long wings held in a shallow V, and white rump. Adult male is unmistakably pale grey; female/juvenile are brown with a pale facial disc.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter visitor to Sri Lanka, mainly in open lowland wetlands, grasslands and paddy landscapes. Look around Bundala, Mannar, Vankalai, Hambantota, Udawalawe and other open-country sites.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Migrant (CBC 2022 M), mainly during the northern winter, broadly September/October to March/April. Individual records outside the main season should be assessed carefully.

species_description.text: Slender, long-winged harrier (about 40–48 cm) with a long tail and graceful buoyant flight. Adult male is grey above with black wing tips and black streaking on the breast; female is brown above and streaked below, with a pale head and dark facial markings. Hunts small birds, mammals, reptiles and large insects over open grassland, marshes and cultivated fields. Breeds on the ground in open habitats in its northern breeding range.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes differ strongly. Adult male is grey with black wing tips and a streaked breast; female is brown and streaked, with a pale facial disc. Male is slimmer and often appears more contrasting.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown, often with rich buff/rufous underparts and less distinct streaking than adult females; immature males gradually acquire grey plumage.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a slim harrier quartering low over grassland with wings held in a shallow V. Adult male's grey body and black wing tips separate it from female/juvenile brown plumage; compare with Western Marsh-harrier, which is larger and heavier.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter visitor, usually in open country, dry grassland, paddy fields and wetland margins. Records from Bundala, Mannar/Vankalai, Hambantota and other open lowland landscapes; can be scarce and easily overlooked.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Migrant (CBC 2022 M), generally present during the northern winter, approximately October–March/April. Exact arrival and departure vary by year.

species_description.text: Tiny grassland warbler, around 10–11 cm, with brown upperparts, streaked back, short rounded wings, long graduated tail and pale underparts. In breeding plumage the bill becomes darker and the tail may appear shorter; the bird often performs a bouncing display flight over grass. Eats small insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; males are more vocal and perform the conspicuous display flight, but plumage alone is not a dependable sexing character.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and more heavily streaked, with less distinct facial markings and a shorter tail.

field_spotting_tips.text: The repeated 'zit-zit-zit' call and bouncing, zig-zag display flight are characteristic. Look for a small brown bird with a rufous rump and white-tipped tail in open grass.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open grassland, paddy fields, marshy edges and rank vegetation across Sri Lanka, especially the dry and intermediate zones. Often overlooked until it rises in display.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is associated with the monsoon/rainy periods; nest is a woven, elongated or purse-like structure attached to grass stems.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022/local checklist convention: all six species resident (R). Grey-breasted Prinia's Sri Lankan subspecies pectoralis is endemic; species is not endemic.

species_description.text: A medium-sized, crested cuckoo (about 33–34 cm) with a dark glossy head and upperparts, chestnut/rufous wings, pale underparts with dark barring, and a long graduated tail with pale tips. Occurs mainly as a migrant in Sri Lanka; uses wooded country, forest edges, plantations and gardens. Feeds chiefly on large insects and caterpillars. A brood parasite: lays eggs in nests of other birds rather than building its own nest.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in overall pattern. Both show the dark head, chestnut wings and barred underparts; sex is not reliably determined from ordinary field views.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner than adults, with less glossy upperparts and less strongly defined chestnut wing colour; details vary with age and feather wear. Use a combination of crest, wing colour and underpart barring rather than one feature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Scan tree canopies and edges for a dark, crested cuckoo with conspicuous chestnut wings. It may sit quietly and be overlooked; listen for calls and check mixed woodland, gardens and plantations during the migrant season.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Primarily a migrant visitor to Sri Lanka. Recorded in wooded habitats, forest edges, gardens and plantations across several regions; sightings are scattered and seasonal rather than concentrated at one guaranteed site.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly recorded during the northern winter migration period; local arrival and departure dates vary between years. Treat it as a migrant, not a resident breeder in Sri Lanka.

species_description.text: A medium-sized, slim, crested cuckoo (about 33 cm) with a black-and-white pattern: black upperparts and breast, white belly, white wing patch and a long tail with white tips. A pale morph occurs in parts of its range, but the Sri Lankan birds are typically the dark-and-white form. Uses open woodland, scrub, cultivation, grassland edges and gardens. Eats mainly insects, especially caterpillars and other large arthropods. It is a brood parasite, laying eggs in the nests of other birds.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and are not reliably separable in the field. The black-and-white pattern, crest and white wing patch are shared by both.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds are generally browner and less sharply contrasting than adults, with less crisp black-and-white patterning; the white wing patch and tail markings may be less distinct. Ageing is best done from a clear photograph.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its repeated, ringing calls, especially in open country. Look on exposed branches, wires and the edges of scrub or cultivation; the strong black-and-white pattern and crest are useful at a distance.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, with records from dry and intermediate zones and open wooded country; also seen in scrub, agricultural landscapes and around protected areas such as Udawalawe and Bundala. Occurrence is local and can be overlooked outside calling periods.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident according to the CBC country list. Calling and breeding activity can be seasonal and influenced by rainfall; do not treat the monsoon association reported elsewhere as a fixed Sri Lankan migration pattern.

species_description.text: Medium-sized pigeon (about 30–35 cm), highly variable in colour. Typical wild-type birds are blue-grey with two dark wing bars, iridescent green-purple neck, pale rump and dark tail band; urban populations include many domestic-derived colour forms. Uses cliffs, rocky outcrops and buildings, especially towns and agricultural areas. Eats seeds, grains and scraps. Nests on ledges, roofs and other sheltered structures; both sexes incubate and feed young with crop milk.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes look alike in the field. Males may be slightly larger and show stronger neck iridescence, but these are unreliable clues; plumage morphs overlap.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less iridescent neck feathers and often a darker iris; cere and eye colour develop with age. Domestic-derived birds show extensive variation.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the two dark wing bars and pale rump in wild-type birds. At urban sites expect colour variation; distinguish from other pigeons by the stocky build, small head and rapid direct flight.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident, particularly in towns, cities, ports, agricultural settlements and around buildings throughout Sri Lanka. Feral and domestic populations make it widespread in human-modified landscapes.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding can occur in multiple months, with timing influenced by food and nesting-site availability.

species_description.text: Large, powerful endemic forest pigeon (about 40 cm) with a grey head and breast, maroon to purplish mantle, dark wings, pale grey belly and a distinctive chequered black-and-white nape patch. Inhabits mature wet-zone and montane forests, feeding mainly on fruits and berries, especially canopy fruit. Usually arboreal and often seen singly or in pairs.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage and not reliably separable in the field. Both show the diagnostic chequered nape and maroon mantle.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immatures are duller, with less distinct nape chequering and less saturated maroon tones; the adult head and neck pattern develops with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its deep, resonant cooing in montane forest. Scan fruiting canopy trees and forest edges; the chequered nape patch and maroon mantle are diagnostic when seen well.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka, mainly in the central hills and wet-zone forests. Key landscapes include Horton Plains, Hakgala, Peak Wilderness, Knuckles and suitable forest patches around Nuwara Eliya and the highlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Breeding records are scattered; reported nesting periods vary by locality, so a single island-wide season should not be assumed.

species_description.text: Small, long-legged robin about 16–17 cm. Male is glossy black or dark slate with a white shoulder patch and chestnut undertail coverts; female is dark grey-brown above, grey below and lacks the white shoulder patch. Both sexes often hold the long tail upright. Feeds mainly on insects, also small frogs and lizards.

male_female_identification.text: Strong sexual dimorphism. Male glossy black with white shoulder patch and chestnut vent; female brown-grey with no white shoulder patch and paler chestnut vent. Sri Lankan southern birds are black-backed.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and mottled/scaled, resembling females but with more obvious pale feather edges; young males develop the black plumage and white shoulder patch gradually.

field_spotting_tips.text: Recognise it by its upright tail, long legs and chestnut undertail coverts. Male's white shoulder patch is conspicuous; female is brown-grey. It runs on the ground and perches on rocks or low thorny shrubs, unlike the more upright, white-bellied magpie-robin.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open dry country, stony scrub, grassland, rocky slopes, cultivated land and around settlements. Widespread in Sri Lanka's dry zone, with scattered populations in wet lowlands and urban open spaces; absent from dense high-elevation forest.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding study at Mihintale recorded two seasons, March–June and July–September. Nests in rock crevices, wall holes, tree hollows and other cavities.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Pied Bushchat R (Sri Lankan hill subspecies atratus endemic); Sri Lanka Shama E; Oriental Magpie-robin R; Indian Robin R; Indian Blue Robin M.

Taxonomy updated to Copsychus fulicatus; older literature Saxicoloides fulicatus.

species_description.text: Medium-sized forest robin about 19–21 cm. Male has glossy blue-black head, back, throat and breast, rich chestnut belly and long graduated tail; female is dark brown above with warmer rufous-brown underparts and a shorter, less glossy tail. Feeds mainly on insects and other invertebrates, often near the forest floor.

male_female_identification.text: Male glossy blue-black above and on throat/breast with chestnut belly; female brown above and rufous-brown below. Both sexes have long tails, but male is typically glossier and more contrasting.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and heavily scaled or spotted, with pale buff feather edges and less distinct adult colour separation. Young males gradually darken.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its rich, varied song in shaded forest and gardens. The male's deep blue-black gloss and chestnut belly distinguish it from Oriental Magpie-robin; female is darker and more rufous than a female magpie-robin. Often forages low or on the ground.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka. Occurs in forests, dense wooded gardens and plantations across wet and intermediate zones, from lowlands to hills. More often encountered in forested areas than the common Oriental Magpie-robin.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding records span a broad period; local observations indicate nests in the first half of the year, but a reliable island-wide month range needs further CBC confirmation.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Pied Bushchat R (Sri Lankan hill subspecies atratus endemic); Sri Lanka Shama E; Oriental Magpie-robin R; Indian Robin R; Indian Blue Robin M.

species_description.text: Common medium-sized robin about 19 cm. Male is glossy black with white shoulder/wing patches, white belly and long tail; female is grey-brown above with pale grey underparts and a white belly. Both sexes have a long tail and slender dark bill. Feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, also taking fruit and scraps.

male_female_identification.text: Male black and white with bold contrast; female grey-brown above and greyish-white below. In some subspecies males have different amounts of white on the wing; Sri Lankan birds are generally nominate C. s. saularis.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and heavily scaled or spotted, with pale buff feather edges; they gradually acquire adult male or female plumage.

field_spotting_tips.text: Male sings loudly from a high exposed perch, often before sunrise and at dusk. Look for white wing patches and long tail; female is grey-brown, unlike the dark brown female Sri Lanka Shama. Ground-feeding birds often flick their tails.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Very common resident across all zones in gardens, cultivation, villages, scrub and open woodland, avoiding deep forest. Often close to human habitation and uses rooftops, walls and lamp posts as song perches.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding mainly March–September, with male territorial singing often extending for many months. Nests in tree holes, walls and cavities, including nest boxes.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Pied Bushchat R (Sri Lankan hill subspecies atratus endemic); Sri Lanka Shama E; Oriental Magpie-robin R; Indian Robin R; Indian Blue Robin M.

species_description.text: A medium-sized, stocky roller, about 26–27 cm long, with a large head, strong bill and vivid blue, turquoise and violet-blue plumage. The crown, face and underparts are brownish with lilac-blue tones; the wings show brilliant blue and deep purplish flight feathers, especially obvious in flight. Favours open dry lowlands, scrub, grassland, cultivation, chena fields, coconut plantations and scattered trees. Often hunts from wires or exposed branches, dropping to catch grasshoppers, beetles, lizards and other small prey. Nests in tree holes, often in dead or decaying trunks.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are very similar in plumage and are difficult to distinguish reliably in the field. Courtship displays include rolling, tumbling and aerobatic flight; display behaviour should not be used as a definitive sex marker without context.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller, with less saturated blue and softer brownish plumage; the adult's vivid blue wing and tail colours become stronger with maturity. Reliable ageing requires close views.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often conspicuous on roadside wires, fence posts and isolated trees. Watch for the spectacular blue wing panels during display or when it flies between perches. Its stocky shape and bright blue wings distinguish it from bee-eaters.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, most frequent in dry lowlands and open country, and less common/local in wet lowlands. Look around chena cultivation, coconut plantations, grassland and roadsides in the dry and intermediate zones.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan accounts report breeding mainly January–June. The species is non-migratory globally, although local seasonal movements may occur.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022); status codes retained as published, including mixed resident/migrant status.

species_description.text: Large, rather long-bodied grey cuckooshrike, around 25–30 cm, with a strong hooked-looking bill, dark wings and tail, and pale underparts. Usually solitary or in pairs, moving deliberately through the middle and upper canopy of forest and wooded country. Feeds mainly on insects and larvae, often taking prey from foliage or hawking insects in flight.

male_female_identification.text: Male is generally darker slate-grey above with a pale throat and breast. Female is similar but usually shows more distinct dark barring on the underparts; plumage variation and subspecies should be considered.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more heavily scaled or barred than adults, with a less clean grey appearance; plumage gradually becomes adult-like.

field_spotting_tips.text: Scan canopy edges for a large grey bird with dark wings and a deliberate, flycatcher-like movement. It may sit quietly for long periods before making short sallies for insects. Check underparts for female barring.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident but uncommon and local in Sri Lanka, mainly in dry and intermediate-zone woodland and forest, from lowlands to middle elevations. Wet-zone records are relatively scarce; records include Wilpattu and other dry-zone forest blocks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding records include May–June; a shallow cup nest is placed on a branch fork and is made with fine twigs, leaf fibres and lichens bound with spider silk.

species_description.text: Large, robust, all-dark crow, typically 45–50 cm, with heavy bill, shaggy throat feathers and a strong, deep call. Occurs in forest, open woodland, agricultural landscapes, villages and towns, often in pairs or small groups. Omnivorous, taking fruit, seeds, insects, carrion, eggs and small vertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; males are slightly larger on average. Bill and head size vary geographically and are not reliable sex characters.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and less glossy, with a less developed shaggy throat and a somewhat weaker bill profile.

field_spotting_tips.text: Much larger and heavier-billed than House Crow, with no grey neck collar. Listen for deep, harsh caws. Check the shaggy throat and massive bill, especially in profile.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident across Sri Lanka, in both wet and dry zones, including forested hills, plantations, villages and urban areas. Sri Lankan birds are often referred to the subspecies group culminatus; taxonomy within the Large-billed Crow complex varies among checklists.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding generally takes place in the dry season/early part of the year, but precise island-wide dates were not established in this batch. Large stick nest placed high in a tree.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Black-hooded Oriole R; Sri Lanka Blue Magpie E; House Crow R; Large-billed Crow R; Indian Pitta M; Cinereous Tit R. Confirm row-level codes if checklist edition changes.

species_description.text: Medium-sized crow about 40 cm, with black head, throat, wings and tail, contrasting grey neck and breast, and a slender bill. Highly adaptable and closely associated with people, towns, markets, ports, rubbish sites, gardens and agricultural land. Omnivorous and opportunistic, eating scraps, fruit, insects, eggs and small animals.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes look alike; males average slightly larger but cannot be reliably sexed in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner than adults, with less sharply defined grey collar and less glossy black plumage.

field_spotting_tips.text: Grey nape and breast against a black head and body distinguish it from Large-billed Crow, which is much larger and uniformly black. Watch its bold behaviour around food and people.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident throughout Sri Lanka, especially towns and villages; abundant in Colombo and other urban/coastal settlements. It is an introduced/commensal species in some parts of the wider world but native to the Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeds in a wide range of months depending on locality; in Sri Lanka nests are usually placed in trees, with multiple nesting attempts possible where food is abundant.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Black-hooded Oriole R; Sri Lanka Blue Magpie E; House Crow R; Large-billed Crow R; Indian Pitta M; Cinereous Tit R. Confirm row-level codes if checklist edition changes.

species_description.text: A medium-sized, rather plain cuckoo (about 33 cm) with grey upperparts, pale underparts crossed by narrow dark bars, a long barred tail and yellowish eye-ring and legs. It favours wooded country, forest edges, plantations and gardens, usually in the canopy. Feeds mainly on hairy caterpillars and other insects. It is a brood parasite, laying eggs in the nests of other birds.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage. The grey upperparts, finely barred underparts and long barred tail are shared by both sexes.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and may show warmer or rufous tones on the upperparts, with less neat barring than adults. Ageing can be difficult at distance; avoid assigning age from a brief view.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for the familiar repeated 'one more bottle' phrase, often delivered from a concealed canopy perch. Scan tall trees when calling; the long barred tail and plain grey upperparts help distinguish it from more boldly patterned cuckoos.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs in Sri Lanka as a resident and migrant component, with records from wooded habitats in both lowlands and hills. More often detected by its voice than seen; check forest edges, plantations and mature garden trees.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC country list records R/M. Calling and breeding can be seasonal; the species' presence in Sri Lanka is not limited to the winter migrant period.

species_description.text: Tiny, active canary-flycatcher about 11–12 cm, with grey head, bright yellow underparts, olive-green upperparts, short bill and a distinctive white eye-ring. Often moves restlessly through foliage, hovering and making short aerial sallies for insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike or very similar in plumage; no reliable external field distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller olive-brown above and pale yellow below, with less sharply defined grey head and eye-ring.

field_spotting_tips.text: Constantly active, often hovering briefly to glean or catch insects. Grey head, yellow body and white eye-ring make it distinctive. Listen for high thin calls in mixed flocks.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in wooded habitats across Sri Lanka, especially forest edges, montane and submontane forest, plantations, gardens and wooded ravines, often near streams. Some populations elsewhere make altitudinal movements.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident in Sri Lanka. Breeding in the wider range often April–June; Sri Lankan nest dates should be verified separately. Nest is a small cup attached to mossy trunks, rocks or banks.

species_description.text: Medium-sized (about 23–25 cm) dry-country wader with long pale legs, large eyes, short straight bill and sandy-buff upperparts. Has dark-and-white facial markings and dark breast banding; long wings and tail. Inhabits open dry grassland, scrub, sparsely vegetated plains and stony ground. Runs after insects and other small invertebrates. Resident in Sri Lanka; ground-nesting.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in general appearance and are not reliably separable in the field. Any subtle size difference is not a useful field character.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller and more diffusely marked, with less sharply defined facial and breast patterning; young birds may show pale feather edges on the upperparts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often detected by its upright, alert stance and rapid running rather than flight. Scan bare ground and short grass; facial pattern, long pale legs and sandy coloration distinguish it from plovers.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Localised in the dry zone, especially open scrub/grassland and arid plains. Search suitable open country in the north and south-east, including areas around Yala and Bundala landscapes; presence is habitat-dependent and not guaranteed at visitor sites.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident; can be encountered throughout the year. Breeding is associated with the dry-country season and local rainfall conditions; avoid assigning a single fixed island-wide month window.

species_description.text: Small, colourful flycatcher about 11–12 cm. Male has bright blue upperparts, orange throat and breast, and white belly; female is duller olive-brown above with yellowish or buff underparts and a pale eye-ring. Feeds on insects, often making short sallies from low perches.

male_female_identification.text: Male blue above and orange below; female olive-brown above and buff-yellow below. Sri Lankan resident subspecies is jerdoni.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and spotted/scaled with buff edges, resembling female but more mottled; young males gradually gain blue and orange.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a blue-and-orange male near woodland edges or streams. Female is olive-brown and yellowish below. The male's orange breast and blue upperparts distinguish it from Dull-blue Flycatcher, which is greyer and lacks orange.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in dry and intermediate zone woodland, scrub, forest edges, gardens and plantations, usually in lowlands and foothills. Sri Lankan subspecies jerdoni occurs locally; species also occurs widely in India.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding mainly March–June. Nest placed in a tree hole, bank or cavity; clutch commonly 3–5 eggs.

species_description.text: Very small, slender swift (about 13 cm) with long narrow wings, deeply forked tail, brown upperparts and paler underparts. Often associates with palms and other tall trees, where it nests using saliva to attach a tiny nest to the underside of a palm frond. Feeds on small flying insects, usually low to medium height over open areas.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage and cannot normally be separated in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and may show pale fringes to feathers; age is not usually identifiable in distant flying birds.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search around coconut palms and watch for a tiny swift with a narrow, deeply forked tail. Its fluttering, buoyant flight and palm-associated nesting behaviour help distinguish it from other swifts.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's lowlands and warmer open country, especially where coconut palms and other palms are common. Frequently seen around villages, plantations, gardens and coastal areas.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Nesting is linked to palm-frond availability and local weather; breeding months can vary by site.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 45–53 පමණ දිගැති, දිගු ගෙල සහ පාද ඇති තාරාවෙකි. සමස්තය රන්-දුඹුරු/fulvous පැහැති අතර පිට සහ පියාපත් තද පැහැති, පැතිවල සුදු-කළු ඉරි ඇත. විවෘත මිරිදිය වැව්, තෙත් තණබිම්, වගාබිම් සහ shallow marshes භාවිත කරයි. ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් ජලජ ශාක, බීජ සහ ධාන්‍ය; සමහරවිට කුඩා ජලජ සතුන්ද. ගස් කුහර/ඝන වෘක්ෂලතා ආශ්‍රිතව කූඩු තැබිය හැක; ලංකාවේ නිශ්චිත breeding months තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

male_female_identification.text: ලිංග දෙකම බොහෝ දුරට සමාන; පිරිමි සාමාන්‍යයෙන් තරමක් විශාල විය හැකි නමුත් field identification සඳහා විශ්වාසදායක වෙනසක් නැත. Juvenile වඩා අඳුරු/අඩු පැහැදිලි, flank barring අඩු විය හැක.

field_spotting_tips.text: විශාල රංචු ලෙස පෙනෙන අතර පියාඹන විට බොහෝවිට ගෙල දිගු කරයි. whistling හඬ සහ රන්-දුඹුරු ශරීරය බලන්න. Lesser Whistling-duck සමඟ වෙන්කරන විට විශාල ප්‍රමාණය සහ පැතිවල පැහැදිලි සුදු-කළු barring බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: පහළබිම් ජලාශ, විශේෂයෙන් වියළි කලාපයේ විශාල වැව් සහ marshes. Bundala, Tissamaharama, Debarawewa, Minneriya, Udawalawe සහ Wilpattu ආශ්‍රිත තෙත්බිම් වාර්තා.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී ජනගහනයක් සමඟ ශීත ඍතුවේදී උතුරින් පැමිණෙන පක්ෂීන් සංඛ්‍යාව වැඩි වේ (CBC 2022: R+M).

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 40–43 පමණ දිගැති, මධ්‍යම ප්‍රමාණයේ දිගු ගෙලැති තාරාවෙකි. දුඹුරු ශරීරය, chestnut පැහැති හිස/ගෙල, තද පැහැති පියාපත් සහ පියාඹන විට පෙනෙන සුදු පියාපත් ඉරි. වැව්, marshes, තෙත් තණබිම්, වී කුඹුරු සහ ජලජ ශාක බහුල ස්ථාන. ජලජ ශාක, බීජ, ධාන්‍ය සහ කුඩා ජලජ අපෘෂ්ඨවංශීන් ආහාරයට ගනී. ගස්වල හෝ ඝන වෘක්ෂලතා තුළ කූඩු තැබිය හැක; ලංකාවේ breeding season ස්ථානය අනුව තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

male_female_identification.text: ලිංග දෙකම පෙනුමෙන් බොහෝ සමානයි. පිරිමි සාමාන්‍යයෙන් තරමක් විශාල; ඇස්/හිස පැහැයේ සුළු වෙනස්කම් field එකේ විශ්වාසදායක නොවේ. Juvenile වඩා dull brown සහ flank pattern අඩු පැහැදිලි.

field_spotting_tips.text: විශාල රංචු ලෙස ජලය මත පාවෙමින් හෝ වැව් අද්දර විවේක ගනී. පියාඹන විට සුදු wing-bar සහ දිගු ගෙල බලන්න. Fulvous Whistling-duck ට වඩා කුඩා සහ chestnut හිසක් ඇත.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: පහළබිම්වල ඉතා පුළුල් ව්‍යාප්තියක්. Bundala, Tissamaharama, Debarawewa, Minneriya, Sigiriya, Wilpattu සහ Anawilundawa වැනි වැව්/තෙත්බිම්වල බහුලව දැකිය හැක.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී සහ ශීත ඍතුවේදී උතුරින් පැමිණෙන අමතර පක්ෂීන් (CBC 2022: R+(M)); අවුරුද්ද පුරා හමුවේ.

species_description.text: Distinctive medium-sized wagtail about 18 cm, brown above with a bold pale supercilium and buff underparts, usually showing two pale wing-bars. Unlike other wagtails, it often walks along branches and horizontal boughs, moving its tail side-to-side. Feeds on insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar. Breeding male may show richer buff tones, but there is no strong reliable field dimorphism.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller brown with softer supercilium and wing-bars; underparts are more buff and less contrasting.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for its unusual sideways tail-swing and habit of walking along horizontal branches. Brown plumage and arboreal behaviour make it unlike typical ground-wagtails.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Migrant visitor, mainly in wooded habitats, forest edges, gardens, plantations and tree-lined streams. Records from Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Kandy and other wooded areas.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular migrant, usually September–April; Limosa occurrence records Jan–Apr and Sep–Dec.

The official CBC 2011 list also corroborates these codes.

species_description.text: Tiny flowerpecker about 8 cm, olive-brown to grey-olive above with pale buff-olive underparts and a short, fine bill that is often pinkish or pale. It feeds on berries, fruit and nectar, especially mistletoe fruits, and is an important seed disperser for parasitic plants.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar; slight differences in bill tone or plumage are not reliable field sexing characters.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and may show softer, less distinct plumage; young birds resemble adults and are difficult to age away from the hand.

field_spotting_tips.text: Smallest-looking flowerpecker in many mixed garden flocks; plain olive-brown with pale underparts and short bill. Watch for it swallowing small berries whole and visiting mistletoe clumps.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident across much of Sri Lanka in gardens, forest, cultivation, shade trees and plantations, from lowlands into the hills. Often visits fruiting and flowering trees.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Sri Lankan breeding records indicate a broad season January–July with peak activity around March; additional breeding specimens have been recorded in September and November.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention retained: Sri Lanka White-eye E; Indian White-eye R; Legge's Flowerpecker E; Thick-billed Flowerpecker R; Pale-billed Flowerpecker R; Purple-rumped Sunbird R; Loten's Sunbird R; Purple Sunbird R. Confirm individual line codes against official list before publication.

species_description.text: Medium-sized drongo, around 25 cm, with glossy blue-black upperparts, a distinct white belly and vent, and a moderately forked tail. Often in pairs in open woodland, scrub, gardens and forest edges. Feeds on insects, catching them in short aerial sallies or gleaning from foliage.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike. White belly and vent are present in both sexes; subtle size differences are not useful for field sexing.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and duller, with less sharply defined white underparts and a shorter, less deeply forked tail.

field_spotting_tips.text: White belly is the quickest clue among Sri Lankan drongos. Look for a dark bird with a pale underside perched on exposed branches or making short sallies. Do not confuse with juvenile Black Drongo, which is more uniformly dark and often pale-edged.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, especially in dry and intermediate-zone open woodland, scrub and human-modified landscapes; also occurs in gardens and forest margins.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding occurs seasonally; precise Sri Lankan months not confirmed in this batch. Nest is a small cup placed on a branch.

species_description.text: Slender, grey drongo, around 25–29 cm, with a long forked tail, dark facial mask and bright red iris. Usually appears paler and slimmer than Black Drongo; some subspecies show white scaling or barring on the throat and breast. Feeds on insects, often in mixed flocks and forest edges.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike. Plumage varies substantially among subspecies; the amount of pale scaling on the underparts is geographic/individual variation, not a sex difference.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and duller, often with more extensive pale scaling on the underparts and a less distinct facial mask.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a slender grey drongo with red eye and no white rictal spot. Compare carefully with Black Drongo: Ashy is grey, slimmer and red-eyed; Black is glossy black and has a white rictal spot.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Scarce winter migrant to Sri Lanka, recorded mainly in wooded habitats and forest edges. Occurrence is irregular and generally much less frequent than resident drongos.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter migrant, mostly during the northern winter; exact arrival/departure months vary and should be checked against CBC seasonal records. Not a Sri Lankan breeder.

species_description.text: Endemic, medium-sized glossy black drongo, about 28–30 cm, with a moderately forked tail but no racket-shaped streamers. Often has a small crest or shaggy forehead feathers, and shows a distinctive pale iris in good light. Inhabits wet-zone rainforest, wooded foothills and forest edges; feeds on insects and follows mixed-species flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage. The crest/forehead feathering and pale iris are species characters, not sex differences.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller black or brownish-black, with less developed crest and tail shape; iris and adult gloss become more apparent with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for loud, varied calls and mimicry in rainforest. Look for a black drongo without rackets, with shaggy crest and pale eye. Often conspicuous when accompanying mixed-species flocks.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident, chiefly in the south-west wet-zone forests and adjoining foothills. Best searched for in Sinharaja, Kanneliya, Kitulgala and other wet-zone forest reserves.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding reported mainly in the early part of the year; nests are placed in trees. More precise local months require confirmation.

species_description.text: Glossy black, medium-sized drongo about 28 cm, with a deeply forked tail, strong bill and small white rictal spot at the base of the bill. Common in open country, cultivation, scrub, villages and urban areas; catches insects in aerial sallies and often perches on wires or exposed branches.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike in plumage; males may average slightly larger, but not reliably separable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller black, with pale or whitish edges/scaling on underparts and shorter, less deeply forked tails. White rictal spot may be less conspicuous.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the deeply forked tail and white rictal spot. Often hawks insects from wires, cattle or ploughs. Compared with Ashy Drongo it is glossy black, bulkier and has a white rictal spot.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common across much of Sri Lanka in open lowlands, agricultural land, towns and scrub. Less tied to closed forest than Greater Racket-tailed and Sri Lanka Drongos.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident with a migrant component in Sri Lanka (CBC R/M). Present year-round; numbers can vary seasonally. Breeding is reported mainly in the dry-season/early monsoon period, but exact local months require verification.

species_description.text: Large, glossy black drongo with long, deeply forked tail and distinctive paired racket-shaped outer tail feathers in adults. Strong bill and active, agile flight. In Sri Lanka it is associated mainly with forest, wooded country and forest edges; feeds on insects caught in flight or picked from foliage, and may join mixed-species flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike in plumage. Adult males and females both develop the elongated outer tail feathers; slight size differences are not reliable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and less glossy, with shorter outer tail feathers and less developed rackets; adult tail streamers develop with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Adult's two long, racket-ended tail streamers are unmistakable at close range. Listen for varied calls and mimicry. Often follows mixed flocks through forest canopy; avoid confusing with the endemic Sri Lanka Drongo, which lacks the rackets.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's forested wet zone and wooded hills, including Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Kanneliya and other mature forest areas. Less associated with open agricultural landscapes than Black Drongo.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding generally occurs in the first half of the year in Sri Lanka; exact timing varies by locality. Cup nest placed high in a tree.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Brown Shrike M; Long-tailed Shrike R; Sri Lanka Wood-shrike E; Greater Racket-tailed Drongo R; Sri Lanka Drongo E; Black Drongo R/M; White-bellied Drongo R; Ashy Drongo M.

species_description.text: A medium-sized flameback, about 28–30 cm, with golden-yellow mantle and wing coverts, black rump and barred underparts. Sri Lanka's northern form is the Jaffna Golden-backed Woodpecker, historically treated as a subspecies of Black-rumped Flameback; its southern counterpart is now often treated separately as Red-backed Flameback, Dinopium psarodes. This species entry should therefore be read as the northern D. benghalense population under the current split treatment. Feeds on ants, termites and wood-boring insects from tree trunks and branches.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a red crown and crest; female has a black crown with white spots. Both sexes show the golden back and black rump in the northern form.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and less sharply patterned; young males gradually develop the red crown. Ageing requires close views of the head and back.

field_spotting_tips.text: Check the back colour and geography carefully. Northern birds show the golden-backed form; southern birds are the red-backed endemic species. There is a documented hybrid zone and intermediate plumages, so photographs from the transition region need cautious identification.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in the north of Sri Lanka, particularly the Jaffna Peninsula and northern dry-zone areas. The southern red-backed population is treated separately as endemic Dinopium psarodes in current split taxonomy; a contact/hybrid zone occurs in the north-central to central region.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. No specific Sri Lankan breeding window was verified for the northern jaffnense population in this batch.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): resident (R) for all non-endemic woodpeckers; endemic (E) for Crimson-backed Flameback. Red-backed Flameback Dinopium psarodes is now treated as a separate endemic species; taxonomy differs from older CBC treatment. Confirm latest CBC row mapping before publication.

species_description.text: A medium-sized endemic flameback, about 28–30 cm, with a striking crimson-red back, black rump and upper tail coverts, golden-yellow crown and crest, and black-and-white patterned underparts. It is the southern Sri Lankan red-backed member of the flameback complex and differs from the northern golden-backed population. It feeds on ants, termites and other insects gleaned from trunks and branches, and nests in a cavity excavated in a tree.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a red crown/crest; female has a black crown with white spotting. Both sexes have the diagnostic crimson back and black rump. Head pattern is more reliable for sexing than back colour.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less saturated red on the back and a less distinct crown. Young males develop the red crown progressively; female-like spotted crown pattern is retained in young females.

field_spotting_tips.text: The red back is the key feature, but be alert to hybrid and intermediate birds in the contact zone. Compare crown colour for sex: red in adult male, black-and-white spotted in female. Study the back and rump together, not one colour patch alone.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident, mainly in southern and south-western Sri Lanka, with a distribution extending through the south and into a contact zone with the northern golden-backed form. Good areas include Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Udawalawe and other wooded southern/intermediate-zone locations.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Local breeding ecology has been studied, but a simple country-wide breeding month window should not be asserted without consulting the full phenology results. Pairing, nesting and parental care are documented in recent Sri Lankan research.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): resident (R) for all non-endemic woodpeckers; endemic (E) for Crimson-backed Flameback. Red-backed Flameback Dinopium psarodes is now treated as a separate endemic species; taxonomy differs from older CBC treatment. Confirm latest CBC row mapping before publication.

species_description.text: Large, distinctive coastal wader (about 38–41 cm) with a mostly white body, black mantle/scapulars and black outer flight feathers. Heavy black bill; grey-blue legs. Feeds mainly on crabs and other crustaceans, also molluscs and marine worms, probing or picking prey on intertidal flats. Breeds colonially in burrows on sandy islands/dunes in the north-western Indian Ocean; it does not breed in Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar in the field. Males may have a somewhat longer/heavier bill, but this is not a dependable field character; do not sex distant birds from bill shape alone.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immatures resemble adults but dark mantle areas are greyer/browner and less sharply black; head/crown and tail may look greyer. Ageing at distance can be difficult.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for large white-and-black flocks on exposed intertidal flats and sandbars, often roosting together at high tide. Check the heavy straight bill and grey-blue legs; scan crab-rich mud/sand at falling tide. Avoid confusing it with smaller gulls or other waders.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Primarily coastal: tidal sandflats and mudflats, lagoons, estuaries, sandbars and sandy islands. Mannar and the north-western coast/Adam's Bridge region are particularly promising; also check suitable coastal lagoons and exposed tidal flats elsewhere. Site use varies with tides.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly a non-breeding visitor. Regional movements suggest southward dispersal Aug–Nov and return north Mar–Apr; Sri Lankan records are most expected during the northern winter, broadly Nov–Mar. Treat exact local peak months as indicative, not a complete national dataset.

species_description.text: විශාල, ශක්තිමත් ශරීරයක් ඇති ගස්වල වාසය කරන පරෙවියෙකි (ආසන්න 45 cm). හිස සහ යටිපස සුදු පැහැති; පිටුපස, පියාපත් සහ වලිගය ලෝහමය කොළ පැහැති දිලිසීමක් දක්වයි; undertail-coverts maroon පැහැතිය. වනාන්තර, ද්විතීයික වනාන්තර, ගෙවතු, මැංග්‍රෝව් සහ ගස් සහිත භූමිවල හමුවේ. විවිධ පලතුරු සහ බීජ අනුභව කරමින් බීජ ව්‍යාප්තියට දායක වේ.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි සහ ගැහැණු පක්ෂීන් පෙනුමෙන් බොහෝ දුරට සමාන බැවින් ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ පිහාටු පමණක් භාවිතයෙන් විශ්වාසදායකව වෙන්කර හඳුනාගැනීම අපහසුය.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: තරුණ පක්ෂීන් වැඩිහිටියන්ට වඩා අඩු දිලිසෙන, මඳ/දුඹුරු පැහැති විය හැකි අතර වැඩිහිටි සුදු-කොළ වෙනස අඩු පැහැදිලි විය හැක. ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ වයස්-අනුව නිශ්චිත ලක්ෂණ සඳහා තරුණ රූප සහ විස්තර තවදුරටත් තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

field_spotting_tips.text: විශාල ප්‍රමාණය, සුදු හිස/යටිපස සහ දිලිසෙන කොළ පිටුපස හඳුනාගැනීමට උපකාරී වේ. ගස් මුදුන්වලින් එන ගැඹුරු, දුරට ඇසෙන හඬ මුලින්ම අවධානයට ලක්විය හැක. පලතුරු දරන ගස් සහ ගෙවතු palm ගස් පරීක්ෂා කරන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ නේවාසික විශේෂයකි. පහතරට වනාන්තර සහ හොඳින් ගස් වැවුණු ප්‍රදේශවල බහුලව හමුවේ; Kitulgala, Tissamaharama, Wilpattu, Kelani forest සහ Nugegoda අවට ගෙවතු/නගර පරිසරවල වාර්තා ඇත. පලතුරු දරන විසිතුරු ගස් ඇති ගෙවතු වෙතද පැමිණේ.

seasonality_months_seen.text: නේවාසික, සංක්‍රමණික නොවන විශේෂයකි. ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ අභිජනන කාලය සඳහා නිශ්චිත මාස මෙම සෙවුමේදී තහවුරු නොවීය; නිශ්චිත මාස සඳහන් කිරීමෙන් වළකින්න.

species_description.text: Small, active babbler about 13–14 cm, with dark brown to blackish forehead and face, olive-brown upperparts, pale greyish or buff underparts and a short rounded tail. Forages in small groups through dense forest undergrowth, ferns and tangled foliage, taking insects and other small invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; no dependable external field sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with a browner, less sharply defined dark face and softer underpart markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for small parties rummaging in waist-high ferns and low foliage. Dark forehead/face contrasts with the paler throat and breast. Check habitat and local subspecies range.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident across Sri Lanka in forest undergrowth and dense scrub. Sri Lankan subspecies siccata occurs in dry zone and drier hills; nigrifrons occurs in wet zone and southwestern hills. Both subspecies are endemic, while the species also occurs outside Sri Lanka.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Main breeding season reported February–May, possibly with a second period October–November. Nest is a ball of dead leaves with a side entrance, placed on a fork or in dense vegetation.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Sri Lanka Scimitar-babbler E; Yellow-eyed Babbler R; Tawny-bellied Babbler R; Dark-fronted Babbler R; Sri Lanka Orange-billed Babbler E; Sri Lanka Ashy-headed Laughing-thrush E; Yellow-billed Babbler R; Sri Lanka Brown-capped Babbler E. Several resident species have endemic Sri Lankan subspecies only.

species_description.text: Small, compact babbler about 13–14 cm, with warm rufous-brown upperparts, rich tawny/rufous belly and flanks, pale throat in Sri Lankan race phillipsi, short rounded wings and a short tail. Usually in small groups, skulking through low scrub, grass tussocks and tangled undergrowth, feeding on insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar and cannot reliably be separated in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller and less richly coloured, with softer plumage and less distinct throat/belly contrast.

field_spotting_tips.text: Usually detected by rustling and soft calls as a group moves through low cover. The warm rufous belly and pale throat of the Sri Lankan form help separate it from Dark-fronted Babbler.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in scrub, grassland edges, bamboo and dense undergrowth in both dry and wet zones. Sri Lankan subspecies phillipsi is endemic to the island, but the species occurs more widely in India.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Nesting has been recorded in Sri Lanka; season varies locally and should not be stated as a fixed national window without further evidence.

Several resident species have endemic Sri Lankan subspecies only.

species_description.text: Slender, elegant white egret (about 55–65 cm) with a fine black bill, long black legs and bright yellow feet. Breeding adults develop two long nape plumes and delicate plumes on the back and breast. Common around tanks, lagoons, canals, paddy fields, marshes and tidal flats; feeds on fish, frogs, crustaceans, insects and other aquatic prey. Often forages actively in shallow water and nests colonially in trees.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in plumage; males may be slightly larger and have longer breeding plumes. Yellow feet contrasting with black legs and bill are characteristic.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble non-breeding adults but have shorter or absent ornamental plumes and may show duller facial skin and feet.

field_spotting_tips.text: The slim black bill, black legs and vivid yellow feet are the key combination. In breeding plumage, look for fine white plumes on the nape and back. Beware white-morph Western Reef-Heron, which has a heavier bill and duller legs.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common and widespread throughout Sri Lanka in lowland wetlands, reservoirs, canals, paddy fields and coastal lagoons, including urban wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year (CBC category R); numbers can fluctuate locally with water conditions and food supply.

species_description.text: Medium-sized coastal heron (about 55–65 cm), occurring in dark slate-grey and white morphs, with occasional intermediate plumage. It has a relatively heavy bill and yellowish to greenish legs. Feeds on fish, crabs and other intertidal animals on rocky shores, mudflats, reefs, estuaries and coastal lagoons. Sri Lankan birds are principally winter visitors rather than a regular breeding species.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike. Colour morph is not a sex difference: both sexes may be dark or white. Dark birds are slate-grey, often with a white chin/throat; white birds are mostly white and can resemble Little Egret.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immatures are duller and less sharply patterned; dark-morph juveniles may be greyer and show more white on the throat and underparts. CBC image records include immature grey-morph birds.

field_spotting_tips.text: First identify the morph, then check structure: compared with Little Egret, Reef-Heron has a heavier bill and less delicate build. Yellowish/greenish legs and coastal habitat are useful clues. Do not confuse white morph with Little Egret.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Primarily coastal, with records from Mannar, Chilaw sand spits, Lunawa and other western/north-western shorelines, lagoons and estuaries. Search rocky coast, tidal flats and mangrove edges.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter migrant to Sri Lanka (CBC category M); records are concentrated in the northern winter, approximately October–April, though individual arrival/departure dates vary.

species_description.text: A small, pale grey-and-white kite with long pointed wings, a black shoulder patch and red eyes in adults. Often hunts from a conspicuous exposed perch or hovers over open grassland, scrub, farmland and dry open country. Diet is dominated by small rodents, with insects, reptiles and small birds also taken. Builds a stick nest, usually in a tree; both sexes participate in breeding duties.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are very similar in plumage. Females are usually slightly larger, but size overlap makes field sexing unreliable. Adult birds show the distinctive dark shoulder patch and red eye.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more streaked on the breast, with buff or brown edging to upperpart feathers; the adult clean grey-and-white pattern develops with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a pale kite hovering almost motionless over grassland, then dropping vertically onto prey. In flight, note the narrow pointed wings and dark carpal/shoulder patches.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A widespread resident of open lowland country, especially dry-zone scrub, grassland, agricultural landscapes and the edges of settlements. Can be found around tanks, paddy fields and open areas in national parks including Wilpattu.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year; breeding and local movements may vary with rainfall and prey availability. No single island-wide seasonal window should be inferred.

species_description.text: Small, elusive endemic warbler, about 14–15 cm, with dark olive-brown upperparts, greyish or smoky underparts, a pale eye-ring/supercilium and relatively long legs. It keeps close to the ground in dense undergrowth, dwarf bamboo and montane forest-edge vegetation, feeding on insects and other small invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in overall plumage; males may be slightly larger and more vocal. No dependable external field distinction for ordinary birders.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are poorly documented in field references; likely browner and softer in plumage, with less distinct facial markings. Treat age-specific field identification as uncertain.

field_spotting_tips.text: Extremely skulking; listen for calls and watch shaded undergrowth and dwarf bamboo. Move slowly and scan low vegetation. Its restricted highland range makes habitat and elevation strong clues.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka's central highlands and montane zone, especially dense undergrowth and dwarf bamboo in montane forests. Recorded around Horton Plains, Nuwara Eliya, Hakgala and other highland forest patches, generally at higher elevations up to about 1,500 m.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round and not migratory. Breeding biology and precise nesting months are poorly documented; avoid assigning a confident island-wide breeding window.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Blyth's Reed-warbler M; Clamorous Reed-warbler R; Large-billed Leaf-warbler M; Greenish Warbler M; Sri Lanka Bush Warbler E; Velvet-fronted Nuthatch R. Clamorous Reed-warbler has endemic Sri Lankan subspecies meridionalis, not an endemic species.

species_description.text: Very large stork with black head, neck and upperparts, white belly and conspicuous white wing panels; long red legs and massive black bill. Hunts fish, frogs, reptiles and other aquatic animals in open marshes, tanks and flooded grassland. Usually solitary or in pairs.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes differ in iris: adult male dark brown, adult female yellow. Plumage otherwise similar.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles browner and duller, with less sharply defined black-white pattern and paler bare parts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for solitary birds standing in shallow water. Very large black-and-white wings; note female yellow iris versus male dark iris if close.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident but scarce and local in large wetland landscapes, particularly dry-zone tanks, marshes and floodplains; records from Yala, Bundala, Kumana and north-central wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident; low density and wide-ranging behaviour make sightings irregular year-round.
