species_description.text: Small lark about 12–13 cm with sandy-brown, finely streaked upperparts, pale underparts and a short crest. Male has a black face, throat and breast with white patches on sides of head and wings; female is much duller and streaked. Feeds on seeds and insects on bare ground and short grass.

male_female_identification.text: Male has striking black-and-white face and underparts with dark breast; female sandy-brown, heavily streaked and lacks black mask. Both sexes have short crest and pale eyebrow.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble female but are more heavily mottled and scaled, with buff edges to feathers; young males gradually develop black-and-white adult pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Scan bare ground and short grass in open country. Male's black-and-white head and breast are distinctive; female is easily overlooked as a plain brown lark. Often runs or crouches rather than perching high.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open dry-zone country, short grassland, scrub, fallow fields and sandy or stony plains. Particularly associated with Mannar, Jaffna, Bundala and Udawalawe landscapes.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident breeder according to CBC 2022. Seasonal abundance can vary with rainfall and grass growth; local breeding months require more nest-based confirmation.

The official CBC 2011 list also corroborates these codes.

species_description.text: Large, robust shorebird (about 53–59 cm) with grey-brown upperparts, pale underparts, large yellow bill with dark tip, very large yellow eyes and long yellow legs. Inhabits sandy and muddy coasts, tidal flats, estuaries and open coastal scrub, but may also use dry inland flats. Feeds on crabs, molluscs, insects and other invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage; females may be slightly larger with a longer bill, but differences are subtle and not dependable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally browner and more mottled, with pale feather fringes and less cleanly defined head/neck pattern. Bill and leg colours may be duller.

field_spotting_tips.text: Usually roosts or feeds on open coastal flats, often standing motionless. The huge yellow eye and bill, large size and upright stance are distinctive; scan beaches and tidal mudflats at low tide.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's coastal dry-zone habitats, especially sandy and muddy shores, estuaries and coastal lagoons. Look around Bundala, Mannar, Puttalam and other undisturbed coastal flats.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round, with local movements possible according to tides and disturbance. Numbers and visibility vary seasonally.

species_description.text: Large (about 39–46 cm), long-tailed cuckoo. Adult male glossy bluish-black with pale greenish-grey bill and crimson iris; female brown, heavily spotted and barred white/buff. Common around gardens, orchards, plantations, open woodland and town trees. Adults mainly eat fruit and berries (including figs), but also insects and small vertebrates. A brood parasite: lays eggs in nests of crows and other suitable host species; it does not build its own nest.

male_female_identification.text: Strong sexual dimorphism. Male is uniformly glossy black/blue-black with red eye and pale bill. Female is brown with white/buff spotting and barring on head, upperparts and underparts; juvenile resembles female but is usually duller.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds resemble the female: brown, spotted and barred, with less sharply defined patterning; plumage and eye/bill colours change as they mature. Do not identify a juvenile as an adult female from colour alone.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for the familiar rising 'koo-oo' call of the male, especially early morning. The female gives a rapid, sharp kik-kik-kik call. Check fruiting trees and tall roadside trees; female's spotted pattern is a useful distinction from the glossy male.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident across Sri Lanka, including home gardens, parks, orchards, plantations, village landscapes and forest edges. Often detected by voice in urban and suburban areas; not restricted to a particular national park.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Vocal activity commonly increases around the breeding period; South Asian sources give roughly March–August, but exact Sri Lankan laying dates should be treated as locally variable and host-dependent.

species_description.text: Small, neat endemic flycatcher about 13 cm. Male is dull slate-blue to blue-grey above, with paler blue forehead and face, whitish throat and pale grey underparts; female is browner/greyer above with a faint blue wash and pale underparts. Feeds on insects from low perches in forest undergrowth.

male_female_identification.text: Male blue-grey with brighter blue forehead and face; female duller brown-grey, sometimes with a blue tinge. Both have pale underparts and similar shape.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and heavily scaled or spotted, with buff edges and little blue; young males develop blue gradually.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often sits quietly at low or middle levels, making short sallies. The dull blue-grey male is less vivid than Tickell's Blue-flycatcher; listen for its soft, clear whistles and search shaded highland forest edges.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident of the central highlands and surrounding wet-zone hills, especially montane forest, forest edges, gardens and plantations. Frequently seen in Nuwara Eliya, Horton Plains, Hakgala, Peak Wilderness and Knuckles.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding reported mainly March–May and August–September in local accounts; exact variation by elevation requires further checking.

species_description.text: Small finch-like munia about 11 cm, pale sandy-brown above and whitish below, with a short, stout, pale bluish-grey bill and dark tail. Usually travels in flocks and feeds on grass seeds and grain, often on the ground.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; male may be slightly more contrasting but cannot be reliably sexed in the field. Bill is thick and pale, giving a silvery appearance.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller brown above and buff below, with a darker bill that becomes pale as they mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Identify by the chunky pale bill, plain sandy plumage and flocking behaviour. Compare with other munias by its pale bill and lack of strong breast pattern.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in dry-zone scrub, grassland, open woodland, paddy fields and cultivation, especially in northern and south-eastern Sri Lanka. Often near settlements and water.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident; breeding varies with rainfall and food supply. Sri Lankan breeding months need more reliable local confirmation. Nest is a domed grass structure in shrubs or grass.

species_description.text: A powerful, streamlined falcon (about 34–58 cm depending on sex and subspecies) with long pointed wings, a dark hood, strong moustache mark and slate-grey upperparts in adults. Hunts birds in fast, direct pursuit, often stooping at high speed. Occurs on cliffs, rocky hills, coastal headlands, wetlands and cities with suitable prey and nesting structures. Nests on ledges and other elevated sites.

male_female_identification.text: Female is substantially larger than male, although plumage is similar. Sri Lanka has the resident dark Shaheen form (F. p. peregrinator) and migrant populations including calidus; colour and size vary among subspecies. Do not identify sex from colour alone.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner above with pale buff edges to feathers and heavily streaked underparts rather than the adult's transverse barring. Cere and orbital skin are duller than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Identify the heavy moustache, compact powerful body and pointed wings. A fast, steep hunting stoop is characteristic. Note location and season when attempting to distinguish Shaheen from migrant subspecies.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: The resident Shaheen is associated especially with rocky highlands and central mountain areas, while migrant Peregrines occur along coastal areas and other open landscapes. Historical records document different distributions for resident peregrinator and wintering calidus.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident Shaheen occurs year-round. Migrant calidus is mainly a winter visitor, with historical Sri Lankan records concentrated approximately October–March.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) is the preferred local authority; status recorded here is provisional pending direct row/subspecies cross-check. R = resident; M = regular migrant. For mixed populations/subspecies retain R/M.

species_description.text: Small falcon (about 32–39 cm) with pointed wings, long tail and a characteristic hovering flight. Upperparts usually rufous-brown with dark spotting; underparts pale with dark streaks. Uses open country, grassland, scrub, agricultural land, coastal plains and urban edges. Hunts mainly small mammals, lizards, large insects and occasionally small birds, often from a perch or by hovering. Nests in cavities, buildings or other sheltered sites; breeding locally should be confirmed from current Sri Lankan records.

male_female_identification.text: Female is generally larger and more heavily barred/streaked, with a more extensively barred tail. Adult male has a blue-grey head and tail, rufous back with dark spots and less heavily marked underparts. Plumage and age can make sexing at distance difficult.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble adult females but are generally more heavily streaked and have buff-edged upperpart feathers. Look for a pale, streaked breast and barred tail; ageing in field photographs can be difficult.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for hovering into the wind over open fields, then dropping onto prey. The small size, pointed wings, long tail and facial moustache distinguish it from larger kites and buzzards.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Recorded in open lowland and dry-zone landscapes, agricultural areas, coastal plains and around settlements. Check open country around the northern and eastern plains, tanks, paddy fields and coastal scrub; sightings are seasonal and localised.

seasonality_months_seen.text: A resident and migrant component is reported in Sri Lanka. Migrants are most likely during the northern winter, broadly October–April; do not assume every sighting is a migrant because resident birds also occur.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) is the preferred local authority; status recorded here is provisional pending direct row/subspecies cross-check. R = resident; M = regular migrant. For mixed populations/subspecies retain R/M.

species_description.text: Small, scarce migratory flycatcher about 13 cm. Breeding male has slate-blue upperparts, dark head, orange-red throat and breast and pale belly; female is brownish olive above with buffy underparts and a warm orange wash on throat/breast. It catches insects from low perches.

male_female_identification.text: Strong sexual dimorphism: male blue-grey above with orange-red throat and breast; female olive-brown above with buff/orange underparts. Non-breeding male may be duller.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and scaly, with buff spots on upperparts and breast; young males gradually acquire blue and orange adult plumage.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search montane gardens, forest edges and wooded ravines in the central hills. Male's blue-and-orange pattern is distinctive; female is easily confused with other brown flycatchers, so check orange throat/breast and structure.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Scarce winter visitor to Sri Lanka, mainly in the central highlands and montane forest edges, gardens and wooded ravines. Important wintering areas include Nuwara Eliya and Horton Plains.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter migrant, generally October–April, though monthly records vary. Limosa records Oct–Nov and Jan–Apr; some datasets show additional August records.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 31 පමණ දිගැති, තරමක් තද පැහැති බිම්වාසී francolin එකකි. රතු-තැඹිලි මුහුණ/උගුර, ඉහළ හා පහළ පිහාටු මත පැහැදිලි සුදු තිත්. තෘණබිම්, පඳුරු සහ වගාබිම් ආශ්‍රිත ආවරණ සහිත ස්ථාන භාවිත කරයි. බීජ හා කෘමීන් ප්‍රධාන ආහාරය බව සාමාන්‍ය francolin ecology අනුව සැලකිය හැකි නමුත් ලංකා-විශේෂිත ආහාර දත්ත තවදුරටත් තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි. ප්‍රජනනයේදී හඬින් හඳුනාගැනීම පහසු විය හැක; ලංකාවේ නිශ්චිත breeding months තහවුරු වී නැත.

male_female_identification.text: ලිංග දෙකේම වර්ණ බොහෝ දුරට සමානයි. පිරිමි පක්ෂියාගේ උගුර සාමාන්‍යයෙන් වඩා තද chestnut; ගැහැනුගේ උගුර සුදු පැහැයට හැරිය හැක. ගැහැනුගේ ඉහළ පිහාටු තිත් අඩු හෝ buff edging නිසා අඩු පැහැදිලි විය හැක.

field_spotting_tips.text: පඳුරු/තෘණ ආවරණයේදී බොහෝවිට නොපෙනී සිටී. හඬට සවන් දෙන්න; පාර අයිනේ හෝ තණබිම් අසල උදෑසන/සවස සෙමින් නිරීක්ෂණය කරන්න. Grey Francolin සමඟ වෙන්කරන විට සුදු තිත් සහ රතු-තැඹිලි මුහුණ බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් පහළ රටේ වියළි/අර්ධ වියළි ප්‍රදේශවල patchy ව්‍යාප්තියක්. Uva සහ ගිනිකොනදිග පහළබිම් සම්බන්ධ වාර්තා ඇත; වර්තමාන abundance/hotspots ස්ථානිකව තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී. late summer සහ මෝසම් සමයේ හඬ ක්‍රියාකාරීත්වය වැඩි විය හැක; වාර්ෂික ලංකා මාසික වාර්තා තවදුරටත් පරීක්ෂා කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: Medium-large blackish waterbird (about 36–39 cm) with rounded body, white bill and white frontal shield, dark head and body, and lobed toes rather than webbed feet. Lives on open freshwater lakes, reservoirs, ponds and marshes, diving for aquatic vegetation and invertebrates. Builds floating or anchored nests among reeds.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage. Males are often slightly larger, but field separation is unreliable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are grey-brown with whitish throat and breast and lack the fully white adult shield; the bill and shield become whiter with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the white bill and shield against the dark body. It dives frequently and may run across the water with wings flapping; distinguish from moorhen by the white frontal shield and lack of red bill.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs in Sri Lanka on larger freshwater bodies and wetlands; resident populations and migrant/wintering birds occur. Important sites include large tanks and reservoirs in the dry zone and lowland wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC status R/M. Numbers can increase during the northern winter; exact abundance varies with water levels and seasonal movements.

species_description.text: Large, secretive rail (about 42–43 cm) with long legs, short tail and heavy bill. Adult male is mostly dark slate-black with a conspicuous red frontal shield and bill; female is brown, heavily streaked and barred, with a pale eyebrow and buff underparts. Lives in marshes, reedbeds, flooded grassland and paddy fields. Eats seeds, shoots, insects, worms, molluscs and small aquatic animals.

male_female_identification.text: Strong sexual dimorphism: male is dark slate-black with red frontal shield; female is brown and cryptically patterned with streaking and barring. Female is often more readily seen in open wet grass.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble the female but are duller and more uniformly brown, with less obvious barring and a less developed frontal shield. Young males darken progressively as they mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its loud, booming or clucking calls at night and early morning. Search dense reeds at dawn; the male's black plumage and red shield are unmistakable, while the female's streaked brown pattern blends into vegetation.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's wetlands, particularly lowland marshes, paddy fields, reedbeds and seasonally flooded grassland. Local and often secretive; suitable sites include large marshes and tank margins.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is seasonal and often follows monsoon rains; exact months vary among wetland systems.

species_description.text: Small, compact snipe (about 25–27 cm including bill) with cryptic brown, buff and black streaked plumage, long straight bill and relatively short legs. Upperparts show bold pale buff/golden stripes; underparts are whitish with brown barring on the flanks. Uses wet grassland, marshes, flooded paddy fields and muddy margins. Feeds on worms, insect larvae and other invertebrates, probing soft mud.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and difficult to distinguish in the field. Reliable sexing generally requires measurements or examination in the hand.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are similar to adults but often have more buff-edged upperpart feathers and a fresher, more scalloped appearance. Ageing and separation from other *Gallinago* snipes can be difficult.

field_spotting_tips.text: Flushes suddenly from wet grass or mud with a zig-zag flight and a sharp call. Identification from other snipes is challenging; note size, bill, tail pattern and flight call. Do not rely on a brief view—photographs of the spread tail can help distinguish Pin-tailed from Common Snipe.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter visitor to wetlands and flooded fields across Sri Lanka, including Bundala, Yala, Udawalawe and other Dry Zone tanks and marshes. Can occur in suitable urban and agricultural wetlands, but is easily overlooked.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Migrant, mainly during the northern winter. CBC image records include a Bundala bird in February; Limosa monthly checklist shows Jan–May and Sep–Dec records. Most expected roughly Sep–Apr.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC 2022 Country List lists Pin-tailed Snipe as M; CBC image record and seasonal checklists support winter migrant.

species_description.text: Medium-sized rail (about 30–38 cm) with dark slate body, white undertail and flank stripe, red bill and frontal shield with yellow tip, and greenish legs. Occupies ponds, lakes, marshes, canals, reservoirs and vegetated urban wetlands. Omnivorous, feeding on aquatic plants, seeds, insects, snails, worms and small fish. Builds a platform nest among emergent vegetation.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; males are usually slightly larger with a larger shield, but overlap is substantial and field sexing is unsafe.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and lack the bright red bill and frontal shield; underparts are paler and legs/bill are duller. Immatures gradually acquire adult dark plumage and red shield.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the white undertail flicked conspicuously as it swims or walks along the water edge. The red frontal shield and white flank stripe distinguish it from White-breasted Waterhen.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident in suitable wetlands across Sri Lanka, including tanks, reservoirs, marshes, ponds, canals and urban lakes.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding can occur in different months depending on rainfall, water levels and vegetation growth.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 37 පමණ දිග, partridge ප්‍රමාණයට ආසන්න නමුත් වඩා පිරුණු ශරීරයක් ඇති, බිම වාසය කරන endemic පක්ෂියෙකි. ගැඹුරු වනාන්තර, තෙත් කලාපයේ rainforest, කඳුකර වනාන්තර සහ ඇතැම් ගංගාබඩ වනාන්තරවල පඳුරු/පත්‍ර තට්ටුව තුළ ආහාර සොයයි. බීජ, වැටුණු පලතුරු සහ කෘමීන් ආහාරයට ගනී. බිම කූඩු තනයි; මුල් වසරේදී ප්‍රජනනය සිදුවන බව CBC සඳහන් කරයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි: maroon-දුඹුරු ශරීරය, කළු-සුදු කොරපොතු/තිත් රටා, හිස හා යටපස වඩා පැහැදිලි; කකුල්වල spurs දෙකක්. ගැහැනු: සරල reddish-brown යටපස සහ අඩු රටා. දෙපාර්ශ්වයේම හොට සහ පාද රතු.

field_spotting_tips.text: ඉතා ලජ්ජාශීලී සහ බොහෝවිට හඬින් පළමුව හඳුනාගත හැක. උදෑසන වනාන්තර මාර්ග, පත්‍ර තට්ටුව සහ ගස් මුල් අසල සෙමින් බලන්න. පලා යන විට කෙටි දුරක් වේගයෙන් දුවන නිසා චලනය ගැන අවධානය යොමු කරන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: තෙත් කලාපයේ ගැඹුරු වනාන්තරවල වඩා සාමාන්‍ය; Sinharaja, Kalugala සහ Rakwana ආශ්‍රිත වනාන්තර වාර්තා. කඳුකර සහ වියළි කලාපයේ ඇතැම් ගංගාබඩ වනාන්තරවලද හමුවේ.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී. CBC අනුව ප්‍රජනන කාලය වසරේ මුල් භාගය; නිශ්චිත මාස/ප්‍රදේශ වෙනස් විය හැක.

species_description.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවට ආවේණික, කුකුළෙකුට සමාන විශාල බිම්වාසී පක්ෂියෙකි. පිරිමි සෙ.මී. 66–73 පමණ; ගැහැනු සෙ.මී. 35 පමණ. වනාන්තර, scrub, වනාන්තර අද්දර සහ වනාන්තරයට යාබද තේ වතු භාවිත කරයි. බිම සීරමින් බීජ, ධාන්‍ය, වැටුණු පලතුරු සහ කෘමීන් සොයයි. බිම කූඩුවක සාමාන්‍යයෙන් බිත්තර 2–4ක් දමයි. CBC අනුව ප්‍රධාන ප්‍රජනන සමය වසරේ මුල් භාගය; ඇතැම්විට අගෝස්තු–සැප්තැම්බර් දෙවන සමයක්ද ඇත.

male_female_identification.text: ඉතා පැහැදිලි sexual dimorphism. පිරිමි: තැඹිලි-රතු ශරීරය, රන්වන්-කහ ගෙල පිහාටු, දිගු නිල්-කළු වලිගය, රතු comb මැද කහ පැල්ලම. ගැහැනු: කුඩා, අළු-දුඹුරු, සුදු/කළු ඉරි සහිත camouflage පිහාටු.

field_spotting_tips.text: උදෑසන/සවස වනාන්තර මාර්ග සහ විවෘත තැන් අසල සොයන්න. පිරිමිගේ කහ මැදක් ඇති comb සහ metallic tail හොඳ ලක්ෂණ. ගැහැනුගේ wing barring සහ domestic chicken හි නොපෙනෙන ලක්ෂණ සසඳන්න. හඬ ඉතා හඳුනාගත හැක.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: දිවයිනේ සියලුම climatic zones වල වනාන්තර සහ scrub වාසස්ථානවල ව්‍යාප්තයි; පහළබිම් සිට කඳුකරය දක්වා. ජාතික වනෝද්‍යාන, Sinharaja, Kitulgala සහ වනාන්තර අද්දර ප්‍රදේශ නිරීක්ෂණයට සුදුසුය.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී; අවුරුද්ද පුරා. CBC වාර්තාව අනුව ප්‍රජනනය මුල් වසරේදී වැඩි අතර අගෝස්තු–සැප්තැම්බර් දෙවන peak එකක් ඇත.

species_description.text: Large, stocky tern (about 33–42 cm) with a thick black bill, black legs, pale grey upperparts and white underparts. Breeding adults have a black cap; in non-breeding plumage the forehead is white and dark markings remain around the eye/ear. Unlike most terns, it often catches insects and other prey over land as well as fish and aquatic invertebrates. Uses lagoons, saltpans, mudflats, marshes and open wetlands.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; male is usually slightly larger. Black cap versus streaked/white winter head reflects season, not sex.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have brownish or buff-edged feathers on the upperparts and a less clean grey mantle; head pattern is less sharply defined. Adults in winter have a white forehead and dark eye patch.

field_spotting_tips.text: The thick, all-black bill is the key feature; larger and heavier-headed than many terns. Often forages over dry ground or fields for insects, unlike fish-diving terns. Check head pattern and bill shape.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Recorded at coastal lagoons and saltpans, including Bundala, Palatupana and Chilaw sandspit; also occurs at suitable inland tanks and wetlands. Sri Lankan status is mixed in CBC list (R/M), with winter visitors and a possible small resident component reported in older seabird literature.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC Country List 2022 gives R/M. Older CBC image records label winter visitor; seasonal datasets show records throughout much of the year, but this may reflect resident component and uneven reporting. Winter numbers increase.

species_description.text: Medium-sized ground thrush about 21–23 cm. Male is vivid orange on head and underparts with contrasting dark wings and tail; female is duller, with olive-brown upperparts and less saturated orange below. Feeds mainly on insects and other invertebrates in leaf litter, also berries.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes differ strongly: male has a blue-grey to slate upper back and bright orange head/underparts; female has olive-brown upperparts and softer orange underparts. Females may be overlooked as a different ground thrush.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are mottled and spotted, with duller brown/orange tones and less clean adult colour blocks; first-winter birds gradually acquire adult plumage.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search shaded leaf litter and low perches in quiet gardens or forest edges. The male's bright orange head and underparts are unmistakable; check females carefully for the same shape and orange tones. Often feeds quietly on the ground.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter migrant to Sri Lanka, recorded in wooded gardens, forest edges, scrub and shaded undergrowth in both lowlands and hills. Occasional records from dry/intermediate zone sites such as Sigiriya and Buttala as well as wet-zone wooded localities.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly a northern-winter visitor, generally October–April; some birds begin singing before departure around February–April. Occurrence is local and birds may be solitary.

species_description.text: Medium-sized endemic forest thrush about 21 cm, olive-brown above with two rows of white spots on the wing-coverts, pale cheeks with dark facial stripes, and creamy underparts boldly marked with dark inverted V-shaped spots on breast and flanks. Mostly terrestrial, turning leaf litter for insects and worms; also takes berries.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage and are not reliably separable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have paler, streaked upperparts and buff underparts with coalescing spots; facial pattern is present but less distinct.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for rich, human-like whistling song. Search forest trails and leaf litter, especially at dawn and late afternoon. Two rows of white wing spots and heavily spotted breast are key; sexes look alike.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident in damp evergreen forest, secondary scrub, plantations and gardens adjoining forest, from wet lowlands to about 2,000 m (more frequent below 1,500 m). Scarce and local in dry-zone riverine forest. Good sites include Sinharaja and Kitulgala.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Double-brooded; nests reported March–April and August–November. Usually solitary or in pairs, feeding on forest trails especially morning and evening.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022: Orange-headed Thrush M; Pied Thrush M; Sri Lanka Scaly Thrush E; Ceylon Whistling Thrush E; Spotted-winged Thrush E; Blackbird (Indian Blackbird) R.

species_description.text: Medium-sized thrush about 22 cm. Adult male is striking black-and-white: black head and upperparts, long white supercilium, white spotting on wings and rump, white underparts with black flank spots, and yellow bill and legs. Female is brown and buff with similar patterning but softer contrast. Feeds on insects and other invertebrates on the ground.

male_female_identification.text: Male black above with bold white eyebrow and white wing/rump spotting. Female brown above with buff eyebrow and more buff-scaled underparts; bill and legs yellow in both.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds resemble female but are more uniformly brown and buff, with scaly underparts and less distinct white markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look on damp lawns, leaf litter and shaded paths in hill-country parks. Adult male's black-and-white pattern is unmistakable; female is warmer brown and more cryptic. Often flushes into a tree and sits quietly.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter visitor from Himalayan breeding areas to Sri Lanka's central hills, wooded ravines, open woodland and forest edges. A regular wintering site is Victoria Park, Nuwara Eliya; also reported around other hill-country gardens and forest margins.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter migrant, generally November–March/April. Birds may be easier to see early morning on lawns and leaf litter; they often move into trees later in the day.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022: Orange-headed Thrush M; Pied Thrush M; Sri Lanka Scaly Thrush E; Ceylon Whistling Thrush E; Spotted-winged Thrush E; Blackbird (Indian Blackbird) R.

species_description.text: Small (about 16–18 cm) slender pratincole with long pointed wings, short bill, short legs and forked tail. Grey-brown above, pale below, with dark throat bordered by a pale line in breeding plumage; flight shows agile, swallow-like turns. Favours sandy riverbanks, exposed islands, reservoirs and open water margins. Catches flying insects, often on the wing; nests on bare sand or gravel.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike or only subtly different; field separation is not reliable. Breeding plumage and throat pattern vary with season rather than sex alone.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with pale/buff feather edges giving a scaled appearance on the upperparts; throat and breast markings are less sharply defined.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often seen hawking insects low over water or resting in groups on bare sand. The long pointed wings, forked tail and tern/swallow-like flight separate it from small waders.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in suitable dry-zone riverine and reservoir habitats. Look along broad sandy riverbeds, tank margins and exposed shorelines; Bundala and other dry-zone wetlands may produce records, though open riverine sandbars are characteristic habitat.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident, with local movements linked to water levels and exposed sandbar availability. Breeding timing can vary with hydrology; avoid treating a single month range as universal.

species_description.text: Medium-sized (about 23–25 cm) elegant pratincole with long pointed wings, long forked tail, short bill and short legs. Brown upperparts, pale underparts and a dark chestnut throat bordered by black in breeding plumage; non-breeding birds have a plainer pale throat. Feeds mainly on flying insects caught in aerial pursuit, but also takes prey from the ground. Uses open grassland, dry plains, floodplains and wetland edges; nests on bare ground.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; males may show a more extensive/darker breeding throat, but plumage and wear make field sexing uncertain.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have scaly-looking upperparts with pale feather edges and a less distinct throat pattern; they lack the strong adult breeding contrast.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a long-winged bird with a forked tail, often feeding in fast, looping flights over open ground. At rest it looks unusually short-legged; do not confuse it with swallows, which have different wing/tail proportions.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs in open country, grassland, floodplains and around wetlands, especially in the dry zone. Search broad open landscapes around Bundala, Yala and large tank systems; flocks may gather on recently exposed ground.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Listed as resident in the CBC country list, although local movements and seasonal changes in numbers may occur. Presence can vary with rainfall, grassland condition and insect availability.

species_description.text: Small, stocky endemic owlet (about 19–21 cm) with a rich chestnut mantle, scapulars and wing coverts, brown facial disc, yellow eyes, white neckband and heavily marked pale underparts. Mainly a wet-zone forest and forest-edge bird, often using tall canopy trees and steep wooded slopes. Feeds on beetles and other insects, and also small mammals, lizards and birds. Nests in tree cavities.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar and cannot normally be distinguished in the field. Size differences are subtle; do not infer sex from colour.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are softer and browner, with less crisp chestnut and barring than adults. Young birds may show fluffier head and body feathers; detailed ageing is difficult away from the nest.

field_spotting_tips.text: Distinguish from Jungle Owlet by the bright chestnut mantle and wings, white neckband and wet-zone forest association. Often detected by its slow, deep repeated 'kraw' calls and by small birds mobbing it.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka's wet-zone forests and adjoining wet hills, reaching roughly 1,800–1,950 m. Particularly associated with Kitulgala and Sinharaja, with records in other remaining wet-zone forest tracts.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident endemic. CBC status E. Breeding has been reported around March–May in secondary species accounts, but the local evidence base is limited; use this as provisional rather than a definitive island-wide season.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022), Version 3: resident (R) or endemic (E) as recorded; E denotes Sri Lankan endemic, not a separate movement code.

species_description.text: Small, compact owl (about 19 cm) with rounded head, short tail, yellow eyes and finely barred brown-and-white plumage. Usually active by day, especially early morning and late afternoon, in dry-zone woodland, scrub, forest edge and wooded cultivation. Feeds on insects, small reptiles, rodents and small birds. Nests in tree cavities; local nest-season data should be treated cautiously.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar in plumage; female is generally larger. No dependable field plumage character separates the sexes.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds are generally fluffier and browner, with softer, less sharply defined barring and pale underparts. Ageing away from the nest is difficult.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often detected by its repeated calls and mobbing birds. Unlike the Chestnut-backed Owlet, it lacks the rich chestnut mantle and wing coverts; compare habitat as well as plumage.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident, mainly in the dry and intermediate zones, in woodland, scrub and forest-edge habitats. Records include dry-zone national parks and wooded landscapes; recent comparative work describes Jungle Owlet as occupying the dry zone while Chestnut-backed Owlet is associated with the wet zone.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. No reliable island-wide seasonal migration pattern; breeding months should be confirmed from local nest records before assigning a firm window.

species_description.text: Large, glossy black myna about 27–30 cm, with a powerful orange-yellow bill, yellow facial wattles extending behind the eye, and conspicuous white wing patches in flight. Strongly arboreal and vocal; feeds mainly on fruit and nectar, also insects and other small invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and are difficult to distinguish visually. Vocal mimicry and a varied repertoire are characteristic.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller brown-black, with less developed facial wattles and a darker bill; white wing patches are present but may be less crisp.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for loud whistles, squeals and imitated sounds high in the canopy. In flight, look for the large white wing patches. Do not confuse with endemic Sri Lanka Myna: compare head wattles, bill pattern and voice.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's wet and intermediate zone forests and wooded country, including forest edges, plantations and large gardens. Current taxonomy recognises the Sri Lankan/Western Ghats population as Southern Hill Myna, Gracula indica, rather than the Himalayan/SE Asian Common Hill Myna G. religiosa.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding dates in South Asian populations vary; local Sri Lankan month-specific data are limited. Tree cavities are used for nesting.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Southern/Common Hill Myna (Gracula indica) R; Sri Lanka Myna E; Common Myna R; Rosy Starling M; Brahminy Starling M; White-faced Starling E. Confirm codes against the list before publication.

conservation.iucn_source_note: Global IUCN LC. Current taxonomy: Southern Hill Myna Gracula indica; older/plate name Common Hill Myna. Not the same taxon as Gracula religiosa.

species_description.text: Large, glossy black endemic myna about 28–30 cm, with a purple-green sheen, orange-red bill with a dark base, and only two small yellow-orange wattles on the nape. It is a canopy fruit-eater, especially fond of wild figs and other large fruits; also takes seeds and some invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar, but iris colour may help: male brown and female pale/whitish according to CBC account. This is subtle and should not be used as the sole sexing character.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less glossy plumage and less developed facial wattles; bill and eye colours are less vivid.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for carrying, clear whistles and the distinctive throaty calls. Search fruiting trees in the canopy. It has fewer, smaller nape wattles and a dark base to the orange-red bill compared with Southern Hill Myna.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to wet-zone and wet hill forests of Sri Lanka, generally up to about 1,800–2,000 m. Occurs in pairs or small groups in forest canopy, plantations and wooded gardens; key sites include Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Peak Wilderness and Horton Plains.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding mainly February–May, with a possible second season August–September. Nests in tree cavities, often high above ground.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Southern/Common Hill Myna (Gracula indica) R; Sri Lanka Myna E; Common Myna R; Rosy Starling M; Brahminy Starling M; White-faced Starling E. Confirm codes against the list before publication.

species_description.text: Large, unmistakable shorebird (about 40–47 cm) with a black head, neck and upper breast, white lower breast and belly, white rump and a broad white wingbar. The long, strong orange-red bill, red eye and pink legs are distinctive. Feeds on mussels, clams, limpets, worms and other intertidal invertebrates, opening or extracting shellfish with its bill. Breeds on coasts and islands in its northern breeding range; it does not breed in Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Female is usually slightly larger and has a longer, thinner bill than the male; differences are subtle. Bill length varies among geographic populations, so sex should not be assigned confidently from a single distant view.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile resembles adult but has browner, often pale-fringed upperparts, duller bare-part colours and sometimes a dark bill tip. First-winter birds may retain juvenile feathering and look less sharply patterned.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the large black-and-white body, very long orange-red bill and pink legs on exposed shore or mudflat. It is much larger and more robust-billed than most waders. Photograph/document carefully and submit unusual Sri Lankan records with date, location and diagnostic images.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A very rare winter visitor in Sri Lanka. Coastal mudflats and tidal flats in the north and north-west are the most plausible areas to check. A documented southern record occurred at Bundala on 4 November 2010; do not describe it as a regular Bundala species.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Rare winter migrant/visitor; Sri Lankan records are few. The documented Bundala individual was seen in early November. Broad northern-winter timing (roughly Oct–Mar) is a cautious expectation, not evidence of regular annual occurrence.

species_description.text: A striking, medium-large kingfisher, about 28–31 cm, with a glossy black cap, lilac-purple back and wings, white neck and underparts, bright red bill and legs, and a blue rump. The flight is powerful and direct, showing contrasting blue and purple tones. In Sri Lanka it is a scarce winter visitor, usually associated with coastal habitats, estuaries, lagoons, mangroves and other large water bodies. Takes fish, crabs and other aquatic animals from a perch.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are broadly similar in plumage and are difficult to separate in the field. Bill size or slight colour differences are not reliable enough for routine sexing.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less glossy purple and black, and may show browner or sooty tones. The bill and legs are less intensely red than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: The black cap, white throat/underparts, purple body and red bill make it distinctive. Check coastal mangroves, estuary margins and lagoon edges. It is much less frequently encountered than the resident kingfishers.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Scarce migrant to Sri Lanka, chiefly recorded along the coast. CBC photographic records include Thalpitiya, Wadduwa; other suitable coastal wetlands and estuaries may hold occasional birds during the northern winter.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter visitor, mainly during the northern winter months. CBC records include November and February; treat October–March as a broad expected window rather than a strict arrival/departure period.

species_description.text: A robust, medium-sized kingfisher (about 28 cm) with a chocolate-brown head and breast, brilliant turquoise-blue back and wings, white throat and breast band, and a large red bill. It is highly adaptable and occurs in wetlands, paddy fields, gardens, parks, coastal scrub, mangroves and open countryside, often far from water. Feeds on fish, frogs, crabs, insects, earthworms and small reptiles, frequently hunting from wires or exposed branches. Nests in a tunnel excavated in an earthen bank.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in plumage. Both show the brown head and breast, white throat, blue wings and red bill.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller than adults, with less vivid blue and brown plumage and a darker bill; the gape and bill colour brighten as they mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: One of the easiest kingfishers to recognise: brown head/chest, white throat and bright blue wings. Often perches on telephone wires and fences and may catch prey far from water. Its loud rattling call often reveals its presence.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Very common resident across Sri Lanka, from lowlands to hills, in both wet and dry zones. Common around gardens, paddy fields, canals, tanks, marshes and coastal habitats.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding activity is reported through much of the year, with strongest activity around April–July; nests are tunnels in vertical earth banks. A documented artificial nest-box use occurred at Moratuwa in December 2020.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, distinctive kite (about 44–56 cm) with chestnut body, white head and breast, dark flight feathers and broad wings. Common around coasts, estuaries, rivers, reservoirs, lakes, fishing harbours and open lowlands. An opportunistic feeder taking fish, crabs, carrion, insects and other small prey; often scavenges around fishing activity. Builds a stick nest in trees, usually near water.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female look alike; female is generally slightly larger. Plumage is not a reliable sex discriminator.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are mostly brown, streaked and mottled, lacking the clean white head and chestnut body of adults. The adult pattern develops gradually over successive moults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the contrasting white head and breast against the rich chestnut body. Often circles over water or perches near fishing boats; may feed while holding prey in its feet in flight.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common across Sri Lanka's lowlands, especially coastal areas, lagoons, reservoirs, rivers and urban waterways. Frequently seen around Colombo, Negombo, Chilaw, Bundala and major inland tanks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Common resident throughout the year. Numbers and visibility may fluctuate locally with food availability, water levels and fishing activity.

species_description.text: A striking forest-dwelling trogon, about 31–32 cm long, with a broad graduated tail and short, heavy bill. The adult male has a dark head and breast, a narrow white breast band, warm orange-brown upperparts and vivid red underparts; the wings are finely barred. The female is more subdued, with brownish or orange-brown head and upperparts and buffy underparts. Usually sits quietly in the mid-storey of evergreen and moist deciduous forest, often in pairs or small groups. Eats mainly insects such as caterpillars, beetles and cicadas, occasionally other small invertebrates and fruit. Nests in cavities excavated in decaying trunks or stumps.

male_female_identification.text: Strong sexual dimorphism. Male has a dark head and breast, white breast band and bright crimson lower breast/belly. Female is mainly warm brown/orange-brown above and buff below, lacking the male's black-and-red contrast. Both sexes have barred wings and long graduated tails.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Fledglings are documented in Sri Lanka. Young birds are duller and browner than adult males, with softer, less contrasting plumage; they may resemble females until adult male colours develop. CBC image archive includes a fledgling photographed at Sinharaja in May.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search shaded forest trails and mid-storey perches, especially where mixed-species flocks move. The male's red belly and white breast band are conspicuous; the female is more cryptic. Trogons often sit motionless before making short sallies after insects.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in forested parts of Sri Lanka, especially wet-zone rainforests and foothill forests, but also recorded in suitable moist forest elsewhere. Reliable locations include Sinharaja, Kitulgala/Makandawa, Morapitiya and Boralugoda; it occurs locally up to about 1,800 m.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding records indicate approximately March–June, with older accounts noting March and April as the main period. Treat this as a reported window, not a fixed annual schedule.

species_description.text: Distinctive, medium-sized treeswift (about 19–21 cm) with long pointed wings, deeply forked tail, dark upperparts, pale underparts and a narrow crest. Often perches upright on exposed dead branches and sallies after flying insects. Unlike typical swifts, it regularly perches and nests on exposed branches; the tiny nest is glued to a horizontal branch with saliva.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a more prominent dark crest and darker facial markings; female usually has a paler, buffier face and less strongly developed crest. Differences can be subtle at distance.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immatures are duller, with less distinct crest and softer facial pattern; pale feather fringes may be visible in close photographs.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for birds perched conspicuously on bare branches or snags, often in pairs. The upright posture, crest and deeply forked tail distinguish it from ordinary swifts; observe their repeated aerial sallies.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, chiefly in dry and intermediate zones and open woodland, including Yala, Bundala, Udawalawe, Minneriya and other dry-zone landscapes. Usually seen in pairs or small groups over open woodland.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is seasonal, often associated with drier periods, but local nesting dates should be verified rather than generalized across the island.

species_description.text: Small, active, slender forest bird, about 12–13 cm, with a short bill and conspicuous white wing-bar. Sri Lankan birds are the endemic subspecies H. p. leggei. Occurs in forest and wooded foothills, often moving with mixed-species feeding flocks. Feeds on small insects and spiders, gleaned from leaves and twigs or caught in short aerial sallies.

male_female_identification.text: Male has black upperparts, head and breast markings with a bold white wing patch/bar. Female is browner or greyer above, with less sharply contrasting dark markings; sexes are less strikingly different than in minivets.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, often with buff scaling or pale fringes on the upperparts and less sharply defined wing markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for a tiny bird flicking through foliage in mixed flocks. The white wing-bar flashes during short flights. It often moves continuously and rarely remains at one perch for long.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in wooded lowlands and hills, particularly forest and foothill habitats. CBC records include Ambewela, Passara, Nilgala and the wet/intermediate-zone foothills; endemic subspecies leggei occurs in Sri Lanka.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan nesting season mainly February–August. The small lichen-camouflaged cup nest is placed on a horizontal branch, often near a dead branch tip; both sexes incubate.

species_description.text: A medium-large, hawk-like cuckoo (about 34 cm), with grey-brown upperparts, pale underparts marked with fine dark barring, a long tail with dark bars, yellow eye-ring and yellow legs. It inhabits wooded gardens, groves, plantations and forest, often in hill country and foothills. Feeds mainly on caterpillars and other insects, sometimes fruit. Like many cuckoos, it is a brood parasite; in Sri Lanka it is associated with babbler hosts.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in plumage and difficult to distinguish in the field. Both have the hawk-like silhouette, barred underparts and long barred tail.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble adults but are generally browner, with less crisp barring and sometimes warmer/rufous tones. The hawk-like shape can cause confusion with a Shikra; check the tail pattern, bill and flight behaviour carefully.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often heard before seen. Its loud, repeated, rising whistles can continue for long periods, including at night during breeding. Search wooded gardens and forest edges; beware of confusing its hawk-like posture with a Shikra.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in the central hills and foothills as the Sri Lankan race ciceliae; additional migrant birds from the Indian population may occur in lowlands. Often heard in wooded areas, gardens and plantations, including the Peradeniya/Kandy hill-country landscape.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident with some seasonal movement; CBC records R/M. Sri Lankan breeding is reported earlier than in much of India, approximately January–April in some local accounts; dates should be treated as approximate.

species_description.text: Elegant, long-legged wader (about 33–36 cm) with very long pink to reddish legs, a fine straight black bill, white body and contrasting dark wings/back. Usually forages in shallow freshwater and brackish wetlands, lagoons, saltpans, paddy fields and marshes. Eats aquatic insects, small crustaceans, worms and other invertebrates; feeds by picking and probing in shallow water. Nests on bare ground or low islands near water.

male_female_identification.text: Male generally has a glossier, blacker back (sometimes greenish sheen); female often shows a browner back. Head and neck black pattern varies individually and seasonally, so sexing is not always certain.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are greyer/browner above with pale sandy or whitish feather fringes, duller legs and less sharply contrasting plumage. First-winter birds retain some juvenile feathering.

field_spotting_tips.text: The extremely long pink legs and needle-like bill are diagnostic. Watch for a characteristic scissoring stride in shallow water and flocks feeding in flooded fields. In flight, legs trail well beyond the tail and the black-and-white pattern is conspicuous.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs widely in suitable wetlands, especially the Dry Zone; also in western wetlands and coastal lagoons. Colombo/Gampaha marshes, Bellanwila, Pepiliyana, Lunawa, Bundala, lagoons and paddy wetlands are useful places to check. Wet Zone numbers can increase markedly in the northern winter.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident and migrant components occur in Sri Lanka. Numbers generally rise during the north-east winter migration, approximately Oct–Apr, while breeding/resident birds may be present year-round. Local breeding has also been recorded in some western wetlands; do not assume every Wet Zone bird is a migrant.

species_description.text: Large, fast-flying needletail (about 20–21 cm) with dark brown upperparts, a contrasting pale brown to whitish rump, dark underparts and long pointed wings. The tail is short and ends in stiff projecting shafts that give the 'needletail' name. Feeds on flying insects, often in fast, high flight over forests, hills and open country.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar and not safely separable in the field. Tail shape, rump contrast and overall structure are more useful than sex-specific plumage.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are poorly documented in field views and may show softer, less glossy plumage and pale feather fringes. Ageing should be left uncertain unless supported by close photographs.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for a large swift with long pointed wings and a pale rump, moving rapidly and often high overhead. A clear view of the tail shafts is helpful but rarely easy; photographs are valuable for confirmation.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Recorded in Sri Lanka as an uncommon or irregular visitor; sightings may occur over forested hills and open landscapes. Exact regular hotspots are not well established, so avoid treating any single site as dependable.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Occurrence is irregular and may be linked to seasonal movements or weather systems. Precise Sri Lankan months require further verification from dated records.

species_description.text: Small to medium swallow (about 13–14 cm) with dark brown to blackish upperparts, pale underparts and a relatively short, shallowly forked tail. Often has a dusky breast band or darker breast shading. Uses hills, open woodland, cliffs, ravines and nearby human structures; feeds on flying insects and may nest on cliffs or buildings.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage and not reliably separated in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller, with pale fringes to feathers and shorter tail streamers; age is difficult to judge at a distance.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch over ridges, valleys and open slopes. Its compact shape and short tail distinguish it from Barn Swallow; compare the underpart pattern and overall flight style with Sri Lanka Swallow.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, mainly in hill country and upland areas, including central highlands and surrounding foothills. Can be encountered over valleys, ridges, tea country and open slopes.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding timing is likely local and weather-dependent; exact Sri Lankan months need confirmation from nesting records.

species_description.text: Graceful, medium-sized swallow (about 17–19 cm) with glossy blue-black upperparts, rufous forehead and throat, pale underparts and a long deeply forked tail with streamers. Feeds on flying insects, usually low over fields, wetlands, lakes and coastal areas. Builds a mud cup nest, often on buildings and bridges, in its breeding range.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male usually has longer tail streamers and richer rufous throat than female; female is similar but often has shorter streamers and duller tones. Sex differences can be subtle outside breeding plumage.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have shorter tail streamers, duller upperparts and buffier/rufous facial tones; the throat and forehead are less intensely coloured than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for long tail streamers, rufous throat and fast, graceful low flight over water or fields. Often feeds in mixed flocks with other swallows and martins; check the tail shape and throat colour carefully.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common migrant throughout Sri Lanka, especially over wetlands, paddy fields, reservoirs, coasts and open agricultural country. Large roosting flocks can gather in reedbeds and marshes.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly a northern-winter visitor, commonly from about September/October to April/May; exact dates vary annually and among regions.

species_description.text: Large, elegant wetland bird (about 28–31 cm; breeding tail greatly lengthens) with very long toes and claws that distribute its weight on floating vegetation. Non-breeding birds have a dark brown crown/nape, white face and neck, chestnut hindneck and brown upperparts. Breeding adults develop a black cap and neck, golden-yellow hindneck and an extremely long pheasant-like central tail. Feeds on insects, larvae, small molluscs and other invertebrates picked from floating plants.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger and more dominant, and may mate with several males. Male is smaller and undertakes incubation and care of the young. In breeding plumage, both sexes can show the long tail, so size/behaviour and context are more useful than plumage alone.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble non-breeding adults but are duller, with less sharply defined head and neck pattern and shorter toes/tail. Young birds may be seen following the male among floating vegetation.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for exceptionally long toes as it walks over water lilies and floating plants. In breeding season the long tail is unmistakable; outside breeding season, identify by the white face/neck, chestnut hindneck and long toes. Observe floating vegetation rather than open mud alone.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs at freshwater lakes, tanks, marshes and vegetated lagoons across the island. Notable sites include Giant's Tank, Tissa Tank, Bundala, and many Dry Zone irrigation tanks; also occurs in suitable Wet Zone wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident and visible year-round in suitable wetlands. Breeding activity depends on water levels and wetland conditions; no single island-wide breeding window is assigned here.

species_description.text: The world's largest tern (about 47–56 cm), with a massive bright red-orange bill, black legs, pale grey upperwings and white body. Breeding adults have a full black cap; non-breeding adults show a streaked grey-white forehead and reduced dark cap. Feeds mainly on fish, caught by plunge-diving, and also takes aquatic invertebrates. Uses coastal lagoons, estuaries, saltpans, large lakes and reservoirs; nests on open sandy or rocky ground outside Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; males are generally larger and heavier-billed. Head-cap changes are seasonal, not sexual.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show brownish mottling on the upperparts and streaking on the crown/forehead, with a reddish bill often dusky-tipped. Immatures gradually lose brown feathering; non-breeding adults have a less complete dark cap.

field_spotting_tips.text: Very large size and huge red bill make it unmistakable among other terns. In flight look for broad wings, shallowly forked tail and dark outer primary undersides; often rests on mudflats with smaller terns.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs at large coastal wetlands and saltpans, particularly Bundala and Yala lagoons; also reported at other lagoons and tanks. CBC status is R/M, indicating a resident and migrant component; numbers may rise during northern winter.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC Country List 2022 gives R/M. Records can occur in multiple months; winter influx may increase numbers. Treat monthly checklist records as presence evidence, not a measure of abundance.

species_description.text: Small, active monarch about 16 cm. Male is bright azure-blue with a black nape patch and narrow black eye-mask; female is duller blue-green above with greyish-white underparts and lacks the bold black nape. It sallies from perches to catch flying insects and often joins mixed-species flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Male bright blue with black nape and eye stripe; female duller blue-green with pale underparts and no black nape patch. Plumage differences are clear in good light.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brownish or grey-brown with buff scaling and little blue; young males gradually acquire blue plumage and the black nape.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a small blue bird making short aerial sallies from shaded mid-storey perches. Male's black nape patch is diagnostic; both sexes often flick wings and tail while foraging.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in wooded habitats across Sri Lanka, including forests, forest edges, plantations, gardens and riverine woodland. Found in both wet and dry zones, usually where there is adequate tree cover.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding in South Asian populations is generally spring to early summer; Sri Lankan nest dates need more local source checking. Nest is a neat cup suspended from a fork.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, dark, rather long-tailed bulbul, around 23–25 cm, with dark grey-brown body, darker head, pale eye and a square-ended tail. Usually occurs in noisy groups in forest canopy and edges, feeding on fruit, berries and insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; no reliable external field distinction. Slight size differences are not useful in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less contrasting head and softer feather texture; young birds may have a less defined pale eye.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for loud, harsh group calls in forest canopy. Its larger size, dark plumage and square-ended tail help separate it from other Sri Lankan bulbuls. Often moves in flocks through fruiting trees.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's wet-zone and central hill forests, including Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Knuckles and other forested uplands. Also occurs in India; the species is not endemic to Sri Lanka.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding timing is not firmly established in the sources consulted for this batch; avoid assigning a precise island-wide breeding window. Nest is a cup in vegetation.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List/local checklist convention: Sri Lanka Black-capped Bulbul E; Sri Lanka Yellow-eared Bulbul E; Red-vented Bulbul R; Square-tailed Bulbul R; White-browed Bulbul R; Yellow-browed Bulbul R. Square-tailed Bulbul is also native to India, so not endemic.

species_description.text: Very large gull (roughly 55–72 cm), with a powerful bill, pale grey upperparts and broad wings. Adult breeding plumage has a distinctive dark chocolate-brown hood (often appearing black at distance), white body and pale grey wings; feeds on fish, aquatic invertebrates and other available prey. Winters around large lakes, lagoons, estuaries and coastal mudflats; breeds inland around central Asian lakes.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; male is generally larger. Hood development is seasonal rather than a sex difference.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and mottled, with a dark bill and dark tail band; head and mantle gradually become paler through immature stages. Non-breeding adults lose the full hood and show dark ear/neck markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: A very large gull with a distinctive dark hood in breeding plumage, heavy bill and pale grey wings. In winter, look for dark ear/neck patches and size; compare carefully with other large gulls.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Scarce winter visitor, particularly on north-western and western coasts; check large lagoons, estuaries and saltpans. Oriental Bird Club notes it is mainly north-western, with occasional birds farther south on the western seaboard. Bundala and other large coastal wetlands are worth checking.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Limosa records Jan–Apr and Oct–Dec. Broadly a winter visitor; occurrence can be irregular and localised. Do not infer resident status from year-round checklist aggregations.

species_description.text: Large, compact fish-eagle (about 61–74 cm) with a grey head and breast, dark brown upperparts, pale belly and powerful hooked bill. Closely associated with freshwater lakes, reservoirs, rivers and marshes. Feeds mainly on fish, sometimes waterbirds and other aquatic prey; usually hunts from a perch or low flight over water. Nests in large trees near wetlands.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; plumage is similar. Adults show a grey head and breast contrasting with dark brown back and pale underparts; sexes are not readily separated in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and streakier, with less uniform grey on the head and breast; adult grey pattern develops gradually.

field_spotting_tips.text: Scan tall dead trees and forest edges overlooking reservoirs. Its grey head and breast, pale belly and heavy fish-eagle shape distinguish it from White-bellied Sea-eagle, which has a white head and tail.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Local but widespread around larger inland water bodies, especially in the Dry Zone. Look around large reservoirs and forest-fringed tanks in Wilpattu, Minneriya, Kaudulla, Wasgamuwa and Yala regions; also recorded at other substantial wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round (CBC 2022 R). Presence is tied to suitable fish-rich water bodies rather than a regular seasonal passage.

species_description.text: Large sea-eagle (about 66–85 cm) with a massive hooked bill, white head, breast and tail, and dark grey-brown wings and back. Found along coasts, estuaries, lagoons and large inland reservoirs. Feeds on fish, waterbirds, carrion and other animals, often taking fish near the surface or pirating prey. Builds a very large stick nest in a tall tree, usually near water.

male_female_identification.text: Female is noticeably larger than male, but plumage is alike. Adults have a white head, underparts and tail contrasting with dark upperparts; bill is massive and grey.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are mostly brown with pale streaking and mottling; the white head, breast and tail develop progressively over several years. Immatures can show variable intermediate plumage.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the broad, plank-like wings, short wedge-shaped white tail in adults and powerful bill. Often perches conspicuously near water or flies low over lagoons. Immatures are brown and lack the adult white head and tail.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident around Sri Lankan coasts and large reservoirs. Regular at Bundala, Yala, Kumana, Mannar, major tanks and coastal lagoons; often seen perched on exposed trees or circling over water.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round (CBC 2022 R). Local activity and breeding vary with food and water conditions; do not infer migration from seasonal changes in sightings.

species_description.text: Large, dark forest eagle (about 65–80 cm) with very broad, long wings and a relatively long tail. Adults are almost uniformly blackish-brown, with a small crest and pale barring visible on the tail and flight feathers. Often soars over forested hills and canopies; its broad wings and slow flight are distinctive. Feeds on birds, mammals and reptiles, and is especially known for taking nestlings and eggs from arboreal nests. Nests on large trees or cliff ledges in forested landscapes.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; plumage is similar in both sexes. Adults are dark overall with subtle pale barring, so sex cannot usually be determined from a single field view.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more mottled, with pale streaking or scaling on the body and more conspicuous pale markings on the wings and tail. The uniformly dark adult appearance develops gradually.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for an enormous dark eagle with long, broad wings and a slow, buoyant soaring style. It often flies low over the canopy and may glide with wings held in a shallow V.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in forested lowlands and hills, especially large tracts of wet-zone and montane forest. Can be encountered over forest reserves and wooded mountain slopes, but is generally less frequently seen than common lowland kites.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is associated with forest territories; precise Sri Lankan breeding months should be confirmed from local nest records.

species_description.text: Very large forest eagle-owl (about 50–60 cm) with prominent ear tufts, large orange-yellow eyes, a powerful bill and heavily patterned brown, buff and white plumage. The underparts are boldly streaked and barred; the upperparts are mottled for camouflage. Occupies forest, wooded hills, rocky slopes and forest edges, often near water but not restricted to it. Hunts mammals, birds, reptiles and other prey, usually from a perch. Nests on ledges or large branches.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; plumage is similar. Ear tufts and eye colour are shared by both sexes and should not be used to sex the bird.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are downy and paler, with softer brown-and-buff patterning; the bold adult barring and ear tufts become more obvious as they mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Its enormous size, long ear tufts, orange eyes and bold underpart streaking are diagnostic. Listen for deep booming hoots at night; do not confuse with Brown Fish-owl, which is more closely associated with water and has a different facial appearance.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in forested and wooded areas across Sri Lanka, especially large forest reserves and hilly landscapes. Occurs in both wet and dry-zone forests; often recorded in Wilpattu, Yala and other protected areas.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding months are not sufficiently verified for a reliable Sri Lanka-wide statement; nesting details vary among regional sources.

species_description.text: Large, bulky fish-owl (about 48–58 cm) with ear tufts, bright yellow eyes, a heavy brow, brown upperparts, finely streaked breast and a pale throat or bib. Strongly associated with wooded areas beside rivers, streams, lakes, tanks and wetlands, from lowlands to hills. Hunts from a perch, taking fish, freshwater crabs, frogs, reptiles and small mammals, often dropping into shallow water. Nests in natural tree cavities, large branch forks or sheltered ledges.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; plumage is broadly similar. No dependable sex-specific colour character for field use.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are softer and fluffier, with more diffuse streaking and pale down around the head and body. Adult ear tufts and crisp facial/breast pattern develop with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search shaded riverbanks and large waterside trees at dusk or after dark. Look for the yellow eyes, heavy brow, ear tufts and pale throat; its deep hoots and shrieks often reveal its presence.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident near water across Sri Lanka, including rivers, tanks, reservoirs and forest streams. Frequently reported from Wilpattu, Yala, Sinharaja and village tanks; can occur from lowlands into the hills.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding records and nesting chronology are not sufficiently documented here for a precise Sri Lankan month range.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, slender cuckooshrike, about 20 cm, with a contrasting dark head and upperparts and pale underparts; wings and tail are dark. It is an uncommon, local bird in Sri Lanka, usually in open woodland, forest edges and wooded dry-zone landscapes. Feeds mainly on insects, including caterpillars, taken from foliage or caught in short aerial sallies.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male has a blackish head and upperparts contrasting with pale underparts. Female is browner and greyer, with more obvious scaling or streaking on the underparts; exact pattern varies with age and subspecies.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner than adults, with pale fringes/scaling on the upperparts and more marked underparts. They can resemble a dull female until the adult dark head develops.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a small-to-medium cuckooshrike moving through the canopy or along woodland edges. Compare the dark-headed adult with Indian Cuckooshrike, which is larger and greyer overall. Calls and quiet movement can make it easy to overlook.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Uncommon and local resident in Sri Lanka. Search dry-zone and intermediate-zone woodland, scrub with scattered trees and forest margins; it is not generally a common wet-zone garden bird.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. A reliable Sri Lankan breeding-month window was not established in this batch; avoid assigning dates from other parts of its range.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 classification convention: resident (R). Confirm current CBC row-level code before publication.

species_description.text: Small, compact shrike about 19 cm, with a brown back, pale eyebrow, blackish eye-mask, pale buff underparts and a fairly long tail. Perches on exposed twigs, wires and bushes, watching for insects and occasionally small vertebrates. Uses open scrub, grassland edges, paddy bunds, plantations, gardens and forest clearings.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are broadly similar. Adult males tend to have a richer brown crown/back and stronger mask; females may show more barring on the flanks, but ageing and subspecies variation complicate sexing.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more heavily barred/scaly on the upperparts and underparts, with a less sharply defined facial mask. First-winter birds can retain barring.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a solitary bird on an exposed perch, with a dark bandit mask and brown back. It often makes short flights to catch prey and returns to the same lookout. Check for juvenile barring when ageing.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Migrant visitor across Sri Lanka, occurring in open and semi-open habitats from northern lowlands to the hills and wet-zone gardens. Regular at Wilpattu, Mannar, Jaffna, Colombo wetlands, Horton Plains and forest-edge clearings.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular northern-hemisphere winter migrant, generally arriving around October and departing by April/early May. Not a Sri Lankan breeder.

species_description.text: Medium-sized shrike, around 20–25 cm, with a long graduated tail, dark facial mask, grey crown, rufous-brown back and rump, pale underparts and dark wings. Often perches prominently on shrubs, fences and wires in open scrub, grassland, agricultural land and dry woodland. Hunts large insects, lizards and small birds.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; males tend to be more richly coloured, while females may show more barring below. Plumage forms vary geographically, including dark melanistic birds.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have browner, barred upperparts, a less extensive facial mask and vermiculated/buff-marked underparts. Immatures gradually acquire the cleaner adult pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Long tail, rufous back and dark mask are key. Check the locality: Sri Lankan records are concentrated in the north. Do not mistake Brown Shrike for it; Brown Shrike is a winter migrant with a browner overall appearance.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, especially in the north and north-west, including Mannar and Jaffna; uncommon or absent in much of the rest of the island. CBC records identify resident northern subspecies L. s. caniceps.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round in northern Sri Lanka. Breeding season and nesting details need a stronger Sri Lankan source; do not infer from mainland populations.

species_description.text: Large gull (about 52–64 cm), with a heavy yellow bill and dark grey to nearly black mantle in adults. Non-breeding adults show streaking on the head; legs usually yellow. Uses coasts, estuaries, lagoons, saltpans and refuse sites; feeds opportunistically on fish, invertebrates, carrion and discarded food. Breeds in colonies in northern Europe/Asia, not in Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Adult sexes are alike in field appearance; male averages larger. Adult mantle shade varies among subspecies and is useful but not sufficient alone for identification.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and heavily mottled/scaled, with a dark bill and variable pale-edged upperparts; they acquire adult-like grey mantle over several years. First-winter and immature birds retain brown wing coverts and tail markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for large size, dark mantle, yellow legs and bill, and broad-winged gull flight. Compare mantle shade, head streaking, leg colour and bill pattern with other large gulls; age and subspecies complicate ID.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A winter visitor to Sri Lanka, mainly along the coast. Check north-western and western shores, lagoons, estuaries and saltpans; Bundala and other large coastal wetlands can produce records. Avoid assuming every dark-backed gull is this species; identify subspecies/complex carefully.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Limosa monthly records show Sri Lankan records Sep–Apr, with peak winter occurrence; Birdfact GBIF/eBird-derived records indicate regular Sep–Apr. Individual records outside this window do not establish regular presence.
