species_description.text: Small, shy robin about 14 cm. Breeding male has deep blue upperparts, bright blue crown and back, orange-rufous throat and breast, and a white belly; female is olive-brown above with buffy underparts and a pale eye-ring. Feeds on insects and other small invertebrates, usually on or near the forest floor.

male_female_identification.text: Marked sexual dimorphism: male blue above with orange-rufous throat/breast; female olive-brown above, buff below and much less conspicuous. Non-breeding male may be duller with brownish feather edges.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and heavily scaled, with buff spots on the upperparts and breast; young males acquire blue and orange gradually.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search damp shaded ravines and leaf litter, especially near streams and in montane forest. Male's blue-and-orange plumage is striking but often stays low and skulking; female is easily overlooked as a plain brown bird.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter migrant to Sri Lanka from Himalayan breeding grounds. Mainly found in shaded forest undergrowth, montane forest, ravines, plantations and wooded gardens, especially in the central hills and wet-zone forests.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter visitor, generally from September/October to April/May. IUCN records Sri Lanka as a non-breeding range; birds leave for Himalayan breeding grounds in spring.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Pied Bushchat R (Sri Lankan hill subspecies atratus endemic); Sri Lanka Shama E; Oriental Magpie-robin R; Indian Robin R; Indian Blue Robin M.

species_description.text: A small pied woodpecker, about 17–18 cm, with black-and-white barred upperparts, pale underparts, a yellowish crown and nape, and a short stout bill. Usually occupies open dry woodland, scrub, thorn forest, plantations and scattered trees, often in pairs. Feeds on ants, termites, beetle larvae and other insects gleaned from bark and branches; it may forage low and occasionally on the ground.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a red patch on the crown; female has a yellow crown without red. The yellow forehead/crown and black-and-white back are useful marks in both sexes.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and less crisply marked; young males may show reduced red on the crown. Bill and facial markings are less sharply defined than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look in open scrub and dry woodland, often lower down on trunks and branches. Male's red crown patch is a key sex mark; the species is smaller and more pied than the larger flamebacks.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident, mainly in the dry lowlands and arid zone, including the north-western coast and Hambantota district; locally reaches foothills and open country east of the central hills. Recorded in Yala, Palatupana, Udawalawe and other dry-zone sites.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Local field accounts report breeding approximately June–August, with nesting in a tree cavity. The period should be treated as an observed regional window, not an invariant annual season.

species_description.text: Small sunbird about 10 cm. Adult male has glossy green crown and upperparts, iridescent purple rump and throat, dark chest and bright yellow belly; female is olive-brown above with yellowish underparts and pale throat. Usually perches while feeding on nectar, but can hover briefly; also takes insects and spiders.

male_female_identification.text: Male is iridescent with purple rump and dark throat/chest, yellow belly; female is olive above with yellow-buff underparts and whitish throat. Male is readily distinguished from Purple Sunbird by its brighter yellow belly and purple rump.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immature males resemble females before acquiring iridescent adult plumage; juveniles are dull olive-brown above and pale yellow below.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for a tiny sunbird visiting flowers in gardens. The male's purple rump and yellow belly are key; female's whitish throat helps distinguish it from female Purple Sunbird.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident throughout Sri Lanka in gardens, scrub, plantations, open woodland and forest edges, especially wherever flowering shrubs and trees are available.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident; may breed over an extended period and sometimes raise more than one brood. Nest is a hanging pouch of plant fibres, cobwebs and lichens, usually built by female.

species_description.text: Large dark, heavy-bodied stork with bare yellowish-orange head, thick bill, dark grey-brown plumage and white belly. Eats carrion and animal prey including fish, frogs, reptiles and large invertebrates. Uses wetlands, open country and forest edges; nests in trees.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes similar; males average larger with heavier bill. Bare head and massive bill characteristic.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds duller and browner, with more feathering on head/neck and less-developed bare-part colours.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search large trees and open wetland margins. Hunched posture, bare yellow-orange head, heavy bill and dark body distinguish it.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident but uncommon and local, especially lowland dry-zone wetlands, marshes and open country; reported from Yala, Bundala, Kumana and northern wetland landscapes.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident; records scattered and no dependable seasonal migration pattern established.

species_description.text: Large, long-billed shorebird (about 37–41 cm) with a long, slightly upturned bill, long legs and relatively short tail. Non-breeding birds are grey-brown above and pale below; breeding birds develop rich rufous/chestnut head, neck and underparts. In flight, the rump and tail are barred rather than showing the Black-tailed Godwit's sharply black tail and broad white wingbar. Feeds on worms, molluscs and crustaceans by probing mud and sand.

male_female_identification.text: Female is generally larger with a longer bill; breeding female tends to be paler and less richly rufous than male. Sexes are difficult to distinguish in non-breeding plumage without close comparison.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show warm buff fringes on the upperparts and pale buff breast with fine streaking. They are less richly coloured than breeding adults and gradually become grey-brown in their first winter.

field_spotting_tips.text: Compare with Black-tailed Godwit: Bar-tailed has a more upturned bill, shorter legs, and barred rump/tail in flight; Black-tailed has a conspicuous white wingbar and black tail. In breeding plumage, both become rufous, so use structure and flight pattern.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter visitor to coastal mudflats, lagoons, estuaries and sandy shores. Recorded at Bundala, Mannar, Puttalam and other suitable coastal wetlands; often associates with other large waders and godwits.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Migrant, mainly Aug–Apr, with northern-winter presence. CBC lists M; Sri Lanka checklists and trip reports confirm occurrence at Bundala and other coastal sites. Exact monthly abundance varies by site and year.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC 2022 Country List classification should be used as source of truth; current workbook retains M, consistent with migratory winter occurrence. Verify line-level status before publication.

species_description.text: Large, long-billed wader (about 36–44 cm) with long dark legs and a long, straight to slightly upturned bill. Non-breeding birds are grey-brown above and pale below, with a pale supercilium and barred tail; breeding plumage is rich orange/chestnut on the head, neck and breast. In flight, a broad white wingbar and black tail are diagnostic. Feeds on worms, molluscs, aquatic insects and other invertebrates in mudflats, shallow lagoons and flooded fields.

male_female_identification.text: Female is usually larger and has a longer bill; breeding female often has paler, less saturated orange underparts than the male. Bill length and plumage vary, and sexing distant non-breeding birds is unreliable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are warm buff on the head and breast, with neat pale fringes on the upperparts. They are less streaked than adults in breeding plumage and gradually become greyer through the first winter.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for long straight bill, long legs and conspicuous white wingbar with black tail in flight. Compare with Bar-tailed Godwit: Black-tailed has a straighter bill and stronger white wingbar/black tail contrast. In non-breeding plumage, note the clean pale underparts and grey-brown upperparts.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Regular winter visitor to coastal wetlands, lagoons, estuaries and saltpans, especially Bundala, Mannar, Puttalam and other extensive mudflats. Also uses flooded fields and inland wetlands. Large flocks have been recorded at Bundala.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly a winter migrant, broadly Aug/Sep–Apr, with peak numbers generally during Oct–Mar. CBC status M; Sri Lanka trip reports record substantial flocks at Bundala.

species_description.text: Small munia about 11 cm, with dark brown upperparts, chestnut-brown underparts and a black throat and upper breast in adult male; female is browner and less sharply marked. Sri Lankan form is kelaarti. Feeds on grass seeds and small grains in flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Male has black throat and upper breast with rich chestnut belly; female is browner with less sharply defined black throat. Sex differences can be subtle outside breeding plumage.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are dull brown above and buff-brown below, lacking the adult male's black throat and rich chestnut belly.

field_spotting_tips.text: Check flocks in grassy scrub and field edges. Adult male's black throat and chestnut belly help distinguish it; do not label the species endemic—the Sri Lankan subspecies is near-endemic.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs in scrub, grassland, forest edges and cultivated areas, especially in the northern and eastern dry zone and locally in hills. The species also occurs in southern India; Sri Lankan population is near-endemic subspecies kelaarti.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Breeding timing in Sri Lanka varies locally and should be confirmed from nest records; likely linked to rains and grass-seed availability.

species_description.text: Small, compact munia about 11 cm. Adult breeding male has glossy black head, throat and upper breast, chestnut back and wings, and white lower belly; female is duller with brown head and less extensive black. Feeds mainly on grass seeds and grains, often in flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Male has black head/throat and chestnut back; female has brown head and less black, with paler underparts. Non-breeding plumage is duller.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are mostly brown and lack the adult black head and chestnut contrast; adult plumage develops gradually.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for small flocks feeding on grass seeds. Adult male's black head and chestnut back are diagnostic; compare with Scaly-breasted Munia, which has a scaly breast and no black head.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open grassland, scrub, paddy fields, cultivation and reed margins; often in small flocks in dry and intermediate lowlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Breeding season varies with rainfall and food; local Sri Lankan nesting months require further verification. Nest is a domed grass structure.

species_description.text: Small munia about 11–12 cm, with brown upperparts, pale underparts and distinctive dark, scale-like crescent markings on breast and flanks. Adult male and female are similar; feeds on grass seeds, rice and other grains, often in large flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike and difficult to distinguish in the field. Adult has a conspicuous scaly pattern on breast and flanks; bill is stout and bluish-grey.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are plain brown above and buff below, without the adult's scaly breast pattern; scaling develops as feathers mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for flocks feeding on grass seeds. The scale-like breast pattern is diagnostic in adults; juveniles are plain and can be mistaken for other munias.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident in open country, grassland, paddy fields, scrub, gardens and cultivation across Sri Lanka. Often gathers in large flocks and roosts communally.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding often follows rains and availability of grass seeds; Sri Lankan breeding months vary by region and need direct local source confirmation.

species_description.text: Small, slender munia about 11–12 cm, with dark brown upperparts, pale underparts and a conspicuous white rump visible in flight. Bill is short and stout; feeds on grass seeds and grain in small flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar. White rump and dark tail are key features; slight plumage differences are not reliable for sexing.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller brown with buff underparts and a less contrasting rump; adult white rump becomes clearer with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for the bright white rump when birds fly up from grass or scrub. Compare with Scaly-breasted Munia: White-rumped lacks the adult's scaly breast pattern.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in forest edges, scrub, grassland, gardens and cultivation, from lowlands to foothills. Often occurs in pairs or small flocks and may join mixed munia flocks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Breeding season varies with rainfall and food availability; Sri Lankan nest timing needs further verification. Builds a domed grass nest in vegetation.

species_description.text: Medium-sized forest hawk (about 38–48 cm) with broad rounded wings, a long tail and a prominent crest. Adults are dark brown above with pale underparts marked by strong dark bars; the head has a dark cap and distinct pale throat markings. Inhabits evergreen and mixed forests, wooded hills and forest edges, often hunting birds and small mammals with rapid ambush flights. Builds a stick nest in a tree.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male, while plumage is broadly similar. Adult birds show a raised crest, barred underparts and contrasting pale throat; size difference is most apparent in a pair.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more buff below, with longitudinal streaking or less distinct barring; the adult's crisp dark barring and head pattern become clearer with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: A raised crest, rounded wings and long tail help identify it. It often moves quickly through the canopy or along forest edges; listen for loud, repeated calls.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in forested lowlands and hills, including wet-zone and montane forest blocks. Look for it in large forest reserves and wooded landscapes rather than open paddy fields.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Breeding timing in Sri Lanka should be treated as incompletely documented here; avoid assigning exact months without a local nest-record source.

species_description.text: Small to medium-sized forest eagle (about 46–61 cm), relatively slender with long wings and a long tail. Adults are dark brown above with rich rufous underparts and a pale throat; the head can look dark and the underwing shows contrasting pale areas. Inhabits mature forest and wooded hills, hunting birds, mammals and reptiles. Usually perches quietly within canopy and makes fast surprise attacks; nests in tall forest trees.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; plumage is similar. Adult rufous underparts and dark upperparts are characteristic, but sex is not reliably determined by plumage.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally paler and more streaked below, with less saturated rufous tones and a less crisp adult pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch forest canopy and ridgelines for a compact eagle with long wings and tail. Do not confuse with larger Changeable Hawk-eagle; note the smaller size, rufous belly and forest association.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Uncommon and local in forested areas, especially the wet-zone and hill forests. Potential areas include Sinharaja, Knuckles, Peak Wilderness and other large forest blocks; sightings are often brief and canopy-level.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident (CBC 2022 R). Records are sparse and detection varies with forest access and observer effort.

species_description.text: Endemic, tiny (c.13 cm), predominantly green parrot with red forehead/crown and rump, orange-washed nape, blue underwing and blue chin patch in males. Arboreal; feeds on fruit, seeds, buds, blossoms and nectar in forest, woodland, gardens and coconut groves.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a distinct blue chin/throat patch; female has much less blue and is generally duller.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles mostly green, with dull facial colours, greenish/orange-brown bill and little or no blue on throat; adult red crown and rump develop with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for sharp squeaky whistles overhead; scan canopy. Scarlet rump flashes in flight; male's blue chin patch is useful at close range.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Across Sri Lanka from lowlands to c.1,600 m, most plentiful in south-west wet zone and foothills; sparse in far north and parts of dry zone. Sinharaja, Kitulgala and Kanneliya are productive areas.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round with local movements following fruit and flowers. Breeding begins around January; nesting commonly March–May in tree cavities.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 42–50 පමණ දිගැති මධ්‍යම ප්‍රමාණයේ dabbling duck එකකි. පිරිමිගේ chestnut හිස, කහ පැහැති forehead සහ අළු ශරීරය කැපී පෙනේ. ගැහැනු දුඹුරු-රතු mottled පැහැති. වැව්, කලපු, marshes සහ ජලජ තණබිම්; බොහෝවිට ජලයේ මතුපිට ශාක කොටස් සහ තණ කමින් සිටී. ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් ශාකභක්ෂකයි. ලංකාවේ ප්‍රජනනය නොකරන ශීත සංචාරකයෙකි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි: රතු-දුඹුරු හිස සහ කහ forehead, අළු පැහැති ශරීරය. ගැහැනු: රතු-දුඹුරු/දුඹුරු mottled ශරීරය, අළු පැහැය අඩු. Eclipse male ගැහැනුට සමාන විය හැක; wing pattern සහ bill colour බලන්න. Juvenile ගැහැනුට සමාන.

field_spotting_tips.text: පිරිමිගේ රතු හිස සහ කහ forehead ඉතා හඳුනාගත හැක. බොහෝවිට තණකොළ කන ලෙස ජල අද්දර හෝ shallow water හි පෙනේ. ගැහැනු හඳුනාගැනීමට bill shape සහ wing speculum/underwing pattern බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් විශාල පහළබිම් ජලාශ, කලපු සහ marshes. Bundala, Tissamaharama සහ වෙනත් දකුණු/වයඹ වෙරළබඩ තෙත්බිම්වල වාර්තා.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශීත සංචාරකයෙක්; සාමාන්‍යයෙන් ඔක්තෝබර්–අප්‍රේල්, වඩාත්ම නොවැම්බර්–මාර්තු (CBC 2022: M; eBird-derived seasonal summary).

species_description.text: Medium-sized bee-eater, about 20–22 cm, with a rich chestnut crown and nape, yellow throat, black eye-stripe, green upperparts and blue-green tail. It has a dark bill and a relatively compact shape compared with Blue-tailed Bee-eater. Feeds on bees, wasps, dragonflies and other flying insects, usually hawking from a perch. Occurs in a wide range of lowland and mid-elevation habitats, including open woodland, forest edges, scrub, farmland and national parks. Excavates a nesting tunnel in soft earth banks or sandy ground, sometimes in colonies.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are very similar in colour and pattern; reliable sexing in the field is difficult. Both show the chestnut crown, yellow throat and black eye-stripe.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less intense chestnut on the crown and softer yellow throat colour; tail streamers and adult feather definition are less developed.

field_spotting_tips.text: The chestnut head and yellow throat are the key marks. Often seen in small groups or colonies around exposed sandy banks during nesting. Less trusting than Blue-tailed Bee-eater; approach nesting colonies cautiously and avoid disturbance.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread breeding resident in Sri Lanka from lowlands to mid-hills, in both wet- and dry-zone landscapes. Recorded in wet-zone forest reserves and dry-zone parks; well-known locations include Wilpattu, Yala, Lunugamvehera, Kitulgala and forest patches near Colombo.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding activity in Sri Lanka is reported mainly from about mid-February to May, when pairs excavate nesting burrows in sandy or soft earth banks.

species_description.text: Small, slender bee-eater, around 16–18 cm, with predominantly green plumage, a black eye-stripe, blue cheek/throat area and a slender black bill. Depending on subspecies and individual, the crown and throat show blue or turquoise tones and the underparts are greenish to yellowish. Frequently perches on wires, dry twigs and low exposed branches in open dry, arid and intermediate-zone country, scrub, farmland and grassland. Eats bees, wasps, dragonflies, beetles and other flying insects, often returning to the same perch. Nests in a tunnel excavated in a sandy or earthen bank.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar. In some populations males have slightly longer central tail feathers, but this is subtle and not a dependable field sexing feature in Sri Lanka.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller green, with less distinct blue on the face/throat and shorter tail feathers. The black eye-stripe may be less sharply defined than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Smallest and most frequently encountered local bee-eater. Look for its green body, black eye-stripe, blue facial patch and habit of returning repeatedly to an exposed perch. Often dust-bathes on sandy tracks and roosts communally.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident in the dry, arid and intermediate zones of Sri Lanka, including open country, scrub, farmland and coastal plains. Often encountered in pairs or small groups and at communal roosts.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Breeding occurs in the dry-season/spring period in many parts of its range; a March–June period is reported in general species accounts, but local Sri Lankan timing can vary with soil and rainfall conditions.

species_description.text: A slender, long-tailed bee-eater, about 23–30 cm including the elongated central tail streamers. Adults have a green body, blue tail and rump, chestnut throat, black eye-stripe and a narrow blue line below it. Feeds almost entirely on flying insects, especially bees, wasps, dragonflies and other large insects, caught from exposed perches. Occurs in open country, wetlands, coastal areas, scrub, farmland and riverbanks; often forms noisy flocks and communal roosts. Nests in tunnels excavated in sandy banks or flat sandy ground.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike or very similar in overall plumage. Tail streamers are usually longer in adult males, but wear and age affect their length; do not rely on streamer length alone to sex a distant bird.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles lack or have much shorter central tail streamers, and their colours are duller; the throat may be less richly chestnut and the black eye-stripe less sharply defined. Adult tail streamers grow with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for long central tail streamers, blue tail/rump, chestnut throat and black eye-stripe. Flocks hawk insects over lagoons, fields and coastal scrub. Distinguish from Chestnut-headed Bee-eater by the blue tail and longer streamers.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A regular migrant and passage/winter visitor in Sri Lanka, with occasional lingering and breeding reports in the south-east. Frequently seen around Bundala, Kalametiya and other coastal wetlands, lagoons and open lowlands during the northern winter.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly present during the northern winter, with numbers increasing around October–November and declining through March; many depart by late spring. CBC classifies it R/M because a resident/breeding component or occasional breeding records are also recognised. Avoid describing every individual as a winter migrant.

species_description.text: Small, compact dark waterbird (about 50 cm) with short stout bill, rounded/steep forehead, short neck and relatively long tail. Adults are glossy black; feeds mainly on fish by diving. Uses ponds, tanks, rivers, paddy-field channels, lagoons and estuaries; often perches with wings spread to dry.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are essentially alike in field plumage; males average somewhat larger. Breeding adults can show tiny pale facial filoplumes/spots; these are not a reliable sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles and non-breeding birds are browner and duller, often with pale or whitish throat and brownish underparts; adult gloss develops with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Smallest and most compact of the three regular cormorants; short bill, dark eye and long-looking tail. Often feeds alone or in small groups; compare carefully with Indian Cormorant.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Very common and widespread in Sri Lankan lowland wetlands, including village tanks, rivers, paddy fields, urban ponds and lagoons. Often the most frequently encountered cormorant.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident (CBC 2022 R); seen throughout the year. Breeding is not assigned a precise island-wide month window here because local timing varies and a robust Sri Lanka source was not located.

species_description.text: A medium-sized, uniformly rich rufous-brown woodpecker, about 25–27 cm, with a slightly shaggy or barred appearance and a long, strong bill. It is associated with forest, plantations and wooded lowlands, often feeding on ants and termites, especially from decaying wood and ant nests. Unlike most woodpeckers, it may forage on the ground, on rotten logs and around termite or ant nests. Nests in a cavity in a tree.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a red moustachial stripe; female has a dark or black moustachial stripe. Plumage is otherwise similar, with the overall rufous colour distinctive.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and less richly rufous, with less distinct facial markings. The male's red moustachial stripe develops with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Its plain rufous-brown colour makes it unlike the barred or boldly patterned woodpeckers. Search decaying logs, ant nests and lower tree trunks; it may descend to the ground to feed. The male's red moustache is a close-view sexing mark.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident but uncommon and local in Sri Lanka's low country, especially wooded wet-zone and intermediate-zone areas and forest edges. Records include Ingiriya, Haldummulla, Kitulgala and other forested lowland locations; not usually a common garden bird.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. A Sri Lankan breeding period of approximately January–May is reported; nests are cavities excavated in trees, sometimes relatively low on the trunk.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): resident (R) for all non-endemic woodpeckers; endemic (E) for Crimson-backed Flameback. Red-backed Flameback Dinopium psarodes is now treated as a separate endemic species; taxonomy differs from older CBC treatment. Confirm latest CBC row mapping before publication.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, broad-winged kite (about 48–60 cm) with long wings, slightly forked tail and variable plumage. Sri Lankan birds are generally associated with open country, wetlands, agricultural landscapes, towns and coastal areas. Feeds opportunistically on small mammals, birds, reptiles, insects, fish and carrion; frequently scavenges around refuse and fishing sites. Builds a stick nest in trees or other elevated structures.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in plumage; females are usually larger. Dark and paler plumage forms/subspecies occur across the species' wide range, so colour variation should not automatically be interpreted as sex.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked, with pale feather edges and a less sharply defined head pattern. Plumage varies among geographic forms.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for long, slightly angled wings and a shallowly forked tail. Often soars in groups over towns or follows food sources; distinguish from Brahminy Kite by its less contrasting plumage.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident and widespread in Sri Lanka, especially lowlands, towns, agricultural areas, wetlands and coastal settlements. Regularly seen over Colombo and other urban areas, reservoirs, paddy fields and fishing harbours.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Local abundance can change with food supply, weather and roosting behaviour; no fixed migrant season should be assigned to the resident Sri Lankan population.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) is the preferred local authority; status recorded here is provisional pending direct row/subspecies cross-check. R = resident; M = regular migrant. For mixed populations/subspecies retain R/M.

species_description.text: Slender wagtail about 18–19 cm with grey upperparts, yellow face and underparts in breeding plumage, white wing-bars and a constantly bobbing tail. Non-breeding birds are duller grey and yellow-white; feeds on insects along streams, ponds, lawns and wet fields.

male_female_identification.text: Adult breeding male has bright yellow face and underparts with grey back; female and non-breeding birds are duller, often yellowish-white below with less distinct markings.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are grey-brown above and pale buff below, with weak yellow tones and less sharply defined wing-bars.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a slim grey wagtail with yellow underparts bobbing its tail beside running water. In non-breeding plumage it can be much paler; check the grey back and yellow wash.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Migrant to Sri Lanka, often in highlands and lowlands near streams, reservoirs, paddy fields, gardens and wet grassland. Common wintering locations include Nuwara Eliya, Horton Plains, Victoria Park and wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter migrant, generally August/September–April. Limosa open records show Aug–Apr with some gaps; peak numbers often during northern winter.

species_description.text: Wagtail complex about 16–18 cm, with long tail, white outer tail feathers and variable head and underpart colours among subspecies. Sri Lankan winter visitors include several western and eastern forms; males may have yellow or pale underparts and distinctive head patterns. Feeds on insects in wet fields and along water.

male_female_identification.text: Highly variable by subspecies and season. Breeding males from different populations have distinct head patterns; females and non-breeding birds are duller and often yellowish or whitish below. Do not assume one single male/female pattern for all birds.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are dull grey-brown above with pale buff/yellowish underparts and weak head pattern; subspecies identification can be difficult.

field_spotting_tips.text: Observe head pattern, ear-coverts, throat and back carefully; photograph from multiple angles. Yellow wagtail taxonomy is complex, and eastern tschutschensis may be treated as a separate species, so avoid overconfident subspecies claims.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Migrant to Sri Lanka in wetlands, paddy fields, reservoirs, coastal marshes, grasslands and open country. Several subspecies and populations may occur; taxonomic treatment of Eastern Yellow Wagtail as separate species varies among authorities.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter migrant, mainly August/September–April. Limosa records Western Yellow Wagtail Jan–Apr, Aug, Oct–Dec; some records may be assigned differently under revised taxonomy.

species_description.text: Small, plain flycatcher about 12–13 cm, with grey-brown upperparts, pale grey-brown breast, whitish belly, dark bill and legs, and a subtle pale eye-ring. Feeds on flying insects from exposed or shaded perches, often making quick sallies and returning to the same spot.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar and difficult to separate in the field. Male may show slightly darker upperparts and more distinct eye-ring, but this is not dependable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are spotted and scaled, with buff-edged feathers on upperparts and breast; they gradually become plain grey-brown.

field_spotting_tips.text: Very plain brown flycatcher with a pale eye-ring and whitish belly. Compare breast colour and bill: Asian Brown is generally greyer and paler below than Brown-breasted Flycatcher. It frequently returns to the same perch after catching insects.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common winter migrant throughout Sri Lanka in gardens, parks, plantations, scrub, forest edges and wooded wetlands. Often occurs near human habitation and can be found in both lowlands and hills.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular winter migrant, usually September/October–April/May. Limosa monthly checklist records Jan–Apr and Sep–Dec.

species_description.text: Small, compact flycatcher about 12–13 cm, with grey-brown upperparts, warm buff-brown breast and flanks, pale belly and fine bill. It often sits quietly in shaded lower and middle storeys, making short sallies for insects and returning to the same perch.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are broadly similar; male may be slightly darker or more contrasting, but field sexing is unreliable without close views or song.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more heavily spotted/scaled on the upperparts and breast, with buff feather edges; adult breast becomes more uniformly warm brown.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a small brown flycatcher with a distinctly warm brown breast, often perched quietly in shade. Compare with Asian Brown Flycatcher: Brown-breasted is warmer and more buff below, usually with a stronger breast wash.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter migrant to Sri Lanka, using forest edges, plantations, gardens, wooded ravines and other shaded habitats in both lowlands and hills.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular migrant, generally present September–April, with some records in May. Limosa monthly records list Jan–Apr and Sep–Dec.

species_description.text: Large white stork with black flight feathers, bare orange-yellow face, long yellow bill and pink tertial feathers. Eats fish, frogs, aquatic invertebrates and small vertebrates in marshes, tanks and lagoons; nests colonially in trees near wetlands.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes look alike; males slightly larger. Yellow bill and pink tertials are key adult features.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles duller brown-grey on head/neck, with less contrasting plumage and less-developed pink tertials.

field_spotting_tips.text: Identify by white body, black flight feathers, yellow bill and pink tertials. Often feeds by tactile sweeping of its partly open bill.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in suitable wetlands, especially dry-zone tanks, marshes and lagoons; Bundala, Kumana, Yala, Vankalai/Mannar and Jaffna wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident; local abundance and breeding respond to rainfall, water levels and food availability.

species_description.text: Small, elusive montane stream thrush about 20 cm. Male is dark brownish-black with a blue sheen and blue spangling on forehead, supercilium, shoulder and breast; female is dark earth-brown above with warmer rufous-brown underparts. Both sexes have a small bright blue shoulder patch. Feeds on aquatic and terrestrial insects and other invertebrates along stream margins.

male_female_identification.text: Strong sexual dimorphism: male dark with blue sheen/spangles; female brown above and rufous-brown below. Both show a blue shoulder patch.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile resembles female but has paler, indistinct vertical streaking on the underparts and less developed blue markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Visit shaded montane streams at dawn or dusk and listen for the sharp, whistling 'sree' call. Birds often move low through streamside cover and feed among wet rocks. The male's blue sheen is striking in good light.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to high-elevation wet-zone mountains, generally above 900 m, in dense forest close to clear, fast-flowing streams, waterfalls and ravines. Favoured sites include Horton Plains, Peak Wilderness, Knuckles and streams around Nuwara Eliya.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding January–May, possibly with a second period in September. Nest placed on rock ledges beside waterfalls/rapids or in tree forks near streams.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 30–35 පමණ දිගැති ඉතා කුඩා ජලචර තාරාවෙකි. කෙටි හොට, වටකුරු හිස සහ කෙටි ගෙල නිසා අනෙක් තාරාවන්ට වඩා කුඩා පෙනුමක් ඇත. පිරිමිගේ හිස/ගෙල සුදු පැහැති අතර කළු තොප්පියක් සහ කළු පිට/පියාපත්; ගැහැනු අළු-දුඹුරු පැහැතිය. වැව්, පොකුණු, ජලජ ශාක බහුල නිශ්චල ජලය සහ ගස් අතු මත විවේක ගැනීම. ජලජ ශාක බීජ, කුඩා ජලජ අපෘෂ්ඨවංශීන් ආහාරයට ගනී. ලංකාවේ ප්‍රජනන කාලය සහ nesting sites සෘජුව තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමිගේ සුදු හිස සහ කළු crown/පිට කැපී පෙනේ. ගැහැනුගේ හිස දුඹුරු-අළු, ඇස් හරහා අඳුරු ඉරක් සහ අඩු contrast. Juvenile ගැහැනුට සමාන නමුත් වඩා අඳුරු/අපැහැදිලි.

field_spotting_tips.text: කුඩා ප්‍රමාණය සහ සුදු-කළු පිරිමි හිස හොඳම ලක්ෂණ. වැවක මැද ජලජ ශාක අතර සහ ජලයට ඉහළ අතු මත බලන්න. පියාඹන විට වේගවත් කළු-සුදු පියාපත් රටාව පෙනේ.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් පහළබිම් වැව් සහ තෙත්බිම්; Tissamaharama, Bundala, Anawilundawa සහ වෙනත් ශාක බහුල වැව්වල වාර්තා. දේශීය ව්‍යාප්තිය ස්ථානික විය හැක.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් ස්ථිරවාසී (CBC 2022: R). ජල මට්ටම හා වර්ෂාව අනුව දේශීය චලනයන් සිදුවිය හැක.

species_description.text: Medium-sized brown owl (about 30–33 cm) with a rounded head, no ear tufts, large yellow eyes, brown upperparts and pale underparts with fine brown barring. Commonly roosts in trees by day and hunts at night in forests, gardens, plantations and wooded urban areas. Feeds heavily on large insects caught in flight, but also takes small vertebrates. Nests in tree cavities, often reusing suitable hollows.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; female is usually larger. Size is difficult to judge without direct comparison.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and softer in appearance, with buff-edged feathers and less distinct barring. Young birds may retain down around the head and body after fledging.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its repeated, hollow 'koo-ook' call, often on moonlit nights. It may sit on lamp posts, telephone poles and TV antennas; large yellow eyes and lack of ear tufts help separate it from scops-owls.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common breeding resident across much of Sri Lanka in forests, cultivation, gardens and wooded towns and villages; less common at higher elevations. Frequently heard in urban and suburban areas including around Colombo.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Local records report breeding around March–April and again in November, but these periods should be treated as documented local observations rather than a universal schedule.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022), Version 3: resident (R) or endemic (E) as recorded; E denotes Sri Lankan endemic, not a separate movement code.

species_description.text: Large, powerful hawk-eagle (about 60–72 cm) with broad wings, a long tail and variable plumage. Sri Lankan birds belong to the ceylanensis form, traditionally called Crested Hawk-eagle, and generally show a prominent crest, dark upperparts and pale underparts with heavy dark streaking or barring. Occurs in forests, forest edges, wooded hills and adjoining open country. Hunts birds, mammals and reptiles, often from a concealed perch or by soaring over forest. Nests in large trees.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; plumage is similar. The Sri Lankan ceylanensis form has a crest and differs in appearance from some other geographic forms, so use local subspecies context when comparing images.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally paler and browner, with buff or whitish underparts marked by longitudinal streaks and less sharply defined adult barring. Crest and adult pattern become more pronounced with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for the long crest, powerful silhouette and broad wings. The pale underparts with strong dark markings and long tail separate it from the uniformly dark Black Eagle.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in wooded lowlands and hills across Sri Lanka, including dry-zone forest and wet-zone forest edges. CBC lists the Sri Lankan Crested Hawk-eagle form as resident under N. c. ceylanensis.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Breeding timing varies geographically and should not be stated as a precise Sri Lankan window without local nest evidence.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022), Version 3: species listed resident (R); see row-level source note. For Changeable Hawk-eagle, CBC separately names Sri Lankan subspecies ceylanensis as Crested Hawk-eagle.

species_description.text: Large, powerful forest eagle (about 70–72 cm) with a prominent crest, dark brown upperparts and pale underparts marked by strong dark streaks and bars. A rare breeding resident of the hills and foothills, favouring dense evergreen and moist deciduous forest. Hunts birds and mammals, including arboreal prey, and nests high in large trees. The species is restricted to the Western Ghats of India and the hills of Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; the sexes are otherwise similar in plumage. Adults show a conspicuous crest and strong dark streaking below. Size is the most reliable sex distinction in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally paler and more buff below, with streaking rather than the adult's stronger barring; upperparts are browner with pale feather edges. Ageing requires comparison with good reference images.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search forested hill slopes and ridgelines for a large crested eagle. Its rarity and resemblance to other Nisaetus eagles mean photographs should capture crest, underpart pattern and tail to support identification.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Rare and local in Sri Lanka's hill country and foothills, especially the wet-zone and central/southwestern forested highlands. Recent records include Ritigala Forest Reserve, an unusual record outside its usual wet-zone hill distribution.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Rare breeding resident, not a regular migrant. Breeding chronology is incompletely documented in Sri Lanka; a 2023 study from the Western Ghats reports a single chick fledging at about four months, but that timing should not be transferred uncritically to Sri Lanka.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022), Version 3: species listed resident (R); see row-level source note. For Changeable Hawk-eagle, CBC separately names Sri Lankan subspecies ceylanensis as Crested Hawk-eagle.

species_description.text: Very large wader (about 50–60 cm) with long legs, brown streaked plumage and a very long downcurved bill. The head and neck are finely streaked; upperparts are mottled brown and underparts pale with dark streaks. Feeds on crabs, molluscs, worms and other invertebrates, probing deep mud and wet sand. Uses estuaries, tidal flats, lagoons, saltpans and coastal grassland.

male_female_identification.text: Female is noticeably larger on average and has a longer, more strongly curved bill; male is smaller with a shorter bill. There is overlap, so sexing is most reliable when birds are together for direct comparison.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have a shorter bill on average, warmer buff fringes on the upperparts and less strongly marked underparts. Bill length increases with age; juvenile plumage can appear warmer and more neatly patterned.

field_spotting_tips.text: Large size and very long downcurved bill are key. Distinguish from Whimbrel by the Curlew's larger body, longer bill and lack of strong dark crown stripes. Listen for the repeated bubbling 'cur-lee' call; Whimbrel's call is a faster series of whistles.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Uncommon migrant on coastal mudflats, lagoons and estuaries, especially Bundala, Mannar and Puttalam. Also recorded at Yala and other suitable coastal wetlands. Usually in small numbers compared with Whimbrel.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter visitor, broadly Aug–Apr, with most expected during Oct–Mar. CBC lists M; Sri Lanka trip report recorded an individual at Bundala. Occurrence and numbers vary between years.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC 2022 Country List classification should be used as source of truth; current workbook retains M, consistent with migratory winter occurrence. Verify line-level status before publication.

species_description.text: Medium-large wader (about 40–46 cm) with brown streaked plumage, long downcurved bill and dark crown stripes separated by a pale central crown stripe. The bill is shorter than that of Eurasian Curlew and often has a pinkish base. Feeds on crabs, worms, molluscs and other invertebrates on mudflats, rocky shores, estuaries and coastal lagoons.

male_female_identification.text: Female averages slightly larger and has a longer bill than male, but sexes overlap considerably. Plumage is similar; sexing individual birds in the field is unreliable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have warmer buff fringes on the upperparts and a shorter bill. Underparts are finely streaked; juvenile plumage is often warmer and more neatly scaled than adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the smaller size and shorter bill compared with Eurasian Curlew, plus two dark crown stripes and a pale central crown stripe. Often gives a clear, repeated series of whistling notes. Check bill length and head pattern when separating from curlew.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common migrant along coasts, tidal flats, lagoons and estuaries, including Bundala, Yala, Mannar, Puttalam and other coastal sites. Also uses rocky shores and offshore islands; may be seen singly or in small flocks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Migrant, mainly Aug–Apr, with northern-winter occurrence. CBC lists M. Limosa monthly checklist and Sri Lanka trip reports show broad seasonal occurrence; some checklists may show all-year records due to occasional oversummering or broad data aggregation.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC 2022 Country List classification should be used as source of truth; current workbook retains M, consistent with migratory winter occurrence. Verify line-level status before publication.

species_description.text: Medium-sized heron (about 58–65 cm) with a stocky body, short neck and thick black bill. Adults have a glossy black crown and back, grey wings and long white head plumes in breeding condition; underparts are pale grey. Feeds mainly on fish, amphibians, insects and other small aquatic animals. Often roosts communally in trees by day and forages at dusk or night.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male and female are broadly alike; differences are subtle and unreliable in the field. Breeding adults develop conspicuous white head plumes and elongated pale feathers.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner, streaked and spotted, with a less contrasting head and back; they lack the adult’s clean black-and-grey pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search shaded tree roosts near wetlands during daylight. At dusk, watch shallow margins for slow, deliberate feeding; its hunched posture and heavy bill help distinguish it.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident around marshes, tanks, lagoons, mangroves and wooded wetlands. Notable sites include Bundala/Hambantota, Bellanwila–Attidiya and other wetland roosts; may be overlooked by day.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round in Sri Lanka (CBC 2022 R). Local movements can follow water levels and food availability.

species_description.text: A medium-sized endemic hornbill, around 45 cm, with a grey body, pale underparts, a rufous vent and a long tail. It lacks the large casque of the Malabar Pied-Hornbill. Usually found in pairs or small groups in lowland moist forest, dry-zone woodland, forest edges, gardens and cultivated landscapes with mature trees. Eats a wide range of fruit, especially figs, as well as insects, scorpions, frogs, lizards and occasionally small vertebrates. Nests in a natural tree cavity; the female seals herself inside during incubation and chick-rearing, while the male delivers food through a narrow opening.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a pale creamy bill and a low casque. Female is smaller and has a darker, blackish bill with a yellow streak. In good views bill colour and size are useful; body plumage is otherwise similar.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have smaller, pale greenish bills and lack the full adult bill profile. Young birds are generally duller and less sharply defined than adults; bill colour and casque develop with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for loud accelerating ka-ka-ka calls, often given in duets. The plain grey appearance, rufous vent and absence of a casque separate it from the larger black-and-white Malabar Pied-Hornbill. Scan fruiting trees and forest edges.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident in Sri Lanka, widespread through lowland moist and dry-zone forests, woodland, forest edges and cultivated country. Recorded in Kitulgala, Sinharaja, Sigiriya, Anuradhapura and many wooded lowland sites; occurs up to about 1,200 m, though less numerous in the hills.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round, with some altitudinal/food-related movements. Breeding season is mainly March–June. After breeding, birds may move locally or upslope in search of fruiting trees.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status applied: endemic (E) for Sri Lanka Grey Hornbill, Yellow-fronted Barbet and Crimson-fronted Barbet; resident (R) for the other three. Verify exact row codes before publication.

species_description.text: මධ්‍යම ප්‍රමාණයේ මුහුදුලිහිණියෙකි (සෙ.මී. 32–35). ඉහළපස අඳුරු charcoal, යටපස සුදු, ඇසට ඉහළින් සුදු පටියක් සහ කළු හිස ඇත; දිගු forked වලිගය. විවෘත මුහුදේ හා දූපත්/ගල්පර ආශ්‍රිතව පියාසර කරයි; කුඩා මසුන් හා මුහුදු මතුපිට ආහාර ගනී. උතුරු ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ කුඩා අභිජනන ජනපද වාර්තා ඇත.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි හා ගැහැනු බාහිරව සමානයි; ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ ලිංගය වෙන්කිරීම සාමාන්‍යයෙන් නොහැක.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile හි ඉහළපස දුඹුරු/අඳුරු කොරපොතු රටා, අඩු පැහැදිලි සුදු නළල/ඇස් පටිය සහ අඳුරු හොටක් පෙනිය හැක. වයස අනුව රටා වෙනස් වේ.

field_spotting_tips.text: අඳුරු ඉහළපසට එරෙහි සුදු යටපස හා ඇසට ඉහළ සුදු පටිය බලන්න. Sooty Tern සමඟ වෙන්කිරීමේදී Bridled හි සුදු ඇස් පටිය ඉතා වැදගත්.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: වෙරළට ආසන්න හා offshore waters; Beruwala–Mirissa දකුණු වෙරළ survey transects, Mannar/Adam’s Bridge සහ උතුරු වෙරළ. පාවෙන ද්‍රව්‍ය මත විවේක ගන්නා ලෙසද වාර්තා වී ඇත.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ වසර පුරා හමුවිය හැකි නමුත් offshore survey වල සැප්තැම්බර්–ඔක්තෝබර් වැඩි සංඛ්‍යාත්මක ගමන් වාර්තා වී ඇත. CBC status R/M ලෙස සටහන්.

species_description.text: විශාල, දිගු පියාපත් ඇති pelagic tern එකකි (සෙ.මී. 38–45). ඉහළපස කළු/අඳුරු දුඹුරු, යටපස සුදු, කළු හිස සහ සුදු නළල/ඇස් පටියක් ඇත; දිගු forked වලිගය. ගැඹුරු මුහුදේ පියාසර කරමින් මතුපිටට ආසන්න මසුන් හා squid අල්ලයි. විශාල දූපත් අභිජනන ජනපද සාදයි; Adam’s Bridge ආශ්‍රිත breeding colony වාර්තා ඇත.

male_female_identification.text: ලිංග දෙකම පෙනුමෙන් සමානයි; ලිංග නිශ්චය ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ කළ නොහැකි තරම් දුෂ්කරය.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile සාමාන්‍යයෙන් වැඩිහිටියාට වඩා දුඹුරු පැහැති, පිට/පියාපත්වල සුදු හෝ buff කොරපොතු රටා සහ අඩු පැහැදිලි හිස රටාවක් දරයි.

field_spotting_tips.text: විශාල, කළු-සුදු pelagic tern; Bridled Tern සමඟ වෙන්කරන විට Sooty හි සුදු ඇස් පටිය/නළල පටිය නොපැහැදිලි හෝ නොමැති බව බලන්න. දුරදක්නයෙන් පියාපත් හැඩය සහ වලිගය නිරීක්ෂණය කරන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් pelagic/offshore මුහුදු ප්‍රදේශ; Mannar–Adam’s Bridge සහ දකුණු වෙරළේ boat surveys. වෙරළෙන් දුරින් පියාසර කරන නිසා සාමාන්‍ය වෙරළ නිරීක්ෂණවල අඩුවෙන් පෙනේ.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ අභිජනන සහ ගමන් වාර්තා ඇත; CBC 2022 අනුව R/M. Boat surveys තුළ සැප්තැම්බර්–ඔක්තෝබර් සහ වෙනත් මාසවල offshore passage වාර්තා තිබේ.

species_description.text: Medium-sized oriole about 25 cm, with bright yellow body, black hood, black wings and tail centre, and a strong pinkish-red bill. It moves through tree crowns in pairs or small family groups, feeding on fruit, berries, nectar and insects. Common in gardens, plantations, open woodland and forest edges.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male has a solid glossy black hood and bright yellow body. Female is duller, with olive-yellow/greenish underparts and less sharply defined black hood; wings and tail retain dark areas.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds resemble females but are duller and show dark streaking on the underparts; the black hood is incomplete, especially on the throat.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for clear, fluty whistles and scan fruiting trees. The bright yellow body and black hood are unmistakable in adults. Female and juvenile birds are greener and more streaked; do not confuse with migrant Golden Oriole.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident across Sri Lanka from lowlands to mid-hills, in wooded gardens, coconut groves, plantations, open forest and village landscapes. Often detected by its fluty calls.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding season reported October–May; a hanging, hammock-like nest is suspended from a fork or leafy branch.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Black-hooded Oriole R; Sri Lanka Blue Magpie E; House Crow R; Large-billed Crow R; Indian Pitta M; Cinereous Tit R. Confirm row-level codes if checklist edition changes.

species_description.text: Very small, slender warbler, about 13 cm, with olive-brown upperparts, pale underparts, long graduated tail, short bill and a pale eyebrow. Famous for sewing leaves together with plant fibres or spider silk to form a cradle for its nest. Feeds mainly on insects and spiders in gardens, scrub, hedges and woodland edges.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage. Males may have a longer tail and more prominent breeding features, but field sexing is unreliable without close examination.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less distinct markings and a shorter-looking tail; young birds may show a yellowish gape.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its loud, repetitive calls in gardens and hedges. Watch for a tiny bird moving restlessly among leaves and for the characteristic stitched-leaf nest. Tail often held cocked.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident across Sri Lanka in gardens, scrub, forest edges, plantations, parks and villages, from lowlands into the hills.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is reported through much of the year, with local peaks varying by rainfall. Nest is a distinctive leaf cradle, lined with soft fibres.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022/local checklist convention: all six species resident (R). Grey-breasted Prinia's Sri Lankan subspecies pectoralis is endemic; species is not endemic.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 30–35 පමණ දිගැති කුඩා, කුකුළු හැඩැති පක්ෂියෙකි. අළු-දුඹුරු/චෙස්නට් ඉහළපස, සුදු-බෆ් යටපස මත සිහින් කළු ඉරි, තැඹිලි පැහැති මුහුණ සහ උගුර වටා කළු necklace රටාව. වියළි තෘණබිම්, පඳුරු, කෘෂිකාර්මික ඉඩම් සහ විවෘත බිම් භාවිත කරයි. බිම ආහාර සොයමින් බීජ, කෘමීන් සහ වෙනත් කුඩා ආහාර ගනී. ලංකාවේ ප්‍රජනන මාස තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි සහ ගැහැනු බොහෝ දුරට සමාන පෙනුමක්. පාදයේ spur තිබීම පිරිමියාට උපකාරී ලක්ෂණයක් විය හැකි නමුත් දුර සිට එය විශ්වාසදායක නොවේ.

field_spotting_tips.text: බොහෝවිට යුගල හෝ කුඩා පවුල් කණ්ඩායම් ලෙස බිම පෙනේ. තැඹිලි මුහුණ, කළු necklace සහ සම්පූර්ණ ශරීරයේ සිහින් barring බලන්න. Painted Francolin සමඟ වෙන්කරන විට එහි සුදු තිත් වෙනුවට Grey Francolin හි සිහින් ඉරි රටාව වැදගත්.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ වියළි පහළබිම් සහ විවෘත scrub/agricultural habitat. වයඹ සහ උතුරු වියළි ප්‍රදේශ ඇතුළු සුදුසු වාසස්ථානවල හමුවිය හැක; නිශ්චිත hotspot ලැයිස්තුව තවදුරටත් eBird/CBC records වලින් සකස් කළ යුතුයි.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී; අවුරුද්ද පුරා සුදුසු වාසස්ථානවල. ප්‍රජනන සමය සඳහා ලංකා-විශේෂිත වාර්තා තවම තහවුරු කර නැත.

species_description.text: Small, nocturnal scops-owl (about 23–25 cm) with prominent ear tufts, yellow to orange eyes and finely patterned brown, grey or rufous plumage. Occurs in wooded country, gardens, plantations and forest edges, often near human settlements. Feeds mainly on large insects, but also takes small reptiles, rodents and other small vertebrates. Nests in tree cavities.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in plumage; female is usually larger. Iris colour and ear tufts are not reliable sex characters.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are downy when very young; fledged juveniles are browner and more softly patterned, with less sharply defined facial and upperpart markings. Age is best assessed from a series of plumage characters.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its regular, repeated mellow hoots after dark. Look for conspicuous ear tufts and yellow-orange eyes; avoid confusing it with Oriental Scops-owl, which is smaller and has two main colour morphs.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka across a range of wooded habitats, including gardens, plantations and forest edges. Often encountered in lowland settlements and well-treed areas.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding season and local timing require verification from Sri Lankan nest records; tree cavities are used for nesting.

species_description.text: Small scops-owl (about 17–19 cm), the smallest owl recorded in Sri Lanka in some field-guide treatments. Has prominent ear tufts, yellow eyes and two principal colour forms: rufous/chestnut and grey-brown. Favours dry-zone forests, open woodland, groves and densely foliaged trees around cultivation; may occur around settlements and streetlights. Feeds on insects and other small prey and nests in tree cavities.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage. Both rufous and grey-brown morphs occur; these are colour morphs, not male and female forms. Female is generally larger.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are softer and more downy, with less distinct patterning; young birds gradually acquire adult-like ear tufts and barred/streaked plumage. Do not label a rufous morph as a sex or age class.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its repeated territorial song, often described as a three-part accelerating or emphatic series. Check ear tufts, small size and colour morph; use voice and habitat to separate it from Indian Scops-owl.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident, chiefly in the dry zone and locally in the wet zone. Sri Lankan subspecies leggei is associated with wooded habitats; records include dry-zone national parks and other wooded localities.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. No established seasonal migrant pattern in Sri Lanka; local calling and breeding periods need more precise source verification.

species_description.text: Small, distinctive reddish-brown scops-owl (about 16.5–17 cm) with a short tail, weakly defined facial disc, no obvious ear tufts and yellow-to-orange eyes. Upperparts are rich rufous with dark markings; underparts paler rufous with dark triangular spots. Restricted to undisturbed lowland wet-zone rainforest and dense undergrowth. Feeds mainly on insects such as beetles and moths, often hunting in the first hours after dusk. Daytime roosts are low in dense vegetation.

male_female_identification.text: Male typically has a more orange iris, while female's iris is more yellowish; plumage is otherwise similar. Iris tone can vary with light and should not be used alone for sexing.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for the distinctive frog-like 'poo-ooo' call in dense rainforest. Search low branches and thick undergrowth during daylight roosting periods; avoid playback or close approach that could disturb this threatened species.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Strictly endemic to the south-western wet zone. Confirmed localities include Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Morapitiya-Runakanda, Kanneliya and Eratna-Gilimale. Range is very restricted and tied to remaining rainforest.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident endemic; not migratory. Active and most often detected by its frog-like call, particularly after dusk. No well-established breeding calendar is available; breeding behaviour remains poorly documented.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022), Version 3: resident (R) or endemic (E) as recorded; E denotes Sri Lankan endemic, not a separate movement code.

species_description.text: Small, compact flowerpecker around 9 cm, with short thick bill, dark olive-brown upperparts and pale underparts, usually with streaking or dusky markings on the breast depending on subspecies. Feeds mainly on berries and small fruits, especially mistletoe, and also takes nectar and insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; males may show slightly darker or more contrasting plumage. Field separation is difficult and should not be forced without close views.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller brown and may show more obvious pale streaking/scaling on the underparts; bill colour and plumage become more adult-like with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a tiny short-billed bird feeding on mistletoe berries high in trees. Its stout bill and flowerpecker shape separate it from sunbirds, which have longer decurved bills.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka in wooded country, forest edges, gardens and plantations. Sri Lankan population is the subspecies P. a. zeylonica.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding reports for the Sri Lankan population include January–July, peaking around March, with additional breeding specimens in September and November.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention retained: Sri Lanka White-eye E; Indian White-eye R; Legge's Flowerpecker E; Thick-billed Flowerpecker R; Pale-billed Flowerpecker R; Purple-rumped Sunbird R; Loten's Sunbird R; Purple Sunbird R. Confirm individual line codes against official list before publication.

species_description.text: Tiny endemic flowerpecker, about 9 cm, with compact body, short stout bill and dark bluish-grey upperparts. Male has a clean white throat and pale underparts; female is duller grey-brown and lacks the sharply contrasting white throat. Feeds on berries, small fruits, nectar and insects, often high in flowering trees.

male_female_identification.text: Male dark blue-grey above with a conspicuous pure-white throat; female duller brownish/grey above with less contrasting pale throat and underparts. Both have short, stout bills.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds are duller and browner, with less distinct throat contrast and often faint scaling; gradually acquire adult plumage.

field_spotting_tips.text: Scan the canopy of wet-zone forest, especially flowering trees. The male's white throat and short thick bill separate it from sunbirds; its rapid movements and high canopy habits make it easy to overlook.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to the south-western wet-zone rainforests and adjacent foothills, mainly in tall forest canopy and forest edges. Can be difficult to see because it forages high in trees.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Breeding reported January–August in older Sri Lankan natural-history accounts. Often easier to detect when red cotton trees and other nectar/fruit sources flower.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention retained: Sri Lanka White-eye E; Indian White-eye R; Legge's Flowerpecker E; Thick-billed Flowerpecker R; Pale-billed Flowerpecker R; Purple-rumped Sunbird R; Loten's Sunbird R; Purple Sunbird R. species_description.text: Large fish-eating raptor (about 54–58 cm) with long, angled wings, white underparts and head, dark eye-stripe, dark brown upperparts and strongly hooked bill. Usually associated with lakes, reservoirs, lagoons, estuaries, rivers and coastal waters. Feeds mainly on fish captured by plunging feet-first into water. Uses large trees, cliffs or artificial structures for nesting in breeding parts of its global range.

male_female_identification.text: Female is generally larger and often has a broader, more heavily streaked breast band; male is smaller and usually cleaner below. Individual variation means sexing from a single distant view is uncertain.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have dark brown upperparts with conspicuous pale/buff feather edges, a more streaked head and breast, and orange-yellow rather than bright yellow eyes. Adult contrast develops with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the distinctive kinked/angled wings in flight and the white head with dark eye-stripe. Often perches prominently near water, then plunges feet-first to catch fish.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A migrant visitor to Sri Lanka, seen at coastal wetlands, lagoons, reservoirs and large inland water bodies. Check Negombo Lagoon, Bundala, Kalametiya, Mannar, major tanks and other fish-rich wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular winter visitor, broadly June–April in some datasets, with many records during the northern winter and passage periods. Occurrence varies between years and sites.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) is the preferred local authority; status recorded here is provisional pending direct row/subspecies cross-check. R = resident; M = regular migrant. For mixed populations/subspecies retain R/M.

species_description.text: Small, active tit about 13–14 cm, with grey upperparts, white cheeks, black cap and throat, broad black central breast/belly stripe, pale underparts and white wing-bar. Forages acrobatically in middle and upper canopy of open woodland, gardens, plantations and forest edges, feeding on insects, larvae and spiders; also takes some seeds.

male_female_identification.text: Male usually has a broader, more extensive black ventral stripe and darker overall markings; female's stripe is narrower and plumage slightly duller. Sexing requires good views and can be subtle.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less sharply defined black cap and ventral stripe; pale yellowish or buff tones may show on underparts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a very active grey-and-white tit with black cap, white cheek and broad black belly stripe. Often joins mixed-species flocks and gives repeated calls. Compare with Great Tit: Cinereous Tit has grey rather than olive-green back and generally paler underparts.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, especially hills and mid-elevations, but also locally in low-country wooded habitats and gardens. Sri Lankan birds are assigned to the subspecies Parus cinereus mahrattarum in some regional treatments.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding in southern India and Sri Lanka mainly February–May, with occasional nests September–November. Nests in tree hollows, old woodpecker/barbet holes, walls or banks.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Black-hooded Oriole R; Sri Lanka Blue Magpie E; House Crow R; Large-billed Crow R; Indian Pitta M; Cinereous Tit R. Confirm row-level codes if checklist edition changes.

species_description.text: Small, familiar sparrow about 14–15 cm, stocky with thick conical bill. Adult male has grey crown and rump, chestnut nape and cheek patch, black bib and pale underparts; female is plain sandy-brown with a pale eyebrow and streaked back. Eats seeds, grain, scraps and insects, especially near people.

male_female_identification.text: Male boldly patterned with grey crown, chestnut nape and black bib. Female plain brown with pale supercilium and streaked back. Juveniles resemble female, with softer plumage and yellowish gape.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are dull brown, streaked above and pale below, with a yellow gape; young males gradually develop grey crown, chestnut nape and black bib.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look around buildings, markets and eateries. Male's black bib and grey crown distinguish it from female; listen for familiar chirping. Flocks gather where grain or food scraps are available.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident around houses, towns, villages, farms and other human settlements throughout Sri Lanka. Also uses open scrub, paddy fields and gardens close to habitation.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding can occur over much of the year, often associated with rainfall and food availability; nests in cavities, roof spaces, nest boxes and suitable holes.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status code R for all eight species. Note older field-guide/plate editions differ for Indian Silverbill and Black-throated Munia (UR); current CBC 2022 checklist lists both R.

species_description.text: Seasonal visitor, about 21–23 cm. Adult breeding male has a pink body, glossy black head, neck, throat, wings and tail, pale orange-pink bill and legs, and a long wispy crest. Female is duller, with shorter crest and less sharply divided pink and black. Winter adults are duller with pale feather edges; juveniles are grey-brown and black.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male in breeding plumage is brighter with longer crest and sharper black-pink contrast. Female is duller with shorter crest. Winter plumage reduces these differences; sexing immature birds is difficult.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are grey-brown above with darker wings and tail, and lack the adult's clear pink body and glossy black hood. First-winter birds develop pink and black unevenly.

field_spotting_tips.text: Scan large mixed starling flocks and open feeding areas. Pink body and black head are diagnostic in adults; check carefully for dull first-winter birds. Large irruptive flocks may appear in some years, while the species can be scarce in others.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Migrant to Sri Lanka, occurring irregularly in open country, grassland, agricultural areas, scrub, lagoons and sometimes urban waste sites. Numbers vary greatly between years; recorded in southern dry-zone sites including Yala/Palatupana.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly a non-breeding visitor during the northern winter, but arrival and departure are irregular and flock sizes vary markedly between years. Do not assume it is present every winter.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Southern/Common Hill Myna (Gracula indica) R; Sri Lanka Myna E; Common Myna R; Rosy Starling M; Brahminy Starling M; White-faced Starling E. Confirm codes against the list before publication.

species_description.text: විශාල, දිගු ගෙලක් සහ ශක්තිමත් පාද ඇති බිම්වාසී පක්ෂියෙකි. පිරිමිගේ දිගු, ඇස්-හැඩැති ocelli සහිත train එක විශේෂත්වයකි. වියළි හා තෙත් වනාන්තර, scrub, ගොවිබිම් සහ ගම්මාන ආශ්‍රිත විවෘත භූමි භාවිත කරයි. බීජ, පලතුරු, ධාන්‍ය, කෘමීන්, කුඩා උරගයන් සහ වෙනත් කුඩා සතුන් ආහාරයට ගනී. බිම සැඟවුණු ස්ථානයක බිත්තර 4–8ක් දමයි; ගැහැනු පමණක් බිත්තර රකින බව ප්‍රධාන species accounts සඳහන් කරයි.

male_female_identification.text: ඉතා පැහැදිලි වෙනසක්. පිරිමි (peacock): දිගු වර්ණවත් train, නිල්-කොළ බෙල්ල/පපුව, හිස මත crest. ගැහැනු (peahen): train නැත; දුඹුරු/අළු පැහැති ශරීරය, කොළ පැහැති බෙල්ලේ කොටස, කෙටි වලිගය. Juvenile පිරිමි ගැහැනුට සමාන විය හැකි අතර train පසුව වර්ධනය වේ.

field_spotting_tips.text: විවෘත බිම්වල උදෑසන/සවස බලන්න; බොහෝවිට හඬින් හෝ විශාල ශරීරයෙන් හඳුනාගත හැක. පිරිමි train එක නොපෙන්වන විටත් දිගු train feathers සහ නිල් බෙල්ල බලන්න. ගැහැනු සහ juvenile අතර වෙන්කිරීමේදී ප්‍රමාණය, හිස/ගෙල පැහැය සහ වලිග වර්ධනය සලකන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ විශේෂයෙන් වියළි කලාපයේ සහ වියළි-අතරමැදි කලාපයේ විවෘත වනාන්තර, scrub, ජලාශ අසල සහ කෘෂිකාර්මික භූමිවල බහුලව හමුවේ. Yala, Wilpattu, Udawalawe සහ Minneriya වැනි වියළි කලාපීය ජාතික වනෝද්‍යාන ප්‍රසිද්ධ නිරීක්ෂණ ස්ථාන.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී. ප්‍රජනනය වැසි සමඟ සම්බන්ධව ප්‍රදේශ අනුව වෙනස් වේ; ලංකාවේ නිශ්චිත peak months වෙනම තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: Sri Lanka's largest kingfisher, a very large and heavy-billed bird (about 35 cm) with a huge reddish-orange bill, chestnut head and underparts, blue-green back and wings, and pale throat. Usually sits quietly on an exposed branch over water, then plunges for fish, crabs, frogs and other aquatic prey. Uses rivers, streams, tanks, marshes, lagoons and mangroves, particularly where wooded banks provide perches. Nests in a hole or tunnel in an earthen bank or tank bund.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in colour. Adult males generally have an all-red bill; females may show a dark tip or dusky area on the lower mandible, but this is not always easy to see in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immatures are duller, with browner or less saturated plumage and a darker bill; the bill gradually becomes the vivid red-orange of adults. CBC image records include immature birds in Wattala.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for its enormous red bill and chestnut head. It often remains motionless on a prominent waterside perch. Its size is substantially greater than the other Sri Lankan kingfishers; listen for its loud, harsh calls.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Uncommon resident in Sri Lanka's lowlands and lower hills, especially near wooded freshwater and brackish wetlands. Records include Wattala, Talangama, Wakarai, Dambulla and Habarana; more frequent in the dry zone.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is reported mainly January–May, with a possible second period around August–September. Nesting is in riverbanks or tank bunds.

species_description.text: Large, pale grey-and-white pelican (about 1.25–1.5 m) with a very large expandable throat pouch, long bill bearing dark spots, grey crest and dark flight feathers. Feeds mainly on fish in freshwater, brackish and coastal wetlands, often by cooperative fishing. Nests colonially in trees, usually near wetlands; Sri Lankan breeding reported mainly December–March/April.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar in the field; males may average larger. Use bill/pouch spotting, crest, facial skin and overall structure rather than sexing a lone bird.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young are duller brownish-grey, with less distinct adult crest and facial colours; plumage becomes progressively paler and more patterned as they mature. Age classes can be difficult to assign at distance.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the enormous bill pouch and spotted bill; flocks may fish cooperatively. In flight, broad wings and heavy silhouette distinguish it from storks.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident breeder at major lowland wetlands. Notable sites include Bundala, Yala, Bellanwila–Attidiya, large tanks and lagoons; may be seen soaring on thermals or resting in large waterside trees.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident (CBC 2022 R); present year-round, with breeding activity reported mainly Dec–Apr. Local abundance varies with water levels and food availability.

species_description.text: Small to medium-sized, shy ground babbler about 16 cm, with dark brown cap, deep grey-brown upperparts and rich rusty-orange/cinnamon underparts and sides of head. Keeps close to the ground, turning over dead leaves and walking as well as hopping while searching for insects and worms.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; no reliable external field distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are poorly documented in modern field references; likely duller and less contrasting, with softer brown cap and underparts. Do not overstate age characters.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its distinctive repeated 'pretty-dear' call and rustling leaf litter. The dark cap, rusty underparts and ground-walking habit are useful; it is the Sri Lankan babbler most likely to walk rather than hop.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident in forest, well-wooded country and thick undergrowth across much of Sri Lanka, absent or scarce in the extremely dry northern and southeastern regions. Dry-zone subspecies babaulti is paler and greyer above; wet-zone birds are darker.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding occurs in the early part of the year. Nest is a dome of dead leaves concealed on the ground in undergrowth, usually with two eggs.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Sri Lanka Scimitar-babbler E; Yellow-eyed Babbler R; Tawny-bellied Babbler R; Dark-fronted Babbler R; Sri Lanka Orange-billed Babbler E; Sri Lanka Ashy-headed Laughing-thrush E; Yellow-billed Babbler R; Sri Lanka Brown-capped Babbler E. Several resident species have endemic Sri Lankan subspecies only.
