species_description.text: Small, slender minivet about 16 cm, with long wings and a dark bill. Male has grey upperparts, orange underparts fading to yellow on belly, and orange rump, tail edges and wing patches. Female is grey above and yellow below, with yellow rump and wing patches. Lives in scrub, thorny jungle, open woodland, wooded gardens and plantations; catches insects and larvae in the canopy.

male_female_identification.text: Male has darker grey head and upperparts, orange breast and yellow belly. Female is paler grey above with yellow underparts and less vivid wing/rump patches. Sri Lankan subspecies is relatively richly coloured.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immatures resemble females but are duller and less sharply marked; young birds often travel in family groups with adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for small flocks moving rapidly through the canopy, with high thin 'swee-swee' calls. The male's orange breast and grey back separate it from the larger Scarlet Minivet; female is yellow below and grey above.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in lowlands and mid-hills across Sri Lanka, including dry and intermediate zones; uses scrub, open forest and wooded gardens but generally avoids dense rainforest interior. Recorded in Wilpattu, Jaffna, Mannar, Knuckles and Peak Wilderness up to c.1,800 m.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding mainly February–May in Sri Lanka; cup nest placed on a small branch or fork, often camouflaged with lichens and cobwebs. Both parents feed young.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 classification convention: resident (R). Confirm current CBC row-level code before publication.

species_description.text: Slender, long-winged minivet about 20 cm, usually in pairs or small family groups. Male is striking scarlet-red and black; female is yellow-orange and grey/olive. It inhabits forest, open woodland, plantations and well-wooded gardens, especially in the hills. Feeds on caterpillars, crickets and other insects, gleaning from foliage and sometimes flycatching.

male_female_identification.text: Male has scarlet-red underparts, rump and wing patches with black head, back and wings. Female is yellow-orange below with grey/olive upperparts and yellowish wing/rump patches. Colour intensity varies geographically.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner/olive, with less saturated red or yellow and often pale-edged/scaly-looking feathers; young birds may be seen with adults in family groups.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a vivid red-and-black male or yellow-grey female moving through canopy with a companion. Minivets often travel in a follow-the-leader sequence from tree to tree while gleaning insects.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common breeding resident throughout Sri Lanka, especially frequent in hills and wooded country. Occurs in forests, forest edges, plantations and tree-rich landscapes; CBC records include Kandy, Hiniduma, Nilgala and Deraniyagala.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeds mainly February–May and again August–September. Nest is a small, well-camouflaged cup high in the canopy, decorated with lichens and bark flakes and bound with cobwebs.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 classification convention: resident (R). Confirm current CBC row-level code before publication.

species_description.text: A large, striking endemic malkoha (about 40–47 cm) with a long graduated tail. Adult has glossy black to metallic green-blue upperparts, white flecking on crown/nape/chin (variable), black throat and breast, white lower underparts, a vivid crimson-red feathered facial patch and a large apple-green bill. Primarily a tall, relatively undisturbed wet-zone rainforest canopy bird, occasionally using suitable riverine forest. Feeds mainly on fruit/berries, while also taking insects and small vertebrates. Usually moves in pairs or small groups and may join mixed-species feeding flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are broadly similar. Female may be distinguished by a pale/white iris in some field accounts, compared with darker iris in male; this is not always easy to assess at canopy distance. Both sexes have the diagnostic red face, green bill and black-and-white body pattern.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles/immatures are duller than adults; facial red, bill colour and glossy upperpart tones are less developed. White flecking and overall contrast may be reduced. Reliable ageing often requires close views or photographs.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its calls and scan the upper canopy during mixed-species bird waves. Look for a long-tailed black-and-white silhouette with a red face and green bill. It may be seen moving between canopy trees rather than sitting in the open; at Sinharaja, scan tall fruiting trees and forest edges.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Sri Lankan endemic. Strongest association is with remaining wet-zone rainforests, especially Sinharaja and nearby forest blocks; also reported from other suitable wet-zone forest remnants and selected riverine habitats. Usually high in the canopy and easily overlooked.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is reported mainly in the first half of the year, with a possible secondary period around August–September; local breeding evidence is not uniform across sites.

species_description.text: A fairly large, slender, long-tailed cuckoo (around 39 cm), with dark green/grey-green upperparts, paler greenish underparts, a conspicuous blue bare-skin patch around the eye, green bill and graduated tail with broad white tips. Uses open dry forest, scrub, thorny thickets, second growth, chena margins and plantations. Eats insects and caterpillars, including grasshoppers, mantids and beetles, plus small lizards and occasional fruit. Unlike many cuckoos, it builds its own nest.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar and difficult to separate reliably in the field. Both show the blue facial patch, green bill and white-tipped graduated tail; do not assign sex from ordinary field views without supporting evidence.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immatures are generally duller than adults and may show more barred or less cleanly defined upperpart plumage. Facial blue and bill colours can be less vivid. Age should be recorded cautiously unless the plumage characters are clear.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch quietly along scrub edges and dry-forest tracks. It often climbs through foliage or makes a short crossing flight between thickets. The blue eye patch and white tail tips are the best quick field marks; distinguish it from Red-faced Malkoha by the absence of a red facial patch.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, especially dry and intermediate lowlands. Recorded in Yala, Wilpattu, Udawalawe, Bundala, Kumana, Lunugamvehera, Wasgamuwa, Minneriya, Kaudulla and scrub/forest patches around village tanks; also occurs locally in other zones where suitable open scrub remains.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Nesting is reported chiefly around March–May, with nesting possible in other months; avoid treating this as a rigid annual window.

species_description.text: Largest of Sri Lanka's regular cormorants, bulky-bodied with thick neck, large head, heavy hooked bill and broad wings. Mostly dark blackish; feeds by diving for fish in larger tanks, reservoirs, rivers and coastal waters. Breeding adults may show white head/neck feathering and a white thigh patch.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage; males are generally larger. Seasonal breeding adornments (white head/neck feathers and thigh patch) are not sex-specific.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and often have extensive pale or whitish underparts, throat and belly; immature plumage varies with age and subspecies.

field_spotting_tips.text: Notice the much heavier body, thick neck and large bill. In flight it looks bulky, with broad wings and slower wingbeats; breeding white flank/thigh patch can be visible.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident but less frequently encountered in Sri Lanka than Little or Indian Cormorant. Look for it at larger reservoirs and tanks, including the dry-zone wetland network; records include Polonnaruwa, Udawalawe and Bundala.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident (CBC 2022 R); present year-round but locally uncommon/less numerous. No precise Sri Lankan breeding months assigned without stronger local evidence.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, slender dark cormorant with elongated oval head, long thin slightly hooked bill, long neck and long tail. Breeding adult glossy black with greenish-blue eye and small white ear-coverts/filoplumes; non-breeding birds browner with paler throat. Feeds mainly on fish, sometimes cooperatively.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in field plumage; males tend to be larger. The blue-green iris and fine, long bill are useful species characters, not sex markers.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immatures are browner and duller, often with a pale breast and lower belly; facial and ear-coverts markings are less crisp than in breeding adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Intermediate in size between Little and Great Cormorants; slimmer than Great, with longer finer bill and neck. Look for the pointed head profile and blue-green eye at close range.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common at extensive freshwater wetlands and coastal lagoons in Sri Lanka. Often seen at tanks, reservoirs, estuaries and coastal wetland systems; frequently associates in groups.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident (CBC 2022 R); present year-round. Seasonal breeding details for Sri Lanka not confidently resolved from the sources reviewed.

species_description.text: Small (17–19 cm) oceanic wader with a very fine needle-like bill, lobed toes and distinctive spinning feeding behaviour. Non-breeding birds are mostly grey above and white below with a dark eye-stripe; breeding females show a bright rufous neck patch and richer grey upperparts. Feeds on tiny aquatic invertebrates and plankton picked from the water surface. Arctic breeder; usually pelagic or on sheltered coastal waters outside breeding season.

male_female_identification.text: Sex-role reversal: females are larger and more brightly coloured in breeding plumage; males are duller and undertake incubation and most chick care. In winter plumage, sex is difficult to determine.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have dark upperparts with warm buff/rufous feather edges and a more patterned appearance than winter adults. First-winter birds become greyer and whiter as they moult.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a tiny wader swimming rather than walking, often spinning rapidly to bring food to the surface. Very fine bill and lobed toes; note that phalaropes are unusually buoyant and may feed on open water.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Scarce migrant in Sri Lanka, recorded on coastal lagoons, salt pans and sheltered waters; Bundala salt pans are a documented site. Also watch coastal wetlands and offshore waters, but sightings are irregular.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Mainly recorded during the northern winter and passage, broadly Oct–Feb in regional datasets; occasional records outside this window are possible.

species_description.text: Very large pink waterbird with long legs, long neck, down-curved pink bill with black tip and black flight feathers. Filter-feeds on algae, diatoms and small invertebrates in shallow saline/brackish lagoons; breeds colonially elsewhere in its range. Sri Lanka is a non-breeding visitor.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike; males average larger with longer legs and neck.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles grey-brown/whitish with dull grey legs and greyish bill; pink colour develops over several years.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for tall pink flocks in shallow lagoons. In flight, note black wing tips, long neck and legs held out; feeding birds sweep the inverted bill side to side.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Large coastal lagoons and saltpans; Bundala, Mannar/Vankalai, Jaffna lagoons and other suitable north-western and south-eastern wetlands. Numbers vary markedly between years.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Migrant; most likely during northern winter, broadly Oct–Mar, but occurrence and numbers are irregular.

species_description.text: Medium-sized leaf-warbler, about 13–14 cm, with olive-green upperparts, pale underparts, a prominent pale supercilium and relatively large bill. Often stays high in forest canopy, where it gleans insects from leaves and branches. Its clear, ascending three-note whistle is a useful clue to its presence.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and cannot reliably be separated in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally similar to adults but may be duller, with softer feather edges and less sharply defined facial markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often detected by its distinctive ascending three-note whistle. Search the canopy of forest and mature trees; it may be heard much more often than seen. Compare bill size and call with other leaf-warblers.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Regular winter migrant across Sri Lanka, favouring forests and well-wooded gardens from the lowlands to the highest hills. Particularly associated with more extensive forest than Greenish Warbler.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter visitor, usually during the northern winter months, approximately October–April. Breeds in the Himalayas and central China; winters in Sri Lanka and the Western Ghats.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Blyth's Reed-warbler M; Clamorous Reed-warbler R; Large-billed Leaf-warbler M; Greenish Warbler M; Sri Lanka Bush Warbler E; Velvet-fronted Nuthatch R. Clamorous Reed-warbler has endemic Sri Lankan subspecies meridionalis, not an endemic species.

species_description.text: Small, active leaf-warbler, about 10–11 cm, with greenish upperparts, pale yellowish-white underparts, a pale supercilium and one or two pale wing-bars depending on subspecies and plumage. It forages rapidly through foliage, taking small insects and spiders.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; no reliable field sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller and more yellowish, with less distinct wing-bars and facial markings; age is difficult to determine away from the breeding grounds.

field_spotting_tips.text: Small size, greenish tone, pale supercilium and wing-bar pattern are useful, but identification among Greenish Warbler complex taxa can be challenging. Listen to calls and check wing-bar number and structure.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter migrant to Sri Lanka, mainly in wooded habitats, gardens, plantations and forest edges. Often occurs in the canopy and mid-storey, sometimes with mixed-species feeding flocks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular winter visitor, generally October–April, with passage birds possible outside the core winter period. Breeds across northern Eurasia and winters in South Asia.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Blyth's Reed-warbler M; Clamorous Reed-warbler R; Large-billed Leaf-warbler M; Greenish Warbler M; Sri Lanka Bush Warbler E; Velvet-fronted Nuthatch R. species_description.text: A medium-sized green woodpecker, about 26–29 cm, with green upperparts, yellowish crown and nape, a red facial/moustachial area in males, and pale underparts marked with dark streaks. It forages on trunks, branches and sometimes the ground, searching for ants, termites and wood-boring insect larvae. Favours moist forest, well-wooded country, forest edges and plantations, often in pairs.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a red moustachial stripe; female has a black moustachial stripe. Both show a yellowish crown and green body. This facial stripe is the most useful sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and more heavily streaked, with less distinct yellow and red facial markings. Young birds may retain a spotted or barred appearance before adult patterning becomes clear.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its loud, ringing calls in forest. Look for a green woodpecker with yellow crown and streaked underparts; male's red moustache contrasts with the female's black. It sometimes descends to fallen logs or the ground to feed.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in wet-zone and adjoining intermediate forests, extending into the mid-hills and occasionally higher elevations. Recorded at Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Horton Plains and other wooded hill-country sites.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan sources report breeding mainly February–May, with cavity nests excavated in tree trunks or branches. It may join mixed-species flocks while foraging.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): resident (R) for all non-endemic woodpeckers; endemic (E) for Crimson-backed Flameback. Red-backed Flameback Dinopium psarodes is now treated as a separate endemic species; taxonomy differs from older CBC treatment. Confirm latest CBC row mapping before publication.

species_description.text: A medium-sized green woodpecker, around 20–22 cm, with green upperparts, pale underparts heavily streaked with dark markings, and a yellowish throat and crown. The male has a red moustachial stripe and the female a dark stripe. It often forages on tree trunks, branches and fallen wood for ants, termites and wood-boring larvae, and may descend to the ground. Favours open woodland, forest edges and well-wooded dry and intermediate landscapes.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a red moustachial stripe; female has a black moustachial stripe. Both have green upperparts and streaked underparts.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and more heavily spotted or streaked, with less distinct facial markings. Young males develop the red moustachial stripe with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a green woodpecker with strongly streaked underparts and a red (male) or black (female) moustachial stripe. It is often found in open woodland and can be confused with Lesser Yellownape; compare throat/breast streaking and facial pattern.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident but local in Sri Lanka's dry and intermediate zones, including open woodland and forest edges. Recorded in Wilpattu, Anuradhapura, Kandy district and other northern/dry-zone localities; not a widespread garden species.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Specific Sri Lankan breeding months were not reliably established in this batch; nest is a cavity excavated in a tree.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): resident (R) for all non-endemic woodpeckers; endemic (E) for Crimson-backed Flameback. Red-backed Flameback Dinopium psarodes is now treated as a separate endemic species; taxonomy differs from older CBC treatment. Confirm latest CBC row mapping before publication.

species_description.text: Colourful, ground-dwelling migrant about 19 cm, with a distinctive black-and-white head pattern, buff breast, green back, blue wing patch, bright blue tail, red vent and pinkish legs. Usually shy and skulking in leaf litter, feeding on insects, worms, snails and other small invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar in plumage; no reliable external field distinction. The striking head pattern and body colours are shared by both sexes.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less vivid blue-green upperparts and a less sharply defined head pattern; young birds are rarely seen in the open.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its distinctive two-note whistle, often heard at dawn and dusk. Search damp leaf litter and shaded undergrowth; it may freeze or run rather than fly. The blue wing patch is conspicuous when it flushes.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter visitor throughout Sri Lanka, favouring moist forest, scrub, gardens with leaf litter, plantations and shaded undergrowth. Often recorded in wet-zone gardens and forest edges as well as dry-zone wooded habitats.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular migrant, usually arriving around September/October and departing by March/April. A few may linger later; not generally treated as a Sri Lankan breeder.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Black-hooded Oriole R; Sri Lanka Blue Magpie E; House Crow R; Large-billed Crow R; Indian Pitta M; Cinereous Tit R. Confirm row-level codes if checklist edition changes.

species_description.text: Large white wader with long black spatulate bill and black legs; breeding birds develop a crest and yellowish breast patch. Sweeps partly open bill side to side in shallow water to catch fish, crustaceans and aquatic invertebrates; often feeds/roosts in groups.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike; males average slightly larger and may have longer, broader bill and more developed breeding crest.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have pale/pinkish bill with yellowish tip, dark primary tips and no developed crest; bill darkens with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Spoon-shaped bill unmistakable at close range. Watch rhythmic side-to-side sweeping while feeding; compare with egrets by bill shape.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Large wetlands, lagoons and shallow tanks, including Bundala, Yala, Kumana, Vankalai/Mannar and Jaffna. CBC lists resident status.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC country list categorises it as resident; local numbers fluctuate with water conditions and movements.

species_description.text: Medium-sized dark ibis with long down-curved bill and glossy plumage showing bronze, green and purple iridescence. Feeds on insects, worms, crustaceans, molluscs and small aquatic animals in marshes, flooded fields and shallow lagoons; often in flocks.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes similar; males slightly larger. Breeding birds show richer gloss and more vivid bare-part colours.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles duller brown, with less iridescence and pale streaking on head and neck; adult gloss develops with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: In bright light look for metallic gloss and slender curved bill. At a distance may appear all-dark; Black-headed Ibis is larger and white.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Mainly a migrant in Sri Lanka, recorded at Bundala, Mannar/Vankalai, Jaffna and other large marshes and paddy fields.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Regular migrant, especially northern winter, broadly Oct–Apr; out-of-season records do not alone imply residency.

species_description.text: Small-to-medium bushlark about 14–15 cm, cryptic sandy-brown with dark streaking, pale supercilium, buff underparts and a short crest. Often sings from a low perch or performs a fluttering display flight; feeds on seeds and insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar and difficult to separate in the field. Male may be slightly more strongly marked and sings in display; female generally duller.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more heavily scaled, with buff feather edges and a less distinct breast pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its song and watch for fluttering display above grassland. More streaked and bush-associated than Ashy-crowned Sparrow-lark; identify by overall shape, call and habitat.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in dry and intermediate zone grassland, scrub, open woodland, fallow cultivation and grassy edges. Recorded commonly in Udawalawe, Yala and Bundala.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident breeder in Sri Lanka. Breeding timing varies with rains; exact months should be confirmed from local nest studies rather than inferred from general range.

species_description.text: Medium-sized weaver about 14–15 cm, with heavily streaked brown upperparts and underparts, pale eyebrow and stout bill. Male in breeding plumage has yellowish face and throat; female and non-breeding male are duller. Feeds on grass and rice seeds and insects in reedbeds and paddy margins.

male_female_identification.text: Breeding male shows yellowish face/throat and more contrasting dark streaking; female is duller brown, heavily streaked and lacks the male's yellow wash. Non-breeding male resembles female.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are dull, with less distinct streaking and pale buff underparts; they resemble adult female.

field_spotting_tips.text: Find colonies in tall reeds at tanks and marshes. Heavy streaking below and absence of a long tubular nest entrance distinguish it from Baya Weaver.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Locally common resident in dry lowland wetlands, especially tall reedbeds around tanks, marshes and paddy fields; also occurs in coastal lowlands and occasionally wet lowlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident breeder. Sri Lankan breeding reported February–April and July–October. Builds globular nests among reeds/bulrushes, with a shorter entrance than Baya Weaver.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status code R for all eight species. Note older field-guide/plate editions differ for Indian Silverbill and Black-throated Munia (UR); current CBC 2022 checklist lists both R.

species_description.text: Small weaver about 15 cm. Breeding male has bright yellow crown, black face mask and dark brown upperparts with yellow underparts; female and non-breeding male are dull olive-brown and streaked. Male constructs elaborate hanging retort-shaped nest with long entrance tunnel. Feeds on seeds, grain and insects.

male_female_identification.text: Breeding male is distinctive with yellow crown and black mask; female is dull brownish-olive, streaked and lacks bright yellow crown. Non-breeding male resembles female.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are dull brown and streaked, similar to female; young males acquire yellow crown and black mask as they mature.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for hanging woven nests with a long entrance tunnel. Breeding male's yellow crown and black mask are unmistakable; distinguish from Streaked Weaver by cleaner underparts and nest architecture.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident in dry lowlands and locally elsewhere, in open country, paddy fields, grassland, scrub and near wetlands. Often nests in colonies in trees, palms or over water.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Sri Lankan breeding peaks reported March–April and August–September. Males weave elaborate hanging nests, often with several nests in one tree; polygynous mating system.

species_description.text: Medium-sized plover (about 23–26 cm). In non-breeding plumage, upperparts are grey-brown with golden/yellow feather fringes, face and underparts pale, and breast sides lightly streaked. Breeding plumage is strikingly black below with golden-spangled upperparts and a white border along the sides. Uses coastal mudflats, lagoons, saltpans, beaches and sometimes flooded fields. Feeds on insects, worms, molluscs and crustaceans, picking prey from the surface.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar outside breeding season. In breeding plumage, females usually show more white mottling on the black underparts and less extensive black than males; differences are variable and difficult to judge outside close views.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble non-breeding adults but are more neatly scaled above, with buff/golden fringes and a more patterned breast. First-winter birds gradually acquire adult-like grey-brown upperparts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a compact, medium-sized plover with golden spangling on the upperparts. In flight, a pale underwing and lack of the Grey Plover's strong black axillary pattern help separate it. Compare carefully with Grey Plover: Pacific Golden is smaller and more finely golden above.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common migrant on suitable coastal wetlands and mudflats, especially Mannar, Puttalam, Bundala, lagoons and saltpans. Also occurs on other suitable tidal flats and coastal wetlands around the island.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Predominantly a northern-winter visitor. Sri Lankan and regional datasets indicate arrivals from Aug/Sep, strongest presence through Oct–Mar, with some records into Apr/May. CBC lists it as M.

species_description.text: Large, robust plover (about 27–30 cm). Non-breeding birds are grey above with pale fringes, pale below and a dark grey breast-side patch. In breeding plumage, face, neck and underparts become black with a bold white border, while upperparts are black-and-white chequered. Feeds on worms, molluscs, crustaceans and insects on mudflats, estuaries and coastal lagoons.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar. Breeding females usually show more white mottling and less solid black on the underparts than males; outside breeding plumage, reliable field sexing is not practical.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have strongly patterned, scaly-looking upperparts with buff fringes, and a pale breast with fine streaking. They gradually become greyer and less distinctly scaled through the first year.

field_spotting_tips.text: Notice its relatively large size, heavy build and grey non-breeding plumage. In flight, the black axillaries are a useful feature. In breeding plumage, the black belly is unmistakable; compare with the smaller Pacific Golden Plover.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common migrant on coastal mudflats, lagoons, estuaries and saltpans, especially Mannar, Puttalam, Bundala and other extensive tidal wetlands. Often feeds on open mudflats at low tide and roosts on sandbars at high tide.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Winter migrant, arriving from Aug/Sep and generally present through Apr or May. CBC 2022 lists M. GBIF-derived records show it most regularly in the northern winter period.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, slender babbler about 20–22 cm, with a long down-curved yellow bill, bold white eyebrow, dark eye-stripe, rufous-brown upperparts and pale throat/breast with darker flanks. Usually in pairs or family groups, probing leaf litter, branches and dense undergrowth for insects, grubs and spiders; also takes berries and nectar.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and are not reliably separable in the field. Pairs often duet, with the two voices closely synchronised.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile plumage is poorly documented in readily available field sources; young birds are likely duller with softer, less sharply defined markings. Do not assign confident age from weak visual clues.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its distinctive bubbling duet, often sounding like one bird. The long sickle-shaped yellow bill and prominent white eyebrow are diagnostic. Search thick cover and mixed-species flocks.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident in suitable wooded habitats across much of Sri Lanka, from lowlands to hills. Uses wet and dry zone forest, dense scrub, bamboo, cardamom shade, estates and well-wooded gardens; scarce in the most open northern dry lowlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding reported mainly December–February. Nest is a loose domed structure concealed in dense foliage, on a bank, bush or near ground level.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Sri Lanka Scimitar-babbler E; Yellow-eyed Babbler R; Tawny-bellied Babbler R; Dark-fronted Babbler R; Sri Lanka Orange-billed Babbler E; Sri Lanka Ashy-headed Laughing-thrush E; Yellow-billed Babbler R; Sri Lanka Brown-capped Babbler E. Several resident species have endemic Sri Lankan subspecies only.

species_description.text: Large, conspicuous rail (about 40–50 cm) with deep purple-blue body, red bill and frontal shield, large red legs and white undertail. Uses reedbeds, marshes, paddy fields, lakes and freshwater swamps with emergent vegetation. Eats shoots, stems, seeds, aquatic plants, insects, molluscs, eggs and small vertebrates; often holds food with its long toes.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; males are usually larger with a larger bill and frontal shield, but size overlaps and is not a reliable standalone sexing feature.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are much duller, mainly brownish or grey-brown, with less purple-blue colour and a smaller, duller frontal shield. Adult colour develops progressively.

field_spotting_tips.text: Large size, purple-blue body and red bill/shield are diagnostic. Watch it walking over floating vegetation or feeding in reedbeds; its loud calls often reveal its presence.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident in lowland wetlands throughout Sri Lanka, especially large marshes, reedbeds, tanks, reservoirs and paddy-field systems.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is linked to water levels and emergent vegetation and may occur in more than one season.

species_description.text: Small, slender prinia, about 11–13 cm, with a long graduated tail, strong pinkish legs, short black bill, grey breast band and white throat. Sri Lankan birds belong to the distinctive pectoralis form, with smoky grey upperparts and a grey band across the breast. Inhabits scrub, open woodland, grass edges and cultivation; feeds on insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are generally similar, but in Sri Lankan pectoralis the female may have an incomplete breast band. This is a useful local distinction but not always obvious in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds resemble non-breeding adults but are browner/rufous above; the lower mandible is pale. The Sri Lankan form retains a relatively grey, breeding-like appearance throughout the year.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the smoky grey breast band contrasting with a white throat, pink legs and rufous wing panel. Do not assume the Sri Lankan endemic subspecies makes the whole species endemic.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident, locally distributed in scrub, open woodland and grassland mosaics in Sri Lanka, including dry and intermediate zone localities. The pectoralis subspecies is endemic to Sri Lanka, but the species itself is not endemic.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding records are seasonal; nests are placed low in tall grass or shrubs, typically with 3–4 eggs. Exact island-wide breeding months require further local source checking.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022/local checklist convention: all six species resident (R). Grey-breasted Prinia's Sri Lankan subspecies pectoralis is endemic; species is not endemic.

species_description.text: Small, long-tailed, brownish warbler, usually 13–15 cm, with streaked or plain brown upperparts, pale buff underparts and a relatively short bill. It frequents grassland, scrub, paddy margins, marsh edges and open cultivation, feeding on insects and other small invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; male may be slightly larger. No reliable field sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally warmer brown and more finely streaked, with a yellowish gape and less crisp facial markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for an active, long-tailed brown bird flicking its tail while moving through grass. Plain Prinia is generally more buff and less contrasting than Grey-breasted Prinia; check habitat and breast pattern.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open country across Sri Lanka, especially dry-zone grassland, scrub, paddy fields and marsh margins; also occurs in lower hills. Sri Lankan birds are often assigned to the insularis subspecies.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round; breeding may occur over an extended period and is influenced by local rainfall. Deep cup nest of grasses placed low in grass tussocks or bushes, sometimes above water.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022/local checklist convention: all six species resident (R). Grey-breasted Prinia's Sri Lankan subspecies pectoralis is endemic; species is not endemic.

species_description.text: Small, active prinia, about 13–14 cm, with grey-brown to olive-brown upperparts, pale underparts, long graduated tail and short bill. The head and throat can look greyer in some plumages. It frequents scrub, gardens, grass edges, open woodland and cultivation, feeding mainly on insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in appearance; males may be slightly larger and more vocal. No dependable external field sex character.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, often with warmer buff tones and less distinct facial markings; plumage varies seasonally.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its repeated sharp calls and watch for tail flicking from low bushes. It is usually greyer and more compact-looking than Plain Prinia; identification should use call, habitat and full plumage.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open scrub, grassland edges, gardens and cultivated landscapes across Sri Lanka, especially dry and intermediate zones, but locally widespread.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding can occur in more than one season and is often associated with rainy periods; nest is a small cup concealed in grass or low vegetation.

species_description.text: Small, rather robust prinia, about 13–15 cm, with brown upperparts, pale buff underparts, a relatively short tail and strong legs. It is associated with dry scrub, thorny bush, forest edges and open woodland, often keeping low in dense cover. Feeds on insects and other small invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage; male is typically more vocal and may show stronger breeding colour, but external sexing is unreliable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and less sharply marked than adults, with softer plumage and a yellowish gape.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search dense scrub and listen for its sharp, repetitive calls. More terrestrial and skulking than Common Tailorbird; distinguish from Plain Prinia by its habitat, proportions and vocalisations.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in dry-zone scrub, thorn forest and open woodland in Sri Lanka, with localised distribution compared with the widespread Common Tailorbird and Ashy Prinia. Recorded at dry-zone sites including Uda Walawe and Bundala.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is seasonal and associated with suitable conditions; local breeding months require further targeted verification. Nest is a cup concealed in grass or low shrub.

species_description.text: A medium-sized endemic barbet, about 21 cm, with green plumage, a bright yellow forehead, blue face and throat, and a stout grey bill. It inhabits wet-zone and hill forests, forest edges, rural gardens and fruit orchards close to forest. Usually seen singly, in pairs or small groups, often high in the canopy. Feeds mainly on fruit and berries, occasionally taking insects. Excavates a cavity in a tree for nesting.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in plumage, with no clear sexual dimorphism reported. The yellow forehead and blue face/throat are shared by both sexes.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less intense yellow and blue facial colours and a less sharply defined head pattern. They can be difficult to age unless seen alongside adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its loud, far-carrying calls in wet-zone forest. The yellow forehead and blue face/throat are diagnostic. It is often easier to hear than see in the canopy; scan fruiting trees and forest-edge crowns.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident, most frequent in the wet zone and central highlands, including Kitulgala, Sinharaja, Udawattakele and suitable forested hill areas. Also visits gardens and orchards near forest. Occurs in lowlands and higher central hills.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding is reported in two periods, approximately February–May and August–September. Nests in excavated tree cavities.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status applied: endemic (E) for Sri Lanka Grey Hornbill, Yellow-fronted Barbet and Crimson-fronted Barbet; resident (R) for the other three. Verify exact row codes before publication.

species_description.text: A small, compact green barbet, around 17 cm, with a crimson forehead and breast patch, yellow throat and greenish-yellow streaked underparts. Its short, stout bill and truncated tail give it a compact profile. Common in gardens, groves, sparse woodland, plantations and urban parks, especially where wild figs and other fruiting trees occur. Mainly frugivorous, feeding on banyan, peepal, figs, berries and drupes, but also catches insects such as winged termites. Excavates a cavity in a branch or tree for nesting and may use cavities for roosting.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are broadly similar. Some references report slightly brighter red and yellow breast bands in males, but this is subtle and not a dependable field sexing feature.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and less brightly marked, with less intense red on the forehead and breast. They may retain a softer, less sharply defined pattern while accompanying adults at feeding and roosting sites.

field_spotting_tips.text: Its repetitive metallic tuk-tuk-tuk call sounds like a small hammer striking metal and is often heard before the bird is found. Search flowering and fruiting trees, especially banyan and peepal. The red forehead and breast patch distinguish it from the larger barbets.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident across Sri Lanka's lowlands and many urban and rural landscapes. Frequently seen around gardens, temple trees, parks, fruit orchards and dry-zone woodland; common around Udawalawe and Tissamaharama as well as towns.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan egg-laying has been reported from December to September, with breeding activity possible through much of the year. Both sexes excavate the nest cavity and share incubation and chick care.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status applied: endemic (E) for Sri Lanka Grey Hornbill, Yellow-fronted Barbet and Crimson-fronted Barbet; resident (R) for the other three. Verify exact row codes before publication.

species_description.text: Sri Lanka's smallest barbet, about 17 cm, with green plumage, a crimson-red forehead, yellow around the eye and throat, pale blue cheek area and a short black bill. It has a compact body, short tail and pinkish-red legs. Usually occurs in forest canopy, forest edges and wooded gardens, singly or in pairs. Feeds on fruits and berries and also takes insects. Excavates a tree cavity for nesting; both parents incubate and feed the young.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are very similar, with no clear sexual dimorphism reported. The crimson forehead and yellow facial markings occur in both sexes.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less saturated red, yellow and blue facial markings. Young birds may show a softer head pattern and are often difficult to age at a distance.

field_spotting_tips.text: Small size and bright red forehead are key. Listen for its characteristic clattering call, often accompanied by head-bobbing. It can be overlooked high in leafy canopy; search fruiting trees and listen carefully in wet-zone forest.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident across Sri Lanka's wet and dry zones, including lowland forest, foothills and upper central highlands. Often encountered in Sinharaja, Kitulgala, the Ramboda area and forested parts of the central hills; can be local and inconspicuous.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding is reported mainly in the first half of the year, approximately January–June. A pair excavates a tree hole and both parents share incubation and chick feeding.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status applied: endemic (E) for Sri Lanka Grey Hornbill, Yellow-fronted Barbet and Crimson-fronted Barbet; resident (R) for the other three. Verify exact row codes before publication.

species_description.text: A large green barbet, around 27 cm, with a brown head and throat, pale streaking on the head and breast, green body and a large stout bill. The bare skin around the eye and base of the bill changes from yellowish to orange during breeding condition. It inhabits wooded country, gardens, plantations and fruit orchards, often in the upper canopy and around cultivated fruit trees. Mainly eats fruit, including figs, mangoes, jackfruit and papaya; adults may also take insects, and chicks are fed fruit and animal food. Nests in a cavity excavated in a tree.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in plumage; no dependable field sex differences are established. Seasonal colour change in the bare facial skin and bill is associated with breeding condition, not a sex distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller and less clearly streaked, with a less developed bill and facial skin. Young birds are often difficult to separate from adults without close views.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its loud, repetitive kura-kura call from the canopy. Look for a large green barbet with a brown head and pale streaking. The bare skin near the eye and bill becomes more orange in breeding condition. Fruiting jak, mango and fig trees are productive places to search.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident across much of Sri Lanka, particularly lowland and intermediate-zone wooded country, gardens, plantations and fruit orchards. Less typical of the highest central hills. Often seen in urban gardens and around fruiting trees.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding is reported mainly February–July, with a secondary period around August–September. It nests in tree cavities and lays approximately 2–4 eggs.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status applied: endemic (E) for Sri Lanka Grey Hornbill, Yellow-fronted Barbet and Crimson-fronted Barbet; resident (R) for the other three. Verify exact row codes before publication.

species_description.text: Endemic medium-sized parakeet, about 29–31 cm including tail, green with lavender-grey head and mantle, broad emerald collar and cobalt-blue tail. Moves in pairs/small flocks through forest canopy and wooded landscapes; eats fruit, seeds, buds and leafy matter. Nests in tree cavities or old woodpecker/barbet holes.

male_female_identification.text: Male has red upper mandible and dark lower mandible; female has a black bill. Bill colour is the most useful sex character.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young of both sexes are green overall with darker head; bill initially orange-red. Adult grey head and collar develop with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for harsh kee-kee calls from canopy. Shorter-tailed than Rose-ringed Parakeet; grey-lavender head, green collar and blue tail are diagnostic.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident, commonest in wet-zone forest and wooded foothills; locally in dry-zone forest patches such as Ritigala and Wasgomuwa. Suitable wooded areas up to c.1,700 m.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding mainly January–May, with secondary period July–September; 2–3 eggs in natural cavity, both parents care for young.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) status convention: E for Sri Lanka Hanging-parrot and Layard's Parakeet; R for the remaining species. Confirm current CBC row-level code before publication.

species_description.text: Green parakeet about 33 cm including tail; adult male has plum-coloured head, green body and long pointed tail. Female has greyish-purple head and pale neck collar. Uses wooded country, forest edges, plantations and gardens; feeds on fruit, seeds, buds, flowers and grain; nests in tree cavities.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male has plum-red head, black chin/throat and narrow bluish-green collar; female has greyish-purple head and lacks male's black throat patch.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble females, with greyish head and no adult male black throat patch; male head colour changes with maturity.

field_spotting_tips.text: Male's plum-coloured head is striking; females and juveniles have greyish heads. Search wooded foothills and fruiting trees; distinguish from Layard's by head pattern and absence of its green collar.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Uncommon breeding resident, chiefly foothills and mid-hills, in wooded low-country and intermediate zone. CBC image records include Mulatiyana, Digana and Passara.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding reported December–April, with occasional July–August records in Sri Lanka; tree-cavity nester.

species_description.text: Sri Lanka's largest parakeet, about 50–58 cm including tail, green with large red bill, maroon shoulder patch, blue-green tail and broad pinkish nape/collar in adult males. Uses wooded country, dry-zone forest, plantations and gardens; eats fruit, seeds, buds, flowers and grain; nests in tree cavities.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male has black-and-pink neck ring and pink nape band; female lacks the complete collar and has a greenish/grey neck. Both sexes show maroon shoulder patch.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble adult females, with green neck and shorter tail; male collar develops over several years. Young bill may be duller.

field_spotting_tips.text: Very large size, heavy red bill and maroon shoulder patch. Adult male's pink-and-black collar is distinctive. Watch feeding/roosting trees and listen for loud calls.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident but local in Sri Lanka; dry-zone woodland and large trees in towns/gardens. Records from Wilpattu, Anuradhapura, Sigiriya, Peradeniya and western lowlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding in tree cavities; a robust island-wide monthly window was not established in this research batch.

species_description.text: Familiar green parakeet, about 40 cm including long pointed tail, red bill and narrow dark chin stripe. Occupies towns, gardens, paddy edges, open woodland, plantations and scrub. Eats seeds, fruit, buds, flowers and crops; nests in tree cavities and sometimes buildings.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male has black chin/neck stripe and pink collar; female lacks the complete collar and has a plain green neck.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble adult females, with green neck and shorter tail; adult male collar develops gradually.

field_spotting_tips.text: Long pointed tail and red bill. Adult male's pink-and-black neck ring is diagnostic; females and young are green-necked. Often noisy in flocks.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Very common resident throughout Sri Lanka, including urban areas, villages, agricultural landscapes, dry-zone woodland and coastal settlements.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeds in tree cavities; local dates vary and no precise island-wide period is asserted here.

species_description.text: Common medium-sized bulbul, about 20 cm, with short pointed crest, dark brown body with pale scale-like feather edges, black head, white rump, bright red vent and white-tipped dark tail. Highly adaptable and feeds on fruit, flowers, nectar, insects and occasionally small vertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; no reliable external field distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less sharply defined head and crest and a less conspicuous red vent; scale-like body pattern is less distinct.

field_spotting_tips.text: Short pointed crest, white rump and red vent are diagnostic. Its loud, varied calls are familiar around houses and gardens. Often seen in pairs or small groups feeding on berries and flowers.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Very common resident throughout Sri Lanka in gardens, towns, villages, scrub, plantations, open woodland and agricultural landscapes. Also present in dry-zone scrub and around human habitation.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding commonly reported June–September, with local variation and possibility of multiple broods. Cup nest in bushes or small trees, often 2–3 m above ground.

Square-tailed Bulbul is also native to India, so not endemic.

species_description.text: Medium-sized bulbul, about 20 cm, with olive-brown upperparts, pale underparts, prominent pale eyebrow and yellow vent. It is often shy and skulking in dense dry scrub, thorny thickets and bushy woodland, feeding on fruit and insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage; no dependable external field distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less distinct eyebrow and yellow vent; young birds can be especially difficult to see in dense scrub.

field_spotting_tips.text: Usually heard before seen: listen for loud, distinctive bursts of calls from dense scrub. Look for pale eyebrow and yellow vent when it briefly emerges. More skulking than Red-vented Bulbul.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in dry-zone and lower-elevation scrub across Sri Lanka, including Tissamaharama, Sigiriya, Wilpattu and other dry lowland habitats. Also occurs in peninsular India.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding season varies locally; exact Sri Lankan months require further CBC/local source verification. Nest is a small cup concealed in dense shrubbery.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, attractive hill bulbul, about 20 cm, with black-and-white head pattern, conspicuous yellow ear tufts, olive-brown upperparts and yellowish underparts. Feeds on fruit, nectar and insects, often in pairs or small groups in forest canopy, gardens and orchards.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage and cannot reliably be separated in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with less contrasting black-and-white head pattern and less conspicuous yellow ear tufts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Distinctive yellow ear tufts and black-and-white head make it unmistakable. Listen for its musical calls, often given while moving between trees. Look for it in fruiting shrubs and forest edges in the highlands.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka's central highlands and montane forests, generally above 1,000 m and most familiar above about 1,300 m. Common around Nuwara Eliya, Horton Plains, Hakgala and montane forest patches.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Two breeding periods reported: February–May and August–October (some CBC accounts give March–May and August–October). Nest is a substantial cup in a small tree or bush, usually 3–5 m above ground.

species_description.text: Small to medium, secretive forest crake (about 25–28 cm) with dark slate-grey head and underparts, brown upperparts, barred flanks and distinctive dull pinkish to reddish legs. Inhabits dense, damp forest undergrowth, stream margins, bamboo and thick vegetation. Feeds on insects, worms, snails and other small invertebrates, probing leaf litter and wet ground.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage and not reliably separable in field conditions.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and more heavily barred or mottled than adults, with less uniform slate-grey underparts. Leg colour may be duller.

field_spotting_tips.text: Usually detected by calls or brief movement in dense cover. Search damp leaf litter and stream edges at quiet dawn periods; patience and playback restraint are important. Note leg colour and barred flanks for identification.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident and locally recorded in Sri Lanka's wet-zone forests and dense, damp habitats; sightings are scarce because of its secretive behaviour. Forest reserves and streamside thickets are the best habitat rather than open marshes.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident, with some seasonal or passage records possible; CBC list indicates R/M. Exact seasonal pattern in Sri Lanka needs further dated-record review.

species_description.text: Large, unmistakable wader (about 42–45 cm) with striking black-and-white plumage, long pale blue-grey legs and a long, slender black bill that curves distinctly upwards. Feeds in shallow fresh or brackish water and on mudflats, sweeping the partly open bill from side to side to catch aquatic invertebrates, including insects, crustaceans and worms. Nests colonially on open ground near water in its breeding range outside Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar. Males tend to have a longer, slightly straighter bill; females usually have a shorter bill with a more pronounced upturn and may show less sharply defined head markings. These differences are subtle and should be used cautiously.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have brownish rather than black dark markings, with duller grey legs and brown/grey mottling or fringes on the pale upperparts. First-year birds retain faded brownish flight feathers.

field_spotting_tips.text: The strongly upcurved bill is the key feature: no other regular Sri Lankan wader has this combination of black-and-white pattern and upturned bill. Observe feeding birds sweeping the bill laterally through shallow water. Check carefully for distant Black-winged Stilts, which have straight bills.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A scarce/irregular visitor in Sri Lanka; search shallow coastal lagoons, saltpans, estuaries and mudflats, particularly in the north-west and other major wader sites such as Mannar and Bundala. Specific regular Sri Lankan hotspots are not firmly established from the sources checked.

seasonality_months_seen.text: A migrant in Sri Lanka. Records should be expected during the northern winter wader season, broadly Oct–Apr, but the species is scarce and the available sources do not establish a reliable Sri Lankan peak month. Record dates and locations carefully.

species_description.text: Small, active fantail about 18–19 cm including long tail. Grey-brown upperparts, white eyebrow and throat, dark eye-line, pale underparts and broad white tips on tail feathers. Constantly fans and flicks its tail while making short aerial sallies for insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; no dependable external field distinction.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner and duller, with buffy edges and less distinct white eyebrow and tail pattern.

field_spotting_tips.text: Tail-fanning is the best clue. It often follows people or livestock, flitting low and returning to a perch. Look for white eyebrow and broad white tail corners; distinguish from other fantails by its grey-brown colour and white brow.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open woodland, scrub, dry forest edges, plantations and gardens, especially in dry and intermediate zones. Sri Lankan subspecies compressirostris is resident.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding generally February–July in Sri Lanka; small cup nest suspended in a fork, often low in a tree or shrub.

species_description.text: Distinctive, secretive wetland wader (about 23–28 cm), with a long pinkish bill, short legs and cryptic, intricately patterned plumage. Adult female is more colourful, with chestnut/rufous neck and breast, dark greenish upperparts and conspicuous white spots; male is smaller-looking and duller brown, with a pale buff face and finely patterned upperparts. Uses marshes, wet grass, paddy fields and vegetated pond margins. Feeds on insects, worms, molluscs and other small invertebrates, often at dusk or night.

male_female_identification.text: Unusual reversed sexual dimorphism: female is brighter and more colourful, with chestnut neck/breast and bold white spotting; male is duller and browner. Female typically courts and may mate with multiple males; male undertakes incubation and chick care.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Male with chicks is often seen; chicks are downy and cryptically striped/spotted in buff, brown and black, matching marsh vegetation. Juveniles are generally duller and less strongly patterned than adult females; ageing can be difficult in poor light.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search slowly along muddy margins with dense sedges and low vegetation, especially at dawn/dusk. Listen for soft calls and scan carefully for a long bill and spotted back. Remember the female is more colourful than the male—opposite to the usual pattern in many birds.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in suitable marshes and wetland vegetation. Known from Colombo wetlands including Pepiliyana, Kimbulawala, Beddagana, Bellanwila-Attidiya and Nedimala; also recorded at Bundala and Vankalai/Mannar. Often hidden in dense marginal vegetation.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident and can be found year-round. Local observations show regular occurrence in Colombo wetlands; breeding and chick records have been documented in different months, so avoid assigning a single island-wide breeding season.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC image database explicitly identifies species as resident in Sri Lanka; resident.

species_description.text: Small to medium-sized forest bulbul, about 19 cm, with olive-green upperparts, bright yellow underparts, black cap and white edges to the outer tail feathers. Feeds on fruit, berries and insects, moving actively through shrubs and canopy in pairs or small parties.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage. Iris is a useful distinction: male typically crimson-red, female deep brown. This is subtle and requires good light.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with a less sharply defined black cap and less vivid yellow underparts; iris colour is not as striking as in adult male.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the black cap, yellow underparts and white tail edges. Do not confuse with Yellow-browed Bulbul, which lacks the black cap. Male's red iris versus female's brown iris can help at close range.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident across Sri Lanka's low-country wet zone and mid-hills, in forest, wooded gardens, forest edges and well-vegetated riverine habitats. Regular at Sinharaja, Kitulgala and other wet-zone forests.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding reported mainly April–May, with a secondary season around August–September, especially in the hills. Cup nest placed low in saplings or shrubs, often supported on a platform of broad leaves.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List/local checklist convention: Sri Lanka Black-capped Bulbul E; Sri Lanka Yellow-eared Bulbul E; Red-vented Bulbul R; Square-tailed Bulbul R; White-browed Bulbul R; Yellow-browed Bulbul R. Square-tailed Bulbul is also native to India, so not endemic.

species_description.text: Small, upright chat about 13 cm. Adult male is mostly black with white rump, lower belly and prominent white wing patch; female is warm dark brown with a rusty rump and paler buff-brown underparts. Feeds chiefly on insects, usually from exposed perches in open country.

male_female_identification.text: Strongly dimorphic. Male black with white wing and rump patches; female brown with rusty rump and no large white wing patch. Non-breeding and first-winter males can show brown/rufous feather fringes.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble females but are more mottled/scaly and less uniform brown. Young males gradually acquire black plumage; first-winter males may retain brown feather fringes.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often sits conspicuously on fence posts, rocks or isolated bushes, dropping to the ground for insects. Look for the male's white wing patch and rump; female is warm brown with rusty rump. Do not assume all Sri Lankan birds are the highland subspecies.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in open grassland, scrub, cultivation, pasture and rocky country. In Sri Lanka, nominate-range populations occur in open lowlands, while the endemic hill subspecies S. c. atratus is resident in the central highlands, including Horton Plains.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. CBC image archive documents hill birds in January, March, April, August and October; breeding reported in the broader range mainly February–May, but local atratus nesting season needs separate verification.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 convention: Pied Bushchat R (Sri Lankan hill subspecies atratus endemic); Sri Lanka Shama E; Oriental Magpie-robin R; Indian Robin R; Indian Blue Robin M.

species_description.text: Small, compact nuthatch, about 11–12 cm, with a long pointed bill, short tail, strong feet and vivid blue upperparts. Underparts are orange-rufous, with a dark eye-stripe and pale supercilium. It climbs head-first down trunks and branches, probing bark crevices for insects and spiders; also takes seeds and small fruits.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a black eye-stripe; female typically has a chestnut-brown eye-stripe and often slightly duller upperparts. Sex distinction is usually visible in good views.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less saturated blue upperparts and paler, less clearly defined facial markings; bill and eye-stripe contrast develop with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Distinctive head-first descent down tree trunks and repeated sharp 'sit-sit' calls. Look for bright blue back, orange underparts and a strong eye-stripe. Often joins mixed feeding flocks in forest canopy.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in forested habitats throughout much of Sri Lanka, from lowlands to montane forests, including Sinharaja, Knuckles, Peak Wilderness, Horton Plains, Yala and Udawalawe riverine woodland. Less frequent in the extreme north.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round and a breeding resident. Nests in tree cavities; breeding months in Sri Lanka require further targeted verification.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Blyth's Reed-warbler M; Clamorous Reed-warbler R; Large-billed Leaf-warbler M; Greenish Warbler M; Sri Lanka Bush Warbler E; Velvet-fronted Nuthatch R. Clamorous Reed-warbler has endemic Sri Lankan subspecies meridionalis, not an endemic species.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 44–52 පමණ දිගැති මධ්‍යම ප්‍රමාණයේ තාරාවෙකි. ඉතා පළල්, spatula හැඩැති හොට ප්‍රධාන ලක්ෂණය. පිරිමිගේ හිස කොළ පැහැති, පපුව සුදු, පැති chestnut; ගැහැනු දුඹුරු mottled සහ හොට අළු-තැඹිලි. Marshes, shallow lakes, lagoons සහ ජලජ ශාක බහුල තෙත්බිම්. හොටේ comb-like lamellae මඟින් ජලයෙන් plankton, කුඩා crustaceans සහ බීජ පෙරහන් කරයි. ලංකාවේ ශීත සංචාරකයෙකි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි breeding plumage හි කොළ හිස, සුදු පපුව, chestnut flank සහ පළල් කළු හොට. ගැහැනු mottled brown, තැඹිලි පැල්ලම් සහිත පළල් හොට. Eclipse male ගැහැනුට සමාන නමුත් පියාපත් රටා/ඇස් පැහැය උපකාරී.

field_spotting_tips.text: හොටේ පළල් spatula හැඩය දුරින්ම හඳුනාගැනීමට උපකාරී. shallow water හි හිස ජලයට දමා පැත්තකට හැරෙමින් filter-feed කරන හැසිරීම බලන්න. පිරිමිගේ කොළ හිස සහ chestnut පැති බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: පහළබිම් කලපු, marshes සහ විශාල වැව්; Bundala, Tissamaharama සහ වයඹ/දකුණු වෙරළබඩ තෙත්බිම්.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශීත සංචාරකයෙක්; සාමාන්‍යයෙන් නොවැම්බර්–මාර්තු, ඇතැම්විට ඔක්තෝබර්/අප්‍රේල් (CBC 2022: M).

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 37–41 පමණ දිගැති කුඩා dabbling duck එකකි. පිරිමිගේ හිස දුඹුරු, ඇස හරහා පුළුල් සුදු crescent එකක්, අළු ශරීරය සහ පියාපතේ ලා නිල්-අළු forewing. ගැහැනු දුඹුරු mottled, ඇස හරහා අඳුරු ඉරක් සහිතයි. Marshes, shallow lakes, flooded grassland සහ rice fields. ජලජ කෘමීන්, කුඩා crustaceans, බීජ සහ ශාක කොටස් ආහාරයට ගනී. ලංකාවේ ශීත සංචාරකයෙකි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමිගේ සුදු crescent facial stripe ඉතා පැහැදිලියි. ගැහැනු mottled brown, ඇස හරහා dark stripe සහ bill base අසල pale patch තිබිය හැක. Juvenile ගැහැනුට සමාන, වඩා අඩු contrast.

field_spotting_tips.text: කුඩා ප්‍රමාණය සහ පිරිමිගේ සුදු ඇස්-ඉර ලක්ෂණය. රංචු ලෙස shallow marshes හි feeding. ගැහැනු හඳුනාගැනීමට bill shape සහ face pattern එක Northern Shoveler/teal සමඟ සසඳන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Bundala, Tissamaharama, Minneriya සහ වෙනත් පහළබිම් marshes/වැව්. වියළි කලාපීය shallow wetlands වඩා හොඳ ස්ථාන.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශීත සංචාරකයෙක්; සාමාන්‍යයෙන් ඔක්තෝබර්–අප්‍රේල් (CBC 2022: M; eBird-derived data).

species_description.text: Medium-sized dove (about 28–32 cm) with pinkish-grey underparts, brown upperparts with dark spotting, and a distinctive black hindneck patch covered in white spots. Tail is long with white outer feathers. Common in gardens, scrub, plantations, farmland and open woodland. Eats seeds and grains, with some small fruits. Builds a loose twig platform nest in shrubs or trees.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar; males may be slightly larger or show richer pink tones, but these differences are subtle and unreliable in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles lack the fully developed black-and-white spotted neck patch and have browner, more uniform plumage with pale feather fringes. Adult neck spotting develops with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: The black nape patch with white spots is the key field mark. Listen for its repeated cooing from garden trees; distinguish from Eurasian Collared-dove by the spotted collar and warmer, more patterned upperparts.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident across Sri Lanka in both wet and dry zones, including gardens, villages, parks, plantations, agricultural land and forest edges.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding can occur in several seasons and is often linked to local rainfall and food availability.

species_description.text: Medium-large forest-edge eagle (about 55–75 cm) with a broad rounded wing, short tail and a distinctive yellow cere and facial skin. Adults are dark brown above, with pale-edged feathers and a conspicuous white-and-brown spotted underside; the head often shows a short crest. Feeds mainly on snakes and other reptiles, also frogs, birds and small mammals. Often hunts from a prominent perch and nests in large trees.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; plumage is alike. Adults show a yellow bare face, short crest and strongly patterned underparts. Sex is difficult to judge without size comparison.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are paler and more heavily streaked or spotted below, with less sharply defined adult patterning and a less developed crest.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its distinctive whistling calls, especially around forest edges. In flight, look for broad rounded wings, short tail and pale-spotted underparts; often circles above tree canopy.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident in forests, wooded country, plantations and forest edges across Sri Lanka, from lowlands to hills. Frequently seen soaring over forest margins and roads in the wet and intermediate zones.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year (CBC 2022 R).

species_description.text: මධ්‍යම ප්‍රමාණයේ සිහින් මුහුදුලිහිණියෙකි (සෙ.මී. 33–38). සුදු/ඉතා ලා අළු ශරීරය, කළු හිස් තොප්පිය, දිගු forked වලිගය සහ අභිජනන සමයේ රතු පැහැති හොට/පාද ලක්ෂණ වේ. වෙරළබඩ මුහුද, වැලි දූපත් හා මසුන් බහුල ජලය භාවිත කරයි; කුඩා මසුන් ප්‍රධාන ආහාරය. Adam’s Bridge දූපත් සමූහයේ අභිජනන වාර්තා ඇත.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි හා ගැහැනු බාහිර පෙනුමෙන් සමානයි; හොටේ/පාදයේ රතු පැහැයේ තීව්‍රතාව හා ශරීර ප්‍රමාණය සුළු වශයෙන් වෙනස් විය හැකි නමුත් ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ ලිංග නිශ්චය විශ්වාසදායක නොවේ.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile හි හිසෙහි කළු පැහැය අඩු/අසම්පූර්ණය; පිට හා පියාපත්වල දුඹුරු පැහැති රටා සහ අඳුරු පියාපත් අග පෙනිය හැක. වයස තීරණයට පිහාටු රටා සමීපව බලන්න.

field_spotting_tips.text: ඉතා සිහින් සිරුර, දිගු forked වලිගය, දිගු පියාපත් සහ කුඩා/සිහින් හොට බලන්න. Common Tern හා වෙන්කරන විට දිගු වලිගය හා සිහින් හැඩය වැදගත්.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: වෙරළබඩ මුහුද; Mannar/Adam’s Bridge, Bundala සහ Yala වෙරළබඩ ප්‍රදේශවල වාර්තා. දකුණු වෙරළේ boat-based surveys වලද හමුවී ඇත.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ අභිජනන/වෙරළබඩ වාර්තා ඇත; CBC 2022 ලැයිස්තුවේ R/M ලෙස සටහන්. පැමිණීමේ නිශ්චිත මාස හා ප්‍රමාණය වසර අනුව වෙනස් විය හැක.

species_description.text: කුඩා මුහුදුලිහිණියෙකි (සෙ.මී. 21–25). ඉහළපස ලා අළු, යටපස සුදු, කහ හොටේ කළු අගක් සහ කහ පාද ඇත; අභිජනන සමයේ කළු තොප්පිය සහ ඇස් අසල සුදු නළල ලක්ෂණ වේ. වෙරළ, කලපු, වැලි තීරු හා නොගැඹුරු ජලයේ කුඩා මසුන් අල්ලයි. ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ අභිජනන වාර්තා සහිත ස්ථිරවාසී පක්ෂියෙකි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි හා ගැහැනු පෙනුමෙන් සමානයි; ලිංගය ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ වෙන් කිරීම සාමාන්‍යයෙන් කළ නොහැක.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: තරුණයන්ගේ පිට/හිසෙහි දුඹුරු-කළු කොරපොතු රටා, අඳුරු හොට සහ අඩු පැහැදිලි හිස් තොප්පියක් ඇත. Saunders’s Tern සමඟ වෙන්කරන විට හොටේ/පාදයේ වර්ණය පමණක් නොව සම්පූර්ණ රටාව බලන්න.

field_spotting_tips.text: කුඩා ප්‍රමාණය, කහ හොටේ කළු අග, කහ පාද සහ සුදු නළල බලන්න. Saunders’s Tern සමඟ ඉතා සමාන බැවින් හොට/පාද වර්ණය සහ පියාපත් රටා හොඳින් නිරීක්ෂණය කරන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: වෙරළබඩ හා කලපු පද්ධති පුරා; Bundala, Yala, Tissa, Mannar, Mirissa සහ Galle ආශ්‍රිත වෙරළ වාර්තා වේ. උතුරු හා නැගෙනහිර වැලි වෙරළවලද සුදුසු වාසස්ථාන ඇත.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022 අනුව R; වසර පුරා වෙරළබඩ වාර්තා. අභිජනනය Adam’s Bridge/වයඹ වැලි දූපත් ආශ්‍රිතව වාර්තා වී ඇත.

species_description.text: Little Tern ට සමාන ඉතා කුඩා මුහුදුලිහිණියෙකි (සෙ.මී. 22–25). සාමාන්‍යයෙන් කළු පැහැති හොට, කහ/තැඹිලි පාද සහ අභිජනන සමයේ කළු හිස තොප්පියක් ඇත. වැලි දූපත්, වෙරළ තීරු හා නොගැඹුරු මුහුදුබඩ ජලය භාවිත කර කුඩා මසුන් අල්ලයි. ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ දුර්ලභ/අඩු සංඛ්‍යාවක අභිජනන පක්ෂියෙකි.

male_female_identification.text: ලිංග දෙකම සමාන පෙනුමක් දරයි; ලිංගය ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ වෙන් කිරීම සාමාන්‍යයෙන් කළ නොහැක.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juvenile හි හිසෙහි කළු පැහැය අඩු අතර පිටේ දුඹුරු-කළු කොරපොතු රටා ඇත. Little Tern සමඟ වෙන්කිරීම දුෂ්කර බැවින් හොටේ කළු පැහැය සහ පාදයේ වර්ණය පමණක් නොව වෙනත් ලක්ෂණද එකට සලකා බලන්න.

field_spotting_tips.text: Little Tern සමඟ වෙන්කිරීමේදී ඉතා ප්‍රවේශමෙන් බලන්න; Saunders’s සාමාන්‍යයෙන් කළු හොටක් දරයි. තනි ලක්ෂණයක් මත පමණක් ID තීරණය නොකර ඡායාරූප/විස්තර සටහන් තබන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් Mannar–Adam’s Bridge වැලි දූපත් සහ වයඹ වෙරළ. CBC image archive හි Adam’s Bridge දූපත්වල nest අසල වැඩිහිටි පක්ෂීන්ගේ වාර්තා ඇත.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC/දේශීය වාර්තා අනුව scarce resident සහ අභිජනන පක්ෂියෙකි. නිරීක්ෂණ වාර්තා සහ breeding colony monitoring මත මාසික රටාව තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, pale sandy-grey dove (about 31–33 cm) with a narrow black half-collar on the hindneck, pinkish legs and a long square-ended tail with white outer edges. Favours open country, villages, gardens, farmland and urban areas. Feeds mainly on seeds and grain. Builds a flimsy platform nest in trees or shrubs, often near people.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in plumage; slight size differences are not dependable for field sexing.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles lack the complete black hindneck collar and have duller, browner plumage with less distinct feather edges. The collar becomes clearer as the bird matures.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the pale sandy body and narrow black half-collar on the back of the neck. Often perches on wires or rooftops; separate from Spotted Dove by the lack of black-and-white neck spots and the cleaner grey-buff body.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, especially in dry and intermediate zones and around settlements, farms, gardens and open scrub. Local abundance varies with suitable open habitat and human settlement.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding may occur over an extended period; local timing can follow rainfall and food availability.

species_description.text: Large forest owl (about 45–48 cm) with a rounded head, dark eyes, broad wings and a long tail. Upperparts are brown with fine pale markings; underparts are pale with strong dark vertical streaks and cross-bars. Occurs in dense evergreen and moist deciduous forest, wooded hills and forest edges, often roosting in thick foliage by day. Feeds on small mammals, birds, reptiles and large insects. Nests in tree cavities or other sheltered sites.

male_female_identification.text: Female is larger than male; plumage is similar in both sexes. No reliable sex-specific colour pattern is known for field identification.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are fluffier and browner, with softer streaking and less sharply defined adult barring. Young birds may retain down around the head and body after fledging.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for deep, resonant hoots at night. The large size, dark eyes and heavily streaked underparts help distinguish it from fish-owls, which have bright yellow eyes and a more waterside association.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in forested lowlands and hills of Sri Lanka, particularly wet-zone and montane forest blocks. Records from Sinharaja and other large forest tracts; usually detected by voice rather than seen.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident throughout the year. Breeding timing in Sri Lanka is not sufficiently established in the sources consulted to give a firm month range.
