species_description.text: Small, elegant starling about 19–20 cm, with pale buff body, grey-brown back, black cap and long wispy crest, pale iris, blue skin around the eye, and orange-yellow bill and legs. Feeds on insects and fruit, often in open scrub, cultivated land and dry woodland.

male_female_identification.text: Adult male has a longer, more pointed crest and stronger black cap; female's crest is shorter and less pronounced, with softer head pattern. Sex differences can be subtle.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and browner, with a less developed crest, less distinct black cap and duller bill/eye skin.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the pale buff body, upright wispy crest and black cap. The blue orbital skin and pale iris are useful at close range. Usually feeds in open vegetation or on the ground.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Regular migrant to Sri Lanka, favouring dry open country, scrub, cultivated areas, plantations and village landscapes. Often seen in small flocks or mixed starling groups.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Seasonal migrant, generally present in the northern winter months. Exact Sri Lankan arrival/departure window not independently confirmed in this batch.

species_description.text: Medium-sized, elusive endemic starling about 20–22 cm, with dark glossy blue-black upperparts, pale/white face and forehead (extent varies), dark underparts, and bluish-brown bill with a blue base to the lower mandible. Forages high in tall forest canopy, eating fruit, invertebrates and nectar.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage and difficult to separate. Amount of white on the face varies individually; some birds have much more extensive white heads.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have a whitish eyebrow, ear-coverts and throat, dull brown upperparts and dark grey underparts; they lack the adult's clean, strongly contrasting facial appearance.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search tall canopy in intact wet-zone forest and listen for its rather quiet starling-like chirps. Watch fruiting trees and mixed-species flocks. White facial extent varies, so do not use it alone for identification.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to the southwestern wet-zone of Sri Lanka, largely confined to relatively undisturbed moist lowland and foothill forest at about 460–1,220 m. Occasional forest-edge records; canopy forager in mixed-species flocks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round and not migratory. Breeding ecology is poorly known and precise nesting months should remain unconfirmed pending stronger local evidence.

species_description.text: A medium-sized, slender cuckoo (about 25–28 cm) with glossy black to dark slate plumage, a long, distinctly forked tail and red to orange-red eyes. It resembles a drongo in silhouette and behaviour. Uses forest, wooded country, plantations and dense gardens, usually in the canopy. Feeds mainly on insects, including caterpillars. It is a brood parasite; host species vary across its range.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in plumage and are not reliably separable in the field. Both show the dark drongo-like body, forked tail and reddish eye.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller brownish-black and may show pale scaling or barring, especially on the underparts; the tail fork and eye colour may be less conspicuous. Age should be assessed cautiously.

field_spotting_tips.text: Check the tail carefully: the long, forked tail and drongo-like shape are key. It may join mixed-species flocks or perch in the canopy; listen for its calls and distinguish it from a true drongo by the cuckoo-like bill and behaviour.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka, but often local and elusive. Recorded in forested landscapes including Sinharaja and other wooded areas; may be encountered in canopy or mixed-species flocks and is easily overlooked.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident according to CBC country list. Calling and breeding are seasonal, but precise island-wide months are not sufficiently established in the sources reviewed.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 15–18 පමණ දිගැති කුඩා, තරමක් තද ශරීරයක් සහිත quail එකකි. තණබිම්, වගාබිම්, තෙත් තණ ආවරණ සහ වගාබිම් අද්දර සැඟවී සිටී. බීජ සහ කුඩා කෘමීන් ආහාරයට ගනී. වර්ණය සහ දෘශ්‍යතාව ලිංගය හා වයස අනුව වෙනස් වේ. ලංකාවේ ප්‍රජනන කාලය සඳහා නිශ්චිත විශ්වාසදායක දත්ත තවදුරටත් අවශ්‍යයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමිගේ මුහුණ/උගුර/පපුවේ නිල්-අළු පැහැය වඩා පැහැදිලි විය හැක; ගැහැනු සාමාන්‍යයෙන් දුඹුරු-බෆ් සහ ඉරි/තිත් සහිත camouflage පිහාටු. Juvenile ගැහැනුට සමාන නමුත් වඩා අඳුරු/අඩු පැහැදිලි විය හැක.

field_spotting_tips.text: බොහෝවිට තණ අතරින් හදිසියේ පියාඹා යන විට පමණක් පෙනේ. විවෘත තණබිම්වල උදෑසන සහ සවස සෙමින් සොයන්න; පියාඹන විට කෙටි, පහත් flight එක සහ පියාපත් රටාව බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ තණබිම් සහ වගාබිම් ආශ්‍රිත පහළබිම් ප්‍රදේශවල හමුවිය හැක. වර්තමාන දිස්ත්‍රික් මට්ටමේ ව්‍යාප්තිය හා ප්‍රධාන hotspots තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් ස්ථිරවාසී/දේශීය චලනයන් සහිත බව පෙනේ; ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ වාර්ෂික seasonal pattern තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: A medium-large, mainly terrestrial malkoha (roughly 42–43 cm), with earthy brown/rufous upperparts, fine dark streaking on head and breast, a long graduated tail with pale/white tips, and a stout red-to-yellowish bill. Favours dry scrub, thorn jungle, open deciduous woodland and secondary growth, mostly in lowlands. Forages on or close to the ground for large insects, lizards and other small prey, and also takes berries and fruit. It is a non-parasitic cuckoo that builds its own nest.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in general plumage; sex is not reliably separable in ordinary field conditions.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are generally duller and less sharply marked than adults; fine streaking and bill colour may be less distinct. Ageing in the field should be conservative.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search low in scrub and along thorny bush edges. It often runs or slips through cover rather than flying far. The red/yellow bill, streaked brown body and white-tipped tail help separate it from the greener, more arboreal malkohas.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's dry and intermediate zones, particularly scrub and open woodland. Reported from Yala, Bundala, Udawalawe and other dry-zone scrub habitats; also locally in suitable secondary forest and thorny country.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan breeding is reported mainly around June–July; this is a reported peak rather than proof that breeding is confined to those months.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 23–29 පමණ දිගැති කුඩා diving waterbird එකකි. කෙටි ගෙල, වටකුරු ශරීරය, කෙටි හොට සහ පසුපසට පිහිටි පාද. breeding plumage හි chestnut ගෙල/කම්මුල් සහ කහ gape patch; non-breeding දුඹුරු-අළු. වැව්, පොකුණු, marshes, slow rivers සහ ජලජ ශාක ආවරණ. කුඩා මාළු, tadpoles, crustaceans සහ ජලජ කෘමීන් ආහාරයට ගනී. පාවෙන ජලජ ශාක මත කූඩුවක් තනා බිත්තර දමයි; ලංකාවේ breeding months තවදුරටත් සෘජුව තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි/ගැහැනු බොහෝ දුරට සමාන; පිරිමි තරමක් විශාල විය හැක. breeding plumage දෙපාර්ශ්වයේම chestnut cheek/throat; non-breeding සහ juvenile දුඹුරු-අළු, juvenile හි මුහුණේ ඉරි/striping පෙනේ.

field_spotting_tips.text: ජලයේ පාවෙමින් හදිසියේ කිමිදීමෙන් හඳුනාගත හැක. කුඩා ප්‍රමාණය, කෙටි හොට සහ පසුපසට දිගු පාද බලන්න. කිමිදුණු ස්ථානයෙන් ටික දුරකින් නැවත මතු විය හැකි නිසා දිගටම scan කරන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: දිවයින පුරා පහළබිම් වැව්, පොකුණු, marshes සහ නගර උද්‍යාන පොකුණු. Tissamaharama, Bundala, Anawilundawa, Colombo wetlands සහ බොහෝ ග්‍රාමීය වැව්.

species_description.text: Very large, powerful swift (about 20–22 cm) with long scythe-shaped wings, dark brown upperparts, a conspicuous white belly and a broad white throat patch separated by a dark breast band. Feeds on aerial insects, often high above open country, hills and escarpments. Nests in colonies on cliffs and buildings in parts of its range.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; males and females cannot be reliably distinguished in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are similar to adults but may show pale fringes or scaling on feathers, especially on upperparts. Such details are difficult to see unless perched or photographed closely.

field_spotting_tips.text: Identify by its very large size, broad white belly and throat, and long powerful wings. Compare directly with smaller swifts; watch high over ridges and open valleys, especially where several individuals circle together.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs in Sri Lanka as a visitor and/or local seasonal bird, especially over open country and hill-country landscapes. Records are scattered; large flocks may pass over ridges, reservoirs and coastal plains.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Usually recorded during the non-breeding season or passage periods; local timing varies. The workbook's existing resident code should be checked against the current CBC country list before final publication.

species_description.text: Small, agile hawk (about 26–36 cm) with short rounded wings and a long, narrow tail. Adult males typically have grey upperparts, rufous-barred underparts and red eyes; females are browner and more heavily barred. Common in open woodland, gardens, plantations, village edges and towns with trees, avoiding the densest forest. Hunts small birds, lizards, rodents and large insects, usually by a sudden dash from a concealed perch. Builds a small stick nest in a tree.

male_female_identification.text: Male is greyer above with fine rufous barring below and usually red iris. Female is larger and browner, with heavier brown barring and often a yellowish to orange iris. Sexing is best based on a combination of size, plumage and iris colour.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown above with pale edges to feathers and buff-white underparts marked by bold longitudinal streaks rather than adult cross-bars. Iris is usually pale yellow; adult barring and eye colour develop with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for sharp repeated calls and watch small birds suddenly mobbing a concealed hawk. The short rounded wings, long tail and quick low flight through trees are useful clues.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common resident in wooded lowlands, gardens, plantations and open country throughout much of Sri Lanka. Often seen around village gardens and urban tree cover, including the wet and intermediate zones as well as dry-zone settlements.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. A local field account reports breeding mainly March–May with a possible second period around August–September; treat these as observed local periods rather than a fixed island-wide calendar.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022), Version 3: species listed resident (R); see row-level source note. For Changeable Hawk-eagle, CBC separately names Sri Lankan subspecies ceylanensis as Crested Hawk-eagle.

species_description.text: Small forest hawk, slightly larger and more robust than Shikra, with short rounded wings and a long tail. Adults have dark slate-grey upperparts, finely barred underparts and a strong pale supercilium; females are larger and browner. Favours forest, forest edge, wooded hills and dense plantations, usually hunting birds by surprise from cover. Nests in trees; local breeding details are not well documented in the sources consulted.

male_female_identification.text: Female is noticeably larger than male and generally browner, with heavier barring. Male is greyer and more compact. Both sexes show a bold pale eyebrow and finely barred underparts; size comparison is most useful when a pair is seen together.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are browner above with buff edges and heavily streaked underparts, rather than the fine cross-barring of adults. A pale eyebrow is usually evident; ageing requires care because plumage varies geographically.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for a compact accipiter flashing through forest gaps, with rounded wings, long tail and pale eyebrow. Distinguish from Shikra by its stronger forest association, heavier build and more prominent supercilium.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in forested and wooded parts of Sri Lanka, particularly the wet-zone and hill-country forests and forest edges. More often detected in wooded habitats than in open agricultural country.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. There is insufficient reliable island-wide monthly evidence to assign a precise seasonal pattern or breeding window; sightings can be difficult because of its secretive habits.

species_description.text: Small, rather plain grey-brown endemic shrike, about 17–18 cm, with a large head, strong hooked bill, white rump and black upper tail-coverts. Male has a dark eye-mask; female is browner and less strongly masked. Usually in pairs in scrub, open woodland and forest edges, feeding mainly on insects gleaned from foliage and branches.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a distinct dark mask through the eye and greyer upperparts; female is browner with a weaker mask. Both have a conspicuous white rump and dark upper tail-coverts.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Young birds are cryptically patterned and can look like a lichen-covered knot on a branch; juvenile plumage is duller and less sharply masked than adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often overlooked because of its dull colour. Listen for its clear, descending, liquid whistle and search in pairs in scrub or large scattered trees. The white rump bordered by dark upper tail-coverts is a useful clue.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident, commonest in the low-country dry zone and on the drier eastern slopes, ascending to about 1,200 m. Scarce and local in wet zone; recorded in Wilpattu, Mannar, Jaffna, Dambulla, Nilgala and Palatupana.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeds in the early part of the year. The small camouflaged cup nest is attached to a horizontal branch or fork, often decorated with cobwebs and flakes.

species_description.text: Elegant long-tailed flycatcher about 19–22 cm excluding streamers. Adult male has glossy black head and crest, blue eye-ring and long ribbon-like tail streamers; body may be chestnut or white depending on morph/subspecies. Female has chestnut upperparts, greyish throat and breast, and no long streamers.

male_female_identification.text: Male has black head and crest, blue eye-ring and long streamers when fully mature; body colour varies from chestnut to white. Female is chestnut above, greyish below, with shorter tail. Resident ceylonensis and migrant nominate paradisi overlap in Sri Lanka.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Immature males lack full streamers and may resemble females; Indian nominate males under about three years may be chestnut with short tails. Young birds are browner with less distinct head gloss.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for the spectacular long streamers of adult males, but do not assume every short-tailed chestnut bird is female: immature males can look similar. Use head/crest, throat colour and race context. Often feeds by aerial sallies.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident endemic subspecies T. p. ceylonensis occurs mainly in dry lowlands and lower hills; migrant nominate T. p. paradisi arrives from India and may occur widely, including gardens, forest edges and wooded wetlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Species-level aggregate R/M. Resident race breeds in Sri Lanka; migrant race mainly visits during the northern winter. CBC image archive records resident birds nesting in April and September; migrant adults recorded in Nov–Dec.

species_description.text: Medium-large coastal tern (about 35–43 cm), with a long orange to orange-yellow bill, black cap in breeding plumage, pale grey upperparts and white underparts. Non-breeding adults have a white forehead and reduced black cap. Feeds mainly on small fish and shrimp, caught by plunge-diving. Strongly coastal; rests and feeds around beaches, sandbars, lagoons, estuaries and saltpans; breeds on sandy islands and beaches outside Sri Lanka.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage; male tends to be slightly larger. Seasonal cap differences are not sex differences.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show mottled/scaly brown-grey upperparts and less solid cap; immature birds gradually acquire adult grey mantle. Non-breeding adults have a white forehead and partial dark cap.

field_spotting_tips.text: Compare with Greater Crested Tern: Lesser Crested is slightly smaller, with a more orange bill (rather than yellow) and often a subtler crest. Look for grey upperwings, black cap and plunge-diving behaviour.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Coastal visitor around Sri Lanka, recorded at Bundala National Park, saltpans and lagoons; check sandy beaches, sandbars and coastal roosts. Often mixed with Greater Crested Terns; CBC lists it as migrant.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC Country List 2022 classifies it M. Limosa monthly records list it across much of the year; presence data do not imply breeding or year-round resident status. Winter coastal flocks are notable.

species_description.text: විශාල මුහුදුලිහිණියෙකි (සෙ.මී. 45–50 පමණ). ඉහළපස අළු, යටපස සුදු, දිගු කහ පැහැති හොට සහ කළු තොප්පියක් ඇත; ශීත/අභිජනන නොවන පිහාටුවල හිසෙහි කළු පැහැය අඩුවේ. මුහුදු වෙරළ, වැලි දූපත්, ගල්පර සහ මුහුදේ මසුන් අල්ලයි. ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් කුඩා මසුන් ගිල දමයි. ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ වයඹ වෙරළේ වැලි දූපත්වල අභිජනන වාර්තා ඇත.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි හා ගැහැනු පෙනුමෙන් බොහෝ දුරට සමානයි. අභිජනන සමයේ කළු හිස් තොප්පිය වඩා පැහැදිලි; ලිංගය වෙන්කර හඳුනාගැනීම ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ අපහසුය.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: තරුණ පක්ෂීන්ගේ ඉහළපස දුඹුරු/අළු පැහැති කොරපොතු රටාවක් සහ අඳුරු පියාපත් අග තිබිය හැක; හොට වැඩිහිටියාට වඩා කෙටි/අඳුරු විය හැක. වයස අනුව වෙනස්වීම් ඡායාරූපයෙන් තහවුරු කරන්න.

field_spotting_tips.text: විශාල ප්‍රමාණය, දිගු කහ හොට, කළු හිස සහ සුදු යටපස එකට බලන්න. Lesser Crested Tern සමඟ සසඳන විට වඩා විශාල හා හොට ඝනයි.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: වෙරළ තීරය පුරා, විශේෂයෙන් Mannar–Adam’s Bridge, Bundala, Yala, Mirissa සහ Galle ආසන්න මුහුදු ප්‍රදේශ. Sand Island/Adam’s Bridge ප්‍රදේශයේ අභිජනන වාර්තා ඇත.

seasonality_months_seen.text: වෙරළබඩ වාර්තා වසර පුරා; අභිජනනය හා දූපත් භාවිතය ස්ථානය/වසර අනුව වෙනස් විය හැක. CBC ලැයිස්තුවේ R ලෙස සටහන්; මාසික වාර්තා එකතු කර තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: Very small plover (about 14–17 cm) with brown upperparts, white underparts and a dark breast-band. Breeding adults show a black forehead, eye-mask and breast-band, a yellow eye-ring and yellowish legs; the bill is dark. Non-breeding plumage is duller brown, with reduced facial and breast markings. Feeds on small insects and other invertebrates on mudflats, paddy fields, pond margins and shallow wetlands.

male_female_identification.text: Male in breeding plumage usually has a broader, blacker breast-band and more extensive black on the face; female tends to have browner and less extensive markings. Sexes are difficult to distinguish in non-breeding plumage.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have buff-edged, scaly upperparts and indistinct brown breast and facial markings. The yellow eye-ring can be less conspicuous than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Very small size, dark bill, yellow eye-ring and yellowish legs are useful. Compare with Common Ringed Plover: Little Ringed is smaller and has a dark bill and a more prominent yellow eye-ring.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread at suitable inland and coastal wetlands, including tanks, paddy fields, marshes, river margins and lagoons. Both resident and migrant populations occur; check wetlands throughout the island, including urban marshes and Dry Zone tanks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident and migrant populations both occur. CBC 2022 separates resident jerdoni and migrant curonicus. Migrants are most evident Aug–Apr, while resident birds may be seen throughout the year.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC 2022: C. d. curonicus — M; C. d. jerdoni — R. Aggregate species classification R/M.

species_description.text: Large white ibis with bare black head and neck, long down-curved black bill and dark legs. Probes mud and shallow water for insects, crustaceans, molluscs, worms, frogs and other prey; uses marshes, lagoons, tanks and wet agricultural land; nests colonially in trees.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike in plumage; males usually slightly larger. Bare black head and neck conspicuous in adults.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have feathered greyish/brown head and neck and shorter-looking bill; bare black skin becomes more extensive with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Watch for deliberate probing and sweeping in soft mud. In flight, large white body, black bare head/neck and trailing legs are useful.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in wetlands across the island, especially Bundala, Kumana, Yala, Vankalai/Mannar, Jaffna wetlands and Colombo wetland network.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round; flock sizes and breeding activity vary with rainfall and wetland conditions.

species_description.text: මධ්‍යම ප්‍රමාණයේ, ගස් මුදුන්වල ජීවත් වන පලතුරුභක්ෂක බටගොයෙකි (ආසන්න දිග 29 cm). කොළ පැහැති ශරීරය, අළු පැහැති හිස/නැප් සහ අළු පැහැති මධ්‍ය වලිග පිහාටු වැදගත් ලක්ෂණ වේ. වනාන්තර, වියළි හා තෙත් පතනශීලී වනාන්තර සහ වෙරළට ආසන්න හොඳින් ගස් වැවුණු ප්‍රදේශවල හමුවේ. පලතුරු හා බීජ, විශේෂයෙන් Ficus වැනි ගස්වල පලතුරු අනුභව කරයි. කුඩා අතු වේදිකාවක කූඩුවක් සාදා සාමාන්‍යයෙන් බිත්තර 2ක් දමයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි: පපුවේ ලිලැක් පැහැති පටියකට පහළින් තද තැඹිලි පටියක්; හිස සාමාන්‍යයෙන් කොළ-අළු පැහැති. ගැහැණු: පපුව කහ-කොළ පැහැති; තැඹිලි/ලිලැක් පටි නොමැත. දෙපාර්ශ්වයේම වලිගයේ මධ්‍ය පිහාටු අළු-ස්ලේටි පැහැති වීම Sri Lanka Green-pigeon සමඟ වෙන්කර හඳුනාගැනීමට උපකාරී වේ.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: තරුණ පක්ෂීන් වැඩිහිටියන්ට වඩා මඳ පැහැති/අඩු පැහැදිලි රටා සහිත විය හැක. ලිංගික වර්ණ වෙනස්කම් තරුණ අවධියේදී සම්පූර්ණයෙන් නොපෙනිය හැක. ශ්‍රී ලංකා තරුණ පිහාටු රටා පිළිබඳ සවිස්තරාත්මක මූලාශ්‍ර තවදුරටත් තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

field_spotting_tips.text: ගස් මුදුන්වල නිහඬව සිටින බැවින් මුලින්ම හඬට සවන් දෙන්න. පලතුරු දරන ගස්, විශේෂයෙන් Ficus, පරීක්ෂා කරන්න. පියාසර කරන විට අළු මධ්‍ය වලිගය හා පිරිමි පක්ෂියාගේ තැඹිලි-ලිලැක් පපුවේ පටි බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ වෙරළබඩට ආසන්න වනාන්තර සහ හොඳින් ගස් වැවුණු පහතරට ප්‍රදේශවල. CBC image records: Ruhuna/Yala, Wilpattu සහ Trincomalee (Periyakulam) අවට වාර්තා. වනාන්තර මායිම් සහ පලතුරු දරන විශාල ගස් ඇති ස්ථාන සොයන්න.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ නේවාසික (resident) විශේෂයකි. ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ අභිජනනය ප්‍රධාන වශයෙන් දෙසැම්බර්–මැයි ලෙස මූලාශ්‍රයක සඳහන් වේ; සමහර ද්විතීයික වාර්තාවල අගෝස්තු–සැප්තැම්බර් දෙවන කාලයක්ද දක්වයි. එම දෙවන කාලය තවත් තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: මධ්‍යම-විශාල ප්‍රමාණයේ (ආසන්න 33 cm) කහ පාද සහිත බටගොයෙකි. අළු පැහැති හිස, කහ පැහැති කොලරය, උරහිසේ ලිලැක් පැහැති ලපය සහ යටිපස/vent ප්‍රදේශයේ chestnut පැහැති ඉරි හඳුනාගැනීමට උපකාරී වේ. වියළි හා තෙත් පතනශීලී වනාන්තර, ගස් සහිත ගොවිබිම් සහ පලතුරු ගස් ඇති ප්‍රදේශවල වාසය කරයි. පලතුරු හා බීජ ප්‍රධාන ආහාරය වේ.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි පක්ෂියාගේ උරහිසේ ලිලැක් පැහැති ලපය සහ පපුවේ වර්ණ තදින් පෙනේ. ගැහැණු පක්ෂියා සාමාන්‍යයෙන් අඩු දීප්තිමත්, වැඩි කොළ/කහ පැහැති වන අතර පිරිමි පක්ෂියාගේ පැහැදිලි පපුවේ රටා අඩුය. දෙපාර්ශ්වයේම කහ පාද සහ අළු හිස වැදගත් ලක්ෂණ වේ. ශ්‍රී ලංකා phillipsi උපවිශේෂයේ සියුම් ලිංගික වෙනස්කම් තවත් තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: තරුණ පක්ෂීන්ගේ පිහාටු වැඩිහිටියන්ට වඩා අඩු දීප්තිමත් වන අතර වැඩිහිටි පිරිමි පක්ෂියාගේ උරහිස්/පපුවේ පැහැදිලි වර්ණ සම්පූර්ණයෙන් නොපෙනිය හැක. ශ්‍රී ලංකා phillipsi සඳහා තරුණ අවධියේ නිශ්චිත ලක්ෂණ තවදුරටත් තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

field_spotting_tips.text: කහ පාද, අළු හිස, කහ කොලරය සහ උරහිසේ ලිලැක් ලපය එකට බලන්න. Nilgala සහ අවට වියළි කලාපීය වනාන්තර/ගස් සහිත ප්‍රදේශවල පලතුරු දරන ගස් පරීක්ෂා කරන්න. Sri Lanka Green-pigeon සමඟ පටලවා නොගන්න: එහි පිරිමි පිටුපස තද maroon පැහැය සහ රතු පාද දක්නට ලැබේ.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ ඉතා සීමිත/දුර්ලභ ව්‍යාප්තියක් ඇති බව CBC image database වාර්තාවල සඳහන්; වියළි කලාපයේ ඊසානදිග පහතරට කඳු පාමුල සහ Nilgala (Bibile ආසන්නය) වැනි ප්‍රදේශ ප්‍රධාන වාර්තා ස්ථාන වේ. Avibase විසින් phillipsi උපවිශේෂය ශ්‍රී ලංකාවට පමණක් සීමා වූ ලෙස ලැයිස්තුගත කරයි. Species-level global range එක දකුණු ආසියාව පුරා විහිදේ.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ නේවාසික (resident) ලෙස වාර්තා වේ; සෘතුමය පැමිණීමක්/නිශ්චිත මාසික රටාවක් සඳහා ප්‍රමාණවත් ශ්‍රී ලංකා දත්ත හමු නොවීය. දුර්ලභ වාර්තා ස්ථානවලදී වසර පුරා සොයා බැලිය හැකි නමුත් සාර්ථකත්වය අඩු විය හැක.

species_description.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවට ආවේණික, මධ්‍යම ප්‍රමාණයේ (ආසන්න 26–28 cm) කොළ පැහැති පරෙවියෙකි. කහ පැහැති මුහුණ/නළල සහ උගුර, පියාපත්වල කහ පැහැති රේඛාව සහ රතු පැහැති පාද ප්‍රධාන ලක්ෂණ වේ. පහතරට සිට පහළ කඳුකරය දක්වා වනාන්තරවල ඉහළ වියනේ තනිව හෝ කුඩා කණ්ඩායම්වල හමුවේ. පලතුරු හා බීජ අනුභව කරයි; ගසක අතු කූඩුවක සාමාන්‍යයෙන් සුදු බිත්තර 2ක් දමයි.

male_female_identification.text: පිරිමි: පිටුපස/මැන්ටලය තද maroon හෝ දම්-දුඹුරු පැහැති. ගැහැණු: එම ප්‍රදේශය කොළ පැහැතිය; යටිපස/vent ප්‍රදේශයේ සුදු-කහ පැහැති කොටසට සිහින් කොළ ඉරි තිබිය හැක. දෙපාර්ශ්වයේම කහ මුහුණ, කහ උගුර සහ රතු පාද දක්නට ලැබේ.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: තරුණ පක්ෂීන් වැඩිහිටි පක්ෂීන්ට වඩා මඳ පැහැති වන අතර පිරිමි පක්ෂියාගේ maroon පිටුපස පැහැය සම්පූර්ණයෙන් වර්ධනය වී නොතිබිය හැක. නිශ්චිත වයස්-අනුව පිහාටු වෙනස්කම් සඳහා වෙනම තරුණ නිදර්ශන තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

field_spotting_tips.text: පිරිමි පක්ෂියාගේ maroon පිටුපස සහ කහ මුහුණ හොඳම ලක්ෂණයයි. Orange-breasted Green-pigeon සමඟ වෙන්කරගැනීමට වලිගයේ මධ්‍ය පිහාටු බලන්න: මෙහි කොළ පැහැතිය; Orange-breasted හි අළු-ස්ලේටි පැහැතිය. ගස් මුදුන්වල හඬට සවන් දෙන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: ශ්‍රී ලංකාවට ආවේණික නේවාසික විශේෂයකි. පහතරට වනාන්තරවල සිට පහළ කඳුකරය දක්වා; මධ්‍යම කඳුකරයේ ඉහළ ප්‍රදේශවල දුර්ලභ/අඩු වශයෙන් වාර්තා වේ. වාර්තා වූ නිරීක්ෂණ ස්ථාන අතර Sinharaja, Kitulgala, Sigiriya, Wilpattu, Nilgala සහ Digana ඇතුළත් වේ.

seasonality_months_seen.text: වසර පුරා නේවාසික විශේෂයකි. මූලාශ්‍රවලින් තහවුරු කළ නිශ්චිත ශ්‍රී ලංකා අභිජනන මාස මෙහි නොදක්වයි; කූඩුව/බිත්තර පිළිබඳ තොරතුරු ඇතත් මාසික කාලසටහන තවදුරටත් තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: Small, slim wader (about 19–23 cm) with a straight fine bill, long yellow-green legs, pale supercilium and conspicuous white spots on the dark brown upperparts. Underparts are white with dark streaking on the breast. Uses shallow marshes, flooded paddy fields, temporary pools, tank margins and wet grassland; feeds on insects, larvae, small crustaceans and other invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in plumage. Females may average slightly larger, but field separation is not reliable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have buff or whitish spots and scalloped fringes on the upperparts, often giving a more strongly spotted appearance than adults. Breast markings are fine and diffuse.

field_spotting_tips.text: Compared with Green Sandpiper, Wood Sandpiper is paler, more spotted above, has longer yellowish legs and a more obvious supercilium. Often feeds in shallow water and flooded fields.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Common migrant at wetlands throughout Sri Lanka, including Bundala, Tissa, Mannar, Puttalam, Udawalawe and numerous inland tanks and paddy fields.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022: M. Commonly encountered during the northern winter, broadly Aug/Sep–Apr; passage birds may occur earlier or later. Limosa monthly records include Jan–May and Jul–Dec, reflecting broad observation coverage.

species_description.text: Large, long-legged wader (about 30–35 cm) with a long, slightly upturned bill, greenish-grey legs and grey-brown upperparts. Non-breeding birds are pale below with fine streaking on the neck and breast. Occurs on mudflats, lagoons, estuaries, saltpans, marshes and flooded fields; feeds on fish, crustaceans, insects, worms and other aquatic prey.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are very similar. Females average slightly larger and may have a marginally longer bill, but reliable field sexing is generally not possible.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have buff-edged upperparts with pale spots and a warmer, more scalloped appearance than adults. Fine breast streaking may be more pronounced.

field_spotting_tips.text: Largest of the common Tringa sandpipers in this plate. Identify by long slightly upturned bill, long greenish legs and clean pale appearance. In flight it lacks the strong white wing-bar of Common Redshank.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Regular migrant across coastal and inland wetlands, including Bundala, Mannar, Puttalam, Tissa, Yala and other large tanks and lagoons.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022: M. Primarily present during the northern winter, broadly Aug/Sep–Apr. Some Sri Lankan monthly checklists show records in most or all months; that reflects recorded occurrence and does not change the CBC migrant classification.

species_description.text: Compact, dark-backed wader (about 20–24 cm) with a short straight bill, dark greenish-brown upperparts, white underparts and dark speckling on the breast. The rump is white and conspicuous in flight. Prefers freshwater pools, shaded streams, marsh edges, ponds and flooded fields; feeds on aquatic insects, larvae, small crustaceans and other invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike; no reliable external plumage difference for field identification.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have small pale buff spots and scalloped edges on the upperparts, creating a more spotted appearance than adults. Underparts remain white with fine breast markings.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the dark upperparts contrasting with white belly and white rump. In flight the rump flashes white; this is a key distinction from the paler Wood Sandpiper. Often flicks its head and bobs while feeding.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A migrant occurring at freshwater wetlands around the island, including Bundala, Tissa, Udawalawe, Mannar and Puttalam, as well as smaller ponds, streams and paddy fields. Often more solitary than other Tringa.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022: M. Broadly expected from Aug/Sep to Apr, with passage and winter records; monthly checklists show Jan–Apr and Aug–Dec occurrence. Local water conditions influence sightings.

species_description.text: Slender, elegant wader (about 22–26 cm) with a fine straight bill, long greenish-grey legs and narrow body. Non-breeding plumage is pale grey above and white below, with fine dark streaking on the breast. Favours shallow freshwater and brackish marshes, flooded paddy fields, pools and lagoon margins; feeds on small aquatic invertebrates and insect larvae.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are alike in plumage. Females average slightly larger, but the difference is not dependable in field conditions.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show warmer buff-edged upperparts and more obvious pale spotting/scalloping than adults. The breast may show fine streaking; ageing requires close views.

field_spotting_tips.text: The very fine straight bill, long legs and slim, pale-grey appearance help separate it from Wood Sandpiper. Often wades in deeper water than smaller sandpipers, picking prey rapidly from the surface.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A regular migrant in shallow wetlands across Sri Lanka. Recorded at Bundala, Tissa, Mannar, Puttalam, Udawalawe and other lagoons, tanks, marshes and flooded fields.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022: M. Mainly a northern-winter visitor, broadly Aug/Sep–Apr, but monthly checklists contain records outside the core season. Numbers vary with water levels and local conditions.

species_description.text: Medium-sized wader (about 28 cm) with a sturdy straight bill, long orange-red legs and grey-brown upperparts in non-breeding plumage. In breeding plumage the head and breast become heavily streaked. Uses mudflats, lagoons, saltpans, estuaries, marshes and flooded fields; feeds by picking or probing for worms, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic insects.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar in non-breeding plumage. In breeding plumage males are often more boldly marked and darker on the breast; females may be slightly larger and heavier-billed, but field sexing is unreliable.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have buff-edged upperpart feathers giving a scaled appearance, with warm buff tones and fine streaking on the breast. Legs may be duller orange than adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for the orange-red legs and bill base, medium-large build and broad white wing-bar in flight. Compare with Spotted Redshank: Common Redshank is shorter-legged and has a shorter, thicker bill; Spotted Redshank is rarer in Sri Lanka.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Winter migrant at coastal lagoons, estuaries, mudflats and inland wetlands. Regularly recorded at Bundala, Mannar, Puttalam, Tissa and other suitable wetland sites; distribution is not limited to these locations.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): M. Most likely during the northern winter, broadly Sep/Oct–Apr; timing and numbers vary by wetland and year. Occasional out-of-season records should not be interpreted as residency.

species_description.text: Medium-sized blackbird about 23–25 cm. Adult male is glossy black with yellow-orange bill and eye-ring; female is dark brown, often with paler throat and subtle streaking. Feeds on earthworms, insects, snails and fruit, often on damp lawns, forest paths and open patches within montane woodland.

male_female_identification.text: Male glossy black with bright yellow-orange bill and eye-ring. Female dark brown, usually with a paler throat and faint streaking; juveniles resemble female.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are brown and mottled, with pale scaling/streaking on the breast and a duller bill and eye-ring.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for males on damp lawns and forest edges after rain, probing for worms. Female is much browner. Listen for blackbird-like fluting song from wooded slopes and garden trees.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's central highlands and montane forests, especially wooded slopes, ravines, gardens and open grassy patches around Horton Plains, Nuwara Eliya and Hakgala. The Sri Lankan form is the endemic subspecies kinnisii; the species also occurs in southern India.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round, with local altitudinal movements. Breeding records mainly in the first half of the year; exact island-wide breeding window needs further local confirmation.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022: Orange-headed Thrush M; Pied Thrush M; Sri Lanka Scaly Thrush E; Ceylon Whistling Thrush E; Spotted-winged Thrush E; Blackbird (Indian Blackbird) R.

species_description.text: සෙ.මී. 13–15 පමණ දිගැති ඉතා කුඩා, කෙටි වලිගයක් සහිත බිම්වාසී පක්ෂියෙකි. තෘණබිම්, වගාබිම්, විවෘත scrub සහ මාර්ග අයිනේ තණ ආවරණය තුළ සැඟවී සිටී. බිම ඇවිදිමින් බීජ සහ කුඩා අපෘෂ්ඨවංශීන් සොයයි. මෙහි sex-role reversal විශේෂත්වයක් ඇත: ගැහැනු පිරිමියාට වඩා විශාල හා වර්ණවත්; පිරිමි බිත්තර රකින භූමිකාව ගනී.

male_female_identification.text: ගැහැනු විශාල සහ වඩා තද/වර්ණවත්; කළු bib හෝ උගුරේ කළු පැල්ලම කැපී පෙනේ. පිරිමි කුඩා සහ සාමාන්‍යයෙන් අඩු වර්ණවත්. සාමාන්‍ය buttonquail වර්ගවල පිරිමි බිත්තර රකින අතර ගැහැනු courtship කරයි.

field_spotting_tips.text: පියාඹනවාට වඩා තණ අතරින් දුවමින් පලා යයි. උදෑසන පාර අයිනේ හෝ තණබිම්වල සෙමින් නිරීක්ෂණය කරන්න. ගැහැනුගේ කළු bib සහ විශාල ශරීරය විශේෂයෙන් බලන්න.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: වියළි කලාපයේ පහළබිම් තෘණබිම්වල සාමාන්‍ය; සුදුසු වාසස්ථානවල තෙත් කලාපය සහ කඳුකරයේද හමුවේ. විවෘත තණබිම්, ගොවිබිම් සහ පාර අද්දර ආවරණ බලන්න.

seasonality_months_seen.text: ස්ථිරවාසී. ප්‍රජනන මාස ප්‍රදේශ/වැසි තත්ත්වය අනුව වෙනස් විය හැකි අතර ලංකා-විශේෂිත මාස තවදුරටත් තහවුරු කළ යුතුයි.

species_description.text: Medium-sized nocturnal owl (about 33–39 cm) with a pale heart-shaped facial disc, dark eyes, long legs and finely mottled buff, grey and brown plumage. Sri Lankan birds belong to the Eastern Barn Owl, Tyto javanica, following the split from the former broad Barn Owl T. alba. Uses open country, farmland, grassland, plantations, villages and buildings, roosting in cavities, barns and other sheltered structures. Feeds mainly on rodents and other small mammals, locating prey by sound. Nests in cavities and buildings.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are similar in general pattern. Females are often larger and may show more spotting on the breast and underparts; individual variation is substantial, so sexing from a single photograph is uncertain.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Nestlings are covered in white down, developing a buff facial disc and juvenile body feathers. Fledged juveniles resemble adults but are generally softer and less sharply patterned; age is best assessed with close views and context.

field_spotting_tips.text: At dusk, watch for its buoyant, silent flight over open fields. The pale heart-shaped face, dark eyes and long legs separate it from other Sri Lankan owls. Listen for harsh screeches rather than relying only on hoots.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident and widespread in suitable open habitats, agricultural landscapes and settlements across Sri Lanka. Often roosts in buildings, old trees and other cavities; local occurrence depends on suitable nesting and roosting sites.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. No regular seasonal migration in Sri Lanka. Breeding can occur when food and nesting cavities are available; exact island-wide months should not be stated without local nest records.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022) and current Sri Lanka checklist sources; all seven taxa are treated as resident (R). Note taxonomic/common-name differences where CBC 2022 uses older combinations.

species_description.text: Distinctive medium-sized bird, about 25–29 cm, with a long slender down-curved bill and a tall erectile crest tipped black and white. Plumage is mainly warm cinnamon-buff, with black-and-white barred wings and tail. Occurs in open country, dry scrub, grassland, cultivation, plantations and lightly wooded habitats, often feeding on the ground. Probes soil for beetles, grubs, ants, crickets and other invertebrates, and may also take small reptiles. Nests in cavities in trees, walls and buildings.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are very similar. Males may have slightly longer bills and more extensive black in the crest, but these differences are subtle and not dependable for field identification.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and often paler, with a shorter crest and a shorter bill. The black-and-white wing pattern is present but may be less crisp than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: The long down-curved bill and large fan-like crest make it unmistakable. Watch for the crest opening when the bird lands or is alarmed. It usually feeds by walking and probing the ground rather than hawking insects in flight.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Occurs in Sri Lanka as a resident and migrant, with seasonal visitors supplementing the local population. Seen in open dry country, agricultural land and coastal scrub; Bundala and other dry-zone/coastal sites are useful locations. It can be scarce and local despite its wide global range.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC classifies Hoopoe as R/M. Local resident birds occur alongside migrants, especially during the northern winter and passage periods. Exact arrival/departure dates vary; avoid assigning a single fixed winter-only window.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022); status codes retained as published, including mixed resident/migrant status.

species_description.text: Large, striking endemic corvid about 42–47 cm, with bright cobalt-blue upperparts, chestnut-brown head and underparts, long graduated blue tail with white tip, red bill, red legs and red bare eye-ring. Usually in noisy groups, searching all forest levels for insects, larvae, frogs, lizards, small reptiles, eggs and fruit.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in colour and pattern. No dependable external field character separates male and female.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with less saturated blue and chestnut plumage, shorter tails and less vivid red bare parts; adult colour and tail length develop with age.

field_spotting_tips.text: Often noisy and conspicuous in small parties, moving acrobatically through the forest. The long blue tail with white tip, chestnut body and red bill/legs are diagnostic. Listen for harsh rattles and clear bell-like notes.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka's wet-zone forests and adjoining hills, from below 150 m to above 2,000 m. Best sites include Sinharaja, Kanneliya, Kitulgala, Knuckles, Peak Wilderness and Horton Plains forest edges.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Breeding commences around January; cooperative groups assist with nest building and feeding. Stick nest is placed in foliage, commonly 5–7 m above ground; usually 3–5 eggs.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention: Black-hooded Oriole R; Sri Lanka Blue Magpie E; House Crow R; Large-billed Crow R; Indian Pitta M; Cinereous Tit R. Confirm row-level codes if checklist edition changes.

species_description.text: Medium-large, noisy lapwing (about 32–35 cm) with bronze-brown upperparts, white underparts, black head, neck and upper breast, and a conspicuous white band running from behind the eye down the sides of the neck. The red bill has a black tip and the face carries prominent red fleshy wattles; legs are yellow. Inhabits open country near water, paddy fields, tanks, grassland, bare ground and urban edges. Feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates; nests in a shallow scrape on open ground.

male_female_identification.text: Male and female are very similar in plumage. Males average slightly larger, with somewhat longer wings/legs, but this is not a reliable field distinction without measurements.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller, with brownish-grey upperparts and a less intense black head/breast; throat and neck-side white markings are less crisp. Facial wattles and bill colours may be less vivid than in adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Listen for its loud, repeated alarm call, often rendered as 'did-you-do-it'. Usually seen in pairs or small groups; it runs in short bursts, pauses and probes the ground. Look for the red facial wattles and broad white neck stripe.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Widespread resident across Sri Lanka in open habitats, including tanks, paddy fields, coastal plains, grasslands and disturbed open ground. Commonly encountered around wetlands and agricultural landscapes throughout the island, including both Dry and Wet Zone lowlands.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident and generally visible year-round. Breeding can occur in different parts of the year depending on rainfall and local conditions; do not assign one narrow island-wide breeding season. Nests/territorial behaviour may be noticed around suitable open ground after rains.

species_description.text: Slimmer and paler than Red-wattled Lapwing (about 26–28 cm), with sandy-buff upperparts, black crown, black chin/throat and upper breast, a narrow white band separating crown from neck, yellow facial wattles and long yellow legs. The bill is yellowish at the base with a dark tip. Favours dry, open, stony ground, short grassland, scrub and sparsely vegetated plains rather than wet margins. Feeds on insects and other ground invertebrates; nests in a shallow scrape on bare ground.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage. Males average slightly larger and may have longer wings and tarsi, but this is not a dependable field sexing character.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles have a browner, less sharply black crown and generally duller, more muted plumage; facial wattles may be less conspicuous. Young birds can look less crisply patterned than adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search dry, open ground rather than the edge of water. The pale sandy body, black cap/throat and yellow facial wattles distinguish it from Red-wattled Lapwing, which is larger, darker above and has red wattles. It may crouch or sit low when disturbed.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A localised resident in Sri Lanka's Dry Zone, especially open arid and semi-arid plains. Reported from the north-western coastal belt (Puttalam–Jaffna), Hambantota, Eastern Province, Udawalawe and Anuradhapura areas. It is less widespread and less frequently encountered than Red-wattled Lapwing.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident, with local movements or changes in detectability associated with rainfall and habitat conditions. Breeding records occur in different Dry Zone localities; avoid presenting one fixed island-wide breeding period without a local dataset.

species_description.text: Distinctive small-to-medium shorebird (about 22–25 cm) with a long, slender bill that curves slightly upward, short orange-yellow legs, grey-brown upperparts and white underparts. Strongly associated with coastal mudflats, sandy shores, estuaries and lagoon margins; feeds on small crabs, molluscs, worms and other invertebrates.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are alike in plumage. Females may average slightly larger with a marginally longer bill, but sex cannot normally be established confidently in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles show buff-fringed, scaly upperparts and a warmer tone than adults. The distinctive upturned bill and short legs are already apparent.

field_spotting_tips.text: The slightly upturned bill is the strongest clue and gives the species its characteristic profile. Also note short orange legs and active, quick feeding behaviour along the waterline.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: A coastal migrant, especially at Bundala, Mannar, Puttalam and other tidal mudflats and lagoons; may also occur inland during passage. Usually found singly or in small groups.

seasonality_months_seen.text: CBC 2022: M. Expected mainly during the northern winter and passage periods, broadly Aug/Sep–Apr. The Limosa checklist records it across a broad range of months, so use local records rather than assuming uniform year-round abundance.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: Verified against CBC Sri Lanka Country List Version 3 (January 2022), which explicitly lists this species as M (regular migrant).

species_description.text: A tiny, active woodpecker, around 13–14 cm, with a brown crown, black-and-white barred back and wings, pale underparts finely streaked or spotted, and a short bill. It forages on small branches and twigs, often in pairs or small family groups, taking ants, beetles, larvae and other small insects. Occurs in open woodland, scrub, gardens, plantations and forest edges, particularly in dry and intermediate country.

male_female_identification.text: Male has a small red patch on the nape; female lacks the red and has a brownish nape. Both have the brown cap and finely patterned body.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller and less sharply patterned than adults; the crown and nape colours are less distinct. Young males may develop the red nape patch gradually.

field_spotting_tips.text: Very small and easily overlooked. Listen for its sharp, repeated calls and watch thin branches rather than large trunks. The brown cap, black-and-white barring and tiny size separate it from larger woodpeckers.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in Sri Lanka's lowlands, especially dry and intermediate zones, but locally found in wooded and cultivated habitats elsewhere. Recorded at Sigiriya, Yala, Wilpattu, Anuradhapura and other open woodland sites.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Sri Lankan field accounts report breeding mainly February–July; nest cavities are excavated in dead branches or trunks. Exact timing may vary locally.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List (2022): resident (R) for all non-endemic woodpeckers; endemic (E) for Crimson-backed Flameback. Red-backed Flameback Dinopium psarodes is now treated as a separate endemic species; taxonomy differs from older CBC treatment. Confirm latest CBC row mapping before publication.

species_description.text: Large, shy endemic thrush about 24 cm, with olive-brown upperparts marked by dark crescent-shaped or scaly markings and warm rufous-buff underparts. Usually solitary or in pairs, feeding on the forest floor among deep leaf litter for insects, worms and other invertebrates; also takes berries.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes are similar and not reliably separable by plumage in the field.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are more buff and heavily patterned, with clearer pale shaft-streaks and scalloped markings; age should be judged cautiously in poor light.

field_spotting_tips.text: Very shy and easily missed. Search quiet forest trails at dawn, watching for a large thrush turning leaf litter. The plain olive-brown back with dark crescent markings and rufous-buff underparts separates it from the white-spotted Spot-winged Thrush.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic resident of the central and southwestern hill forests, typically in dense forest between about 600 and 1,500 m, often above 900 m. Localised in suitable forest; reported from Sinharaja, Horton Plains, Nuwara Eliya and other hill-country forest blocks.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round, with some vertical movement. Breeding reported March–May and July–October; likely double-brooded. Nests are concealed in vegetation and usually contain two eggs.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022: Orange-headed Thrush M; Pied Thrush M; Sri Lanka Scaly Thrush E; Ceylon Whistling Thrush E; Spotted-winged Thrush E; Blackbird (Indian Blackbird) R.

species_description.text: Small, lively white-eye about 11–12 cm, green above with yellowish throat and undertail, pale greyish underparts and a conspicuous white eye-ring. Slightly larger and darker than Indian White-eye; the white orbital ring is characteristically interrupted in front of the eye. Highly social and constantly searches foliage for insects, berries and nectar.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike; no dependable external field distinction. Compare with Indian White-eye: Sri Lanka White-eye is generally larger, darker and greener, with a distinctive break in the eye-ring in front.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles resemble adults but are duller, with less distinct eye-ring and less bright yellow on throat/underparts.

field_spotting_tips.text: Search active flocks in highland gardens and forest edges. Listen for loud, busy chirping. The broken white eye-ring and darker green plumage help separate it from Indian White-eye.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Endemic to Sri Lanka's central highlands and montane zone, especially montane cloud forest, wooded gardens, orchards, tea estates and forest edges. Mainly above 1,000 m, but can descend to lower elevations and overlap with Indian White-eye.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident. Horton Plains breeding study recorded nesting March–May; broader accounts report a second period in August–September.

conservation.occurrence_source_note: CBC Sri Lanka Country List 2022 status convention retained: Sri Lanka White-eye E; Indian White-eye R; Legge's Flowerpecker E; Thick-billed Flowerpecker R; Pale-billed Flowerpecker R; Purple-rumped Sunbird R; Loten's Sunbird R; Purple Sunbird R. Confirm individual line codes against official list before publication.

sources.citation: Endemic. CBC endemic account describes flocking, diet, habitat and breeding; Horton Plains field study documents 46 nests and breeding March–May. Phylogenetic work confirms it is a distinct endemic species, not merely a highland form of Indian White-eye.

species_description.text: Very small, active greenish-yellow white-eye about 10–11 cm, with bright yellow throat and vent, pale underparts, olive-green upperparts and a prominent complete white eye-ring. Gregarious, moving through foliage in pairs or small flocks and feeding on insects, caterpillars, berries, buds and nectar.

male_female_identification.text: Sexes alike. Sri Lankan population is the subspecies Z. p. egregius; it is smaller and brighter-backed/throated than Sri Lanka White-eye.

juvenile_immature_plumage.text: Juveniles are duller olive-green and yellow, with a less sharply defined eye-ring; otherwise similar to adults.

field_spotting_tips.text: Look for small noisy flocks in flowering trees and garden foliage. Complete white eye-ring, brighter yellow throat and smaller size distinguish it from the larger, darker Sri Lanka White-eye.

sri_lanka_distribution_and_hotspots.text: Resident in lowland and mid-elevation Sri Lanka in gardens, groves, orchards, scrub, forest edges and mangroves. The Sri Lankan population is Z. p. egregius; may move locally or seasonally.

seasonality_months_seen.text: Resident year-round. Regional accounts give a broad breeding period February–September, with April a peak; local nesting dates vary.
